title: Recent and Long-term Impacts of Boreal Wildfires Observed through NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) Vegetation Indices
matched_keywords: ['HLS', 'HLS VI', 'HLS VIs', 'HLS vegetation index', 'Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2']
authors: Panshi Wang, Junchang Ju, Paul Montesano, Qiang Zhou, Joseph O Sexton, Matthew J Macander, Gerald V Frost Jr, Margaret Wooten, Saurabh Channan and Christopher S R Neigh
main_session: Wildfire Analysis Using Remote Sensing, Multisensor Fusion, Multisource Data Integration, and Artificial Intelligence I Poster
abstract: Boreal wildfires play a significant role in the global carbon cycle and climate feedback mechanisms, with their escalating severity persisting into 2026. Continued monitoring of trends in boreal wildfire and post-fire ecosystem recovery is vital for understanding the full scope of these impacts. Building upon the rich legacy of the Landsat data archive, NASA's Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) project elevates satellite monitoring capacity to an unprecedented level. Through the radiometric and geometric harmonization of imagery from Landsat and Sentinel-2 satellites, HLS enables vegetation change monitoring at a temporal resolution of 1 to 2 days. The HLS vegetation index (VI) suite provides VIs based on radiometrically and geometrically consistent surface reflectance. We utilized the HLS VI data archive to derive the 2013–2026 annual rates of change for eight vegetation indices (NDVI, NDMI, NDWI, EVI, SAVI, MSAVI, NBR2, and TVI) across Alaska and Canada at a 30-meter resolution. This dataset provides fine-scale details of the vegetation change landscape in the North American Arctic and confirms the dominating role of wildfire in boreal vegetation dynamics. Furthermore, the unparalleled temporal frequency of HLS VIs enables timely monitoring of trajectory shifts, which is invaluable for evaluating recent wildfire impacts within the context of long-term trends.

title: Shock and Recovery: Tracking Post-Hurricane Helene Flood and Vegetation Responses Across Agricultural Parcels Using HLS Observations, Hydrodynamic Modeling, and Open-Source Geospatial Data Layers
authors: Dr. Emine Fidan, Aaron Smith, Savannah Jobkar, Samuel Neary and Brad Wilson
main_session: Vegetation Detection, Characterization, and Monitoring Through Multisensor Remote Sensing and Data Fusion Techniques I Oral
abstract: Agricultural land in mountainous headwater regions is increasingly exposed to extreme flooding, yet post-event damage assessment in these settings remains coarse and disconnected from the parcel-scale units at which recovery decisions are made. Hurricane Helene (September 2024) produced catastrophic flooding across East Tennessee, inundating cropland and pasture throughout the Nolichucky and French Broad watersheds and offering a test of vegetation condition as a measure of agricultural flood damage. We present a framework in which multi-sensor vegetation observations are the primary damage signal. Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) surface reflectance, which merges Landsat 8/9 OLI and Sentinel-2 MSI acquisitions into a single 30-m, near-daily record, is fused with hydrodynamic inundation time series, gridded precipitation, gSSURGO soil properties, USDA Cropland Data Layer classes, and county parcel records. We resolve which crop classes flooded, when, and for how long, then combine these with post-event vegetation response in a parcel-level Flood Impact Index. For each parcel, a multi-year NDVI baseline defines expected growing-season condition; departure from that baseline quantifies the vegetation "shock," and monthly trajectories track recovery and residual deficit. Inundation peaked within 24 hours of Helene's arrival in the southern Appalachians, at midday on 27 September, submerging approximately 60,000 acres of agricultural land, predominantly pasture. Recession diverged sharply by class: pasture drained to a third of peak extent within 72 hours, whereas corn and tomato acreage held near peak for two days and remained above two-thirds of peak at 72 hours, indicating that row crops on low floodplain terraces sustained substantially longer submergence. The highest-impact parcels cluster along the Nolichucky River, with intensity increasing downstream toward Douglas Dam. In severely impacted parcels, post-Helene NDVI fell to the lowest values in the ten-year (2016–2025) HLS record, consistent with near-complete loss of riparian vegetation and burial of the surface by flood sediment. GeoAg, a statewide tool for damage assessment, recovery tracking, scenario modeling, and forecast-driven exposure estimation, operationalizes the framework.

title: Deep Learning-Based Multi-Temporal IUCN-GET Classification Using Landsat and HLS Time Series
authors: Byeongcheol Kim, Minji Koh, Kyungil Lee, Yunyoung Choi and Seonyoung Park
main_session: Advances in Remote Sensing Capabilities Leading to a Better Understanding of Ecosystem and Natural Resource Management III Poster
abstract: Reliable spatial mapping of IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (GET) Ecosystem Functional Groups (EFGs) is essential for standardized ecosystem assessment, biodiversity conservation, and ecosystem monitoring. Existing regional IUCN-GET products are typically generated through rule-based integration of land-cover maps, ecological inventories, and environmental variables rather than direct satellite-based classification. Although this approach provides standardized maps, they are difficult to update consistently and have limited ability to represent phenology, long-term environmental variability, and disturbance history. Despite these limitations, direct data-driven classification of IUCN-GET EFGs from satellite time-series observations remains largely unexplored. This study develops a deep-learning model for multi-temporal IUCN-GET classification using satellite time-series observations and ecological variables. First, a 2022 reference IUCN-GET ecosystem map was established by integrating multiple nationally available thematic spatial datasets, including land-cover, forest, geological, and other ecological datasets, according to the IUCN-GET classification framework. The resulting reference dataset served as the training and validation labels for the deep-learning model. The reference dataset was subsequently combined with both Landsat and Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery to develop a multi-temporal ecosystem classification model. A five-year HLS time series is used to capture seasonal phenological patterns and interannual ecosystem variability, enabling the generation of recent IUCN-GET ecosystem maps. Terrain and land-cover information are incorporated as auxiliary inputs while maintaining consistency with the IUCN-GET class definitions. The proposed model is evaluated using spatially independent validation areas, and the HLS-based classification results are compared with conventional rule-based approaches. This study further explores the potential of multi-temporal IUCN-GET ecosystem maps to support continuous ecosystem monitoring, ecosystem conservation planning, and future IUCN Red List of Ecosystems (RLE) assessments.

title: Emulating Monthly 30 m OpenET Evapotranspiration Using the Prithvi-EO-2.0 Foundation Mode
authors: Euiyoung Choi, Seulgi Kim and Hyunglok Kim
main_session: Geospatial Foundation Model and Remote Sensing for Hydrologic Prediction Across the Terrestrial Water Cycle I Poster
abstract: High-resolution evapotranspiration (ET) products are essential for agricultural water management, drought monitoring, and land–atmosphere studies. OpenET provides six operational 30 m ET products across the conterminous United States (CONUS), but generating these products requires product-specific retrieval algorithms and input datasets. Prithvi-EO-2.0 is a geospatial foundation model pretrained on large-scale Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery to learn transferable geospatial representations for Earth observation tasks. In this study, we developed a framework to emulate monthly 30 m OpenET ET using the Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model together with HLS imagery and auxiliary variables. The proposed framework combines Prithvi-EO-2.0 representations with terrain, soil properties, reference ET, and spatiotemporal information through a deep learning network to reconstruct monthly ET at 30 m resolution. The framework was evaluated using geographically held-out regions, temporally held-out years, and independent flux towers outside the training domain. Initial experiments with the OpenET DisALEXI product demonstrated agreement with flux-tower observations. The proposed framework establishes a scalable foundation for additional OpenET products.

title: Enhancing Global Flood Risk Mapping to Building Level Using AlphaEarth and Prithvi Foundation Models
authors: Zachary Flamig, Tsung-Lin Hsieh, Yi-Cheng Teng, Arman Pouyaei, Jungho Kim, Michael Gomez, Marco Maneta and Edward Joseph Kearns, First Street, New York, United States
main_session: Connections Foster Evolution in Science and in Science Data Stewardship II Oral
abstract: Flood risk mapping underpins disaster preparedness, infrastructure planning, and financial risk assessment, but running physical flood simulations globally requires high resolution datasets that do not yet exist. The best available global flood depth products therefore stop at roughly 90 m resolution, too coarse to distinguish one street or one building from the next. We show how AI-ready Earth observation datasets and pretrained geospatial models can close that gap, bringing existing simulations down to 10 m. We use the AlphaEarth embeddings as inputs to fine tune foundation models (Clay & Prithvi) into a representation of the 10 m refinement from a 90 m digital terrain model (DTM). We then combine this refinement layer with the 90 m hydro conditioned MERIT DTM to create a global 10 m DTM. The downscaled terrain consistently sharpens riverbank boundaries and urban street patterns that MERIT cannot resolve. Measured against high-resolution limited-domain simulations used as ground truth, our method improves flood extent prediction over the unenhanced physical model. We also discuss the practical side of this workflow: how we leveraged cloud-hosted embeddings and open foundation model weights for training and inference. We demonstrate the advantages of the cloud-hosted datasets, and how we chose to use a mix of on-prem & cloud compute for the creation of this dataset.

title: An Overview of NASA’s Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) Project
authors: Madhu Sridhar, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL, United States, Trang Vo, NASA IMPACT, Huntsville, United States, Junchang Ju, University of Maryland, Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center, College Park, MD, United States, Christopher Holden, Development Seed, Boston, United States, Qiang Zhou, Chengdu University of Technology, The Engineering & Technology College, Chengdu, China, Lavanya Ashokkumar, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, United States, Sean Harkins, Development Seed, Washington DC, DC, United States, Christopher S R Neigh, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Biospheric Sciences Laboratory, Greenbelt, MD, United States and Pontus Olofsson, PhD, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, AL, United States
main_session: Accelerating Impact: User‑Driven Earth Observation Solutions from the Satellite Needs Working Group I Poster
abstract: The Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) Project produces global surface reflectance products at 30 m spatial resolution using sensors aboard NASA/USGS Landsat-8 and -9 and ESA’s Sentinel-2A/B/C satellites. The HLS project was one of the first operational solutions to come out of the Satellite Needs Working Group’s (SNWG) survey of federal agency needs in 2016. The HLS archive spans more than a decade, with an overall size of nearly 6 PB. More than 2 PB of HLS data has been transferred to the user community, and HLS is one of the most downloaded datasets within NASA’s Earth Science Data Systems. Several HLS-related SNWG solutions are in various stages of development. A global HLS-derived Vegetation Indices product (SNWG Cycle 3) is in operation from 2025, a low-latency HLS solution (SNWG Cycle 4) is currently in the implementation phase, and 10-m HLS was selected as an SNWG Cycle 5 solution. Additionally, a global HLS vegetation indices composite product is under development to support NASA’s Biodiversity and Ecological Conservation (BDEC) applications. Recently, the HLS data production cloud pipeline was modernized and upgraded. The Cloud masking algorithm was updated in HLS forward production earlier this year, and optimizations to the atmospheric correction algorithm are planned for the near future. This presentation will provide an overview of recent project updates and discuss key timelines for future project milestones.

title: Toward Continental-Scale Crop Residue Mapping: Automated Endmember Learning and Augmented Spectral Mixture Framework Using HLS Time Series
authors: Zhixian Lin, Kaiyu Guan, Sheng Wang, Saibo Li and Mr. Haozheng Ma
main_session: Remote Sensing for Sustainable Agriculture I Poster
abstract: Field-level crop residue and tillage information is essential for tracking soil conservation and carbon outcomes, yet existing national products are either spatially coarse or physically opaque. Spectral mixture analysis (SMA) can recover residue fraction directly from optical spectra, but conventional SMA workflows rely on region-specific endmember libraries that transfer poorly across heterogeneous U.S. soils and cropping systems. We develop an automated endmember learning and spectral unmixing framework for crop residue mapping across major row-crop regions of the contiguous United States using Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) time series. An independently trained tillage classification model is first used as weak supervision to identify high-confidence residue-rich and soil-exposed fields. Within these candidate fields, PlanetScope imagery is used to screen candidate residue and bare-soil endmember samples for spatial homogeneity and material purity. Optical moisture indices, SAR observations, and recent precipitation are then used to characterize the surface moisture condition associated with each candidate endmember. For each HLS observation, a context-specific endmember subset is selected according to crop type, soil spectral class, surface wetness, and regional context. An augmented linear mixing model is used to estimate residue abundance while accounting for illumination, moisture, and regional spectral variability. Uncertainty is quantified from endmember selection and model sensitivity. Initial experiments in parts of the U.S. Midwest demonstrate the feasibility of transferring residue information from airborne hyperspectral data to satellite-based HLS observations. This framework provides a scalable and physically interpretable pathway toward field-level crop residue mapping across the United States at the continental scale.

title: Self-Supervised Floating Algal Bloom Mapping in Coastal Waters Using Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel-2
authors: Thainara Lima, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State, MS, United States and Vitor Martins, Mississippi State University, Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering, Mississippi State, MS, United States
main_session: Advancing Water Quality Through Artificial Intelligence: Lessons, Strategies, and New Frontiers I Poster
abstract: Deep learning approaches for satellite algal bloom monitoring have advanced rapidly but are typically region-specific, often designed to detect either macroalgae or microalgae, and rely on coarse-resolution data that miss the fine-scale structure of surface-floating blooms. We present a new, globally applicable Vision Transformer model that maps both micro- (e.g., single-celled phytoplankton) and macroalgal (e.g., seaweed) blooms from 30-m harmonized Landsat-8/9 and Sentinel-2A/B/C data. To capture the optical variability of coastal waters worldwide, a self-supervised learning strategy was implemented, for the first time, on a global unlabeled dataset comprising 528,856 patches extracted from 1,175 coastal locations (15,751 Landsat and Sentinel-2 images) acquired between 2013 and 2020. The resulting pre-trained model captures a wide range of water composition, algal bloom optical characteristics, phenological dynamics, and environmental conditions across diverse aquatic systems, establishing the first foundation model designed for global aquatic systems. The effectiveness of the self-supervised strategy is demonstrated by comparing the reconstructed and original reflectance across the VNIR bands, with relative differences ranging from 3.32% in the blue band to 29.44% in the NIR band, indicating that the model learned meaningful spectral representations despite the high optical variability of coastal waters. Building on this pre-trained foundation, the ViT model was fine-tuned on a high-quality labeled algal bloom patch dataset (24,265 training and 12,255 validation patches) generated from coastal bloom hotspots worldwide, achieving an overall Dice coefficient of 63% with omission and commission errors of 24.37% and 46.12%, respectively. Further validation against well-documented micro- and macroalgal bloom events reported in the literature shows that the model resolves complex bloom structures, including faint bloom filaments, with minimal misclassification. A one-year time series assessment at four locations, compared against MODIS-derived products, demonstrates the advantage of higher-spatial-resolution 30-m mapping for detecting the fragmented and spatially heterogeneous blooms that region-specific and coarse-resolution approaches cannot reliably resolve.

title: Spectral–Thermal Estimation of Cover Crop Biomass across Illinois: Integrating PlanetScope Red-Edge, HLS SWIR, and Growing Degree Days
authors: Yide Xu, Kaiyu Guan, Sheng Wang, Andrew J Margenot, Eric Potash, Saibo Li, Mr. Haozheng Ma and Zhangliang Chen
main_session: Remote Sensing for Sustainable Agriculture I Poster
abstract: Biomass is a key modulator of the agronomic trade-offs of cover crops. However, scalable methods for estimating cover crop biomass across large agricultural regions remain limited. Using 655 ground measurements of cereal rye and cereal rye–mixture aboveground biomass collected at field and plot levels across Illinois in 2020–2021 and 2024–2025, we evaluated how spectral information, vegetation-index time series, and thermal conditions contribute to remote-sensing-based aboveground biomass estimation. PlanetScope SuperDove imagery, Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 data (HLS), and PRISM temperature data were used to compare vegetation indices, snapshot and time-series features, and machine-learning models incorporating growing degree days (GDD) and shortwave-infrared bands. Red-edge indices performed best among all vegetation indices, with NDRE the strongest overall linear relationship with biomass, with R 2 = 0.413 and RMSE of 0.77 ton ha -1 . Time-series features of vegetation indices generally did not outperform snapshot vegetation indices. Crucially, integrating spring GDD substantially improved machine-learning model performance. For PlanetScope data, XGBoost performance increased from R 2 = 0.45 and RMSE of 0.74 ton ha -1 using only spectral information to R 2 = 0.67 and RMSE of 0.58 ton ha -1 after adding spring GDD. With HLS data, the combination of spectral, red-edge, SWIR, NDRE, and spring GDD information achieved R 2 = 0.71 and RMSE of 0.55 ton ha -1 . Statewide predictions of rye and rye-mixture cover crop biomass from 2020 to 2024 revealed substantial spatial variability, averaging 1.04 ± 0.81 Mg ha -1, slightly below the recommended minimum of 1.12 ton ha -1 for reducing nitrate-N losses. Biomass was generally higher in southern Illinois than in northern Illinois. These results demonstrate that NDVI-related indices, red-edge information, spring thermal time, and SWIR reflectance provide complementary information for regional cover crop biomass estimation. This study advances cover crop biomass estimation from site-specific relationships toward scalable, multi-sensor regional monitoring, providing a framework for statewide assessment of cover crop performance and its associated agroecosystem outcomes.

title: Toward Enhanced Terrestrial Monitoring Through Fusion of PACE, EMIT, and HLS Reflectance Products
authors: Maggie Johnson, Antonio Ferraz, David Schimel, Gregory Hillard Halverson, Jouni Susiluoto, Skyelar Caplan, Amy J Braverman, Michelle M Gierach and Nicholas Parazoo
main_session: Advancing Global Imaging Spectroscopy and Thermal Infrared Measurements: ECOSTRESS, EMIT, and EAGLE IV Poster
abstract: Recently launched hyperspectral visible to shortwave infrared (VSWIR) missions like EMIT and PACE, together with the upcoming EAGLE and CHIME missions, will provide unprecedented data enabling fine-scale understanding of surface properties and dynamics. However, no individual instrument will achieve the sub-weekly revisit and high spatial resolution needed to address high-priority science questions on terrestrial ecosystem change, agriculture management, biodiversity, snow and ice dynamics, and inland and coastal ecosystem health. Data fusion between complementary hyperspectral instruments, along with existing and future multispectral instruments, provides a pathway to achieve the desired science. In this talk, we present new data fusion techniques for producing high spatial (30m), near daily, hyperspectral VSWIR reflectance products through fusion of PACE, EMIT, and Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) land surface reflectance products. The framework explicitly accounts for the different spectral, spatial, and temporal resolutions of individual instruments and does so while appropriately tracking and quantifying the associated uncertainties. We present initial results over the Dangermond Preserve in Southern California and an agricultural site in northeastern Colorado, and discuss the potential impact of the fused products for terrestrial and agricultural monitoring.

title: Enhancing the Temporal Resolution and Consistency of OpenET through Fusion of Daily Harmonized Landsat, Sentinel-2, and PlanetScope (HLSP) surface reflectance and AMSR-2 Passive Microwave data
authors: Rasmus Houborg, Planet Labs, San Francisco, CA, United States and Julie Nutini, Planet Labs PBC, San Francisco, United States
main_session: Evapotranspiration (ET): Advances in In Situ ET Measurements and Remote Sensing–Based ET Estimation, Mapping, and Evaluation I Oral
abstract: OpenET provides a robust, operational benchmark for satellite-based evapotranspiration (ET): flux-validated 30 m ET across the conterminous United States from an ensemble of models combining optical and thermal satellite data with surface meteorology. However, OpenET retrieves ET only on clear-sky Landsat overpasses (8-day repeat at best) and reconstructs daily values by interpolating the reference-ET fraction between overpasses, limiting sensitivity to short-term ET dynamics driven by irrigation, rainfall, and transient stress. We present an approach to enhance the temporal resolution and quality of operational ET products such as OpenET by exploiting the daily 30 m surface reflectance of the Harmonized Landsat, Sentinel-2, and PlanetScope (HLSP) product. HLSP applies the CubeSat-Enabled Spatio-Temporal Enhancement Method (CESTEM) to directly fuse and harmonize clear-sky observations from PlanetScope and public mission sources into a seamless, sensor-agnostic, daily surface reflectance stream. Our approach uses a compact, scalable feature set: HLSP surface reflectance and vegetation indices, incoming solar radiation, and downscaled AMSR-2 passive-microwave brightness temperatures—a cloud-penetrating proxy for surface moisture and temperature. Two complementary tracks are developed. Track A is a gradient-boosted regression model that learns to map these daily predictors to OpenET ensemble ET at clear-sky overpass dates, then applies it to produce ET on every day, including cloudy, non-overpass dates. Track B embeds Track A within the CESTEM reference-sampling framework, using it to propagate the reference ET across dates while suppressing its uncertainty through robust multi-date aggregation. We demonstrate both tracks of our approach over Mead, Nebraska (2021–2025), validating against AmeriFlux eddy-covariance towers spanning irrigated and rainfed maize–soybean systems. We evaluate between-overpass performance, cross-compare with OpenET, characterise uncertainties, and assess feature importance. Preliminary results assess whether optical–microwave fusion can extend robust, OpenET-quality ET to an observation-driven daily cadence for water-resources monitoring and decision-making.

title: Developing a Scalable Global Land Surface Phenology Product from Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 Data for the Post-MODIS Era
authors: Colin A Quinn, Qiang Zhou, Junchang Ju, Margaret Wooten, Amanda Hildt Armstrong, Dr. Shawn Serbin, BA, MS, PhD and Christopher S R Neigh
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat I Oral
abstract: With the upcoming end to MODIS science data collection, establishing the next generation of global Earth observing datasets is critical for supporting research continuity. This effort focuses on developing a global land surface phenology (LSP) algorithm that leverages NASA's Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) v2.0 data in a cloud computing ecosystem. While MODIS products provide daily coverage with 250-500m spatial resolution, our approach utilizes the 30m spatial resolution and a global average ~1.6 day revisit frequency. The phenology algorithm is similar to the MODIS Land Surface Phenology (MCD12Q2) algorithm - we apply robust spline-fitting and QA/QC methods to a 36 month time series of vegetation indices (e.g., Enhanced Vegetation Index 2, EVI2) extracted from quality-screened HLS scenes, incorporating the enhanced Fmask 5.0 to remove cloud, shadows, water, and snow/ice pixels, and calculate a suite of over 20 phenological metrics for each target year. Initial findings using EVI2 indicate that the newly developed HLS LSP dataset captures broad landscape trends, such as the early onset of greenup in Interior Alaska compared to the North Slope. When validated against a North to South 1500km transect in Alaska, HLS-derived greenup for 2024 occurs 28±19 days later than the MODIS MCD12Q2 product, despite strong spatial correlation (r = 0.72). Comparison with the similar HLS-derived Multi-Sensor Land Surface Phenology (MSLSP) product on Alaska’s Seward Peninsula shows a consistent greenup within 2.4 days in 2019. Similarly, in the temperate Mid-Atlantic USA region, the HLS LSP demonstrates consistent seasonal timing compared to the MCD12Q2 dataset (greenup ± 3.1 days, dormancy ± 1.3 days). The HLS LSP reveals fine-scale spatial phenology patterns across the coastal piedmont and Appalachian Mountains driven by topography and land use transitions that are not discernible with the coarser MODIS-based phenology dataset.

title: A Prototype WorldView–HLS Fusion Workflow for Policy-Relevant Monitoring of Crop–Eucalyptus Dynamics in Ethiopia
authors: Woubet G. Alemu, Christopher S R Neigh, Margaret Wooten, Qiang Zhou and François Smith, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Biospheric Sciences Laboratory, Greenbelt, MD, United States
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat II Poster
abstract: Crop–Eucalyptus transitions are reshaping smallholder landscapes in the Ethiopian highlands as farmers respond to rising input costs, labor constraints, climate variability, market returns, and policy pressure to maintain food-crop production while limiting water stress on irrigation systems. In Mecha District, Amhara Region, these dynamics occur at field-to-woodlot scales and seasonal-to-annual time scales. HLS provides Landsat-family temporal continuity, and an experimental 10 m HLS solution offers finer seasonal monitoring, but even 10 m observations can mix crop, Eucalyptus, fallow, homestead, and tree–crop components. Conversely, 2 m WorldView imagery resolves field and woodlot boundaries, but irregular acquisition limits direct phenology monitoring. This study developed a high-spatial/high-temporal fusion workflow that uses 2 m WorldView imagery to structure classification of an experimental 10 m HLS time series. A 2D CNN semantic-segmentation model delineated field- and woodlot-scale units representing crop fields, Eucalyptus/other woody vegetation, grass/fallow, built-up features, and water. HLS reflectance and vegetation-index trajectories were summarized within these WorldView-derived units and classified using a 1D CNN temporal model. WorldView supplies the spatial framework, while HLS supplies the temporal engine for interpreting seasonal trajectories within management units smaller than the HLS pixel. Applied in Mecha, the prototype workflow tracked crop–Eucalyptus dynamics during rapid socioeconomic and policy change. Results indicate crop-to-Eucalyptus succession during 2015–2020, consistent with rising crop-production costs, lower labor requirements, and attractive woodlot returns. After 2020, parts of this trajectory reversed from Eucalyptus/woody cover back to cropland, reflecting policy enforcement and renewed pressure to maintain food-crop production where Eucalyptus expansion raised irrigation-water concerns. More broadly, the workflow provides a transferable prototype for land-use and policy investigations in fragmented smallholder systems: high-resolution imagery defines the management units, HLS captures their temporal behavior, and the fused trajectories reveal policy-relevant transitions that are difficult to detect with either data stream alone.

title: Cross-Sensor Consistency: A Comparison of NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) surface reflectance and MODIS NBAR products
authors: Qiang Zhou, Min Feng, Junchang Ju, Joseph O Sexton, Eric Vermote, Panshi Wang, Amit Angal, Margaret Wooten, Madhu Sridhar, Saurabh Channan, Nathan Thomas and Christopher S R Neigh
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat II Poster
abstract: High-frequency, fine-resolution surface reflectance datasets are critical for global land monitoring. Maintaining observational continuity across datasets is increasingly urgent as legacy coarse-resolution systems like the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) near decommissioning. The NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) Version 2 product addresses this transition by integrating observations from Landsat and Sentinel-2 to deliver high-frequency, 30-meter imagery. This study evaluates the radiometric consistency of HLS against the established MODIS Nadir Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function-Adjusted Reflectance (NBAR) dataset. HLS demonstrates strong agreement with MODIS NBAR across all six shared spectral bands, exhibiting high linear correlations (Pearson r : 0.969–0.993). Globally, mean absolute differences (MADs) remain low, typically staying under 0.03 for visible bands and below 0.05 for NIR and SWIR bands. Spatially, the largest differences occur in high-latitude regions, primarily driven by sub-pixel snow, ice, and water, which are excluded in the 30 meter HLS data but persist as mixed signals within coarser 250-500 meter MODIS pixels. This resolution-driven mismatch offers a mechanistic explanation for historical discrepancies in satellite-derived vegetation trend analyses, demonstrating how coarse-resolution data can confound greening trends in landscapes with dynamic snow, ice, or water fractions. These insights establish a baseline for HLS quality assessment and offer guidance for refining multi-sensor data fusion frameworks.

title: Transferability and operational reliability of a released Prithvi geospatial foundation model for crop type mapping across three continents
authors: Venkatesh Kolluru, Rajat Shinde, Abdelhak Marouane, Caden Helbling, Slesa Adhikari, Deepak Shah, Othneil Drew, Iksha Gurung, Manil Maskey and Rahul Ramachandran
main_session: Advancing AI for Environmental Sustainability: Data, Methods, and Applications II Poster
abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) pretrained on large satellite archives report strong crop classification accuracy and offer improved geographic transferability, potentially reducing dependence on location-specific training data. However, the accuracy of released fine-tuned GeoFMs has been established almost entirely within their training distribution, and their behavior under operational conditions elsewhere remains poorly characterized. To address this gap, we evaluated the operational out-of-distribution performance of a widely adopted GeoFM, namely Prithvi-EO-2.0, a 600-million-parameter temporal Vision Transformer, run in its intended configuration of three temporal frames, 13 classes, and 30 m resolution. We tested the model across 37 events spanning three continents and 12 countries, and validated it against four regionally appropriate reference products (CDL, AAFC, EUCROPMAP, and MapBiomas) and benchmarked it against Prithvi-EO-1.0. We found that the mean overall accuracy declined with distance from the training distribution, from 0.65 within the United States to 0.40 in Europe. We observed that accuracy collapsed when the observation window was misaligned with local crop phenology, while model confidence remained high. A Monte Carlo dropout estimate registered this shift, whereas the reported confidence did not. Much of the cross-continent decline, therefore, reflected phenological misalignment rather than spatial transfer. Aligning the window to the local growing season restored accuracy, and consolidating the 13 classes into 10 raised accuracy at every event by 4%. We also found that compressing the temporal window to less than 30 days for near-real-time use resulted in an 11% decrease in overall accuracy, and upgrading to Prithvi-EO-2.0 improved accuracy without closing the transfer gap. Together, these results show that Prithvi-EO-2.0 transfers usefully across regions only when its observation window is aligned with the local growing season, and that its probabilistic confidence does not register the failures that occur under misalignment. We translate these findings into deployment guidance specifying conditions under which the released model can be applied reliably.

title: NASA HLS V2.0 Surface Reflectance Assessment versus USGS Landsat C2 and ESA Sentinel-2 L2A
authors: Qing Ying, Junchang Ju, Qiang Zhou, Eric Vermote, Madhu Sridhar, Trang Vo, Margaret Wooten and Christopher S R Neigh
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat II Poster
abstract: The NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 Version 2.0 (HLSv2) products provide globally consistent and temporally enhanced terrestrial Surface Reflectance (SR) by harmonizing the US Landsat Operational Land Imager (OLI) and the European Copernicus Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument (MSI) satellite data. The HLS applies atmospheric correction, cloud masking, and Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) normalization to radiometrically calibrated, orthorectified, and geometrically precise Level-1 Landsat and Sentinel-2 data, producing nadir BRDF-adjusted reflectance (NBAR) in a unified tiling and griding system. After bandpass adjustment, HLS generates Landsat-like 30-m Sentinel-2 NBAR, ultimately complementing Landsat 8 and 9 to achieve land observations every 2-3 days on a global average. USGS and ESA have routinely carried out atmospheric correction to Level-1 Landsat and Sentinel-2 data in their native tiling and griding systems, using LaSRC and Sen2Cor algorithms, respectively. To assess the consistency and improvement of HLSv2 reflectance, we compared the HLSv2 intermediate SR and final NBAR with USGS’s Collection 2 (C2) Level-2 Landsat and Sentinel-2 SR on a set of 545 granules with less than 10% cloud cover from 96 tile locations. Using 18 granule-based statistical metrics across all bands, we found consistent agreement between HLSv2 and USGS’s C2 Product surface reflectance. The largest mean absolute difference (MAD) is present in the near-infrared band (NIR, MAD = 0.0059 ± 0.0037). Shortwave visible bands are more susceptible to atmospheric correction than the longwave bands, as demonstrated by the number of outliers. The differences in SR increase when the mean sun zenith angle exceeds 40°, largely due to differences in SR estimates after atmospheric correction over mountainous snow/ice-covered areas. Visualized comparisons showed that BRDF normalization in HLSv2 eliminates reflectance angular variations from adjacent focal plane assemblies, preventing those artifacts from propagating to downstream vegetation indices and modeling products. Our work evaluated HLSv2 surface reflectance products to support HLS improvements to meet urgent needs arising from agricultural monitoring, disaster response, and land resource management.

title: Toward Near-Real-Time Large-Scale Monitoring of Tropical Forest Disturbances Using Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 Data
authors: Na Chen, Di Yang, Chang Liu, Ning Ye, Johan van den Hoogen and Lalasia Bialic-Murphy
main_session: Tropical Forests Under a Changing Environment III Poster
abstract: Timely and early detection of tropical forest disturbances is critical for understanding ecosystem dynamics, quantifying carbon stocks, and supporting sustainable forest management. Although Landsat time-series data have been widely used for tropical forest disturbance monitoring, their relatively limited observation frequency can constrain the detection of rapid disturbance events in tropical regions. The Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) dataset provides an opportunity to address this limitation by integrating Landsat and Sentinel-2 observations into a consistent surface reflectance record with enhanced temporal resolution. However, the potential of HLS for large-scale tropical forest disturbance monitoring remains largely unexplored. Here, we integrated dense time-series data, the Breaks For Additive Season and Trend Monitor ( BFAST Monitor) algorithm, and machine learning approaches to characterize tropical forest disturbances at regional scales in near real time. Using HLS time series observations from 2016 to 2020, we analyzed Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI) temporal trajectories and applied the BFAST Monitor algorithm to detect forest disturbances across Mato Grosso, Brazil. We assessed the accuracy of the detected forest disturbances using 400 stratified reference samples that were visually interpreted. Our preliminary results show that the overall accuracy of forest disturbance mapping in Mato Grosso in 2020 is 83.75%, while also revealing substantial spatial and temporal variability in disturbance patterns across the region. These results demonstrate the potential of HLS for large-scale tropical forest disturbance monitoring. This study provides baseline information for near-real-time forest disturbance monitoring and early warning systems using HLS, offering valuable information for tracking forest changes and supporting sustainable forest management across the Amazon.

title: Mapping Changes in Daytime and Nighttime Urban Heat Islands Using ECOSTRESS and Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 Data
authors: Andrews Korah, Michael C Wimberly, Bright Andoh, Shomen Mukherjee and Ankitha Jayanth
main_session: Urbanization and the Environment: Data, Models, and Applications I Poster
abstract: Satellite-based observations, including VIIRS, MODIS, ASTER, and Landsat, are often used to map land surface temperature (LST) and quantify urban heat islands. However, these products are limited in either spatial or temporal resolution. Since late 2018, the ECOSTRESS mission has provided a unique combination of spatial and temporal resolutions compared with previous LST products, capturing diurnal patterns of urban heat exposure at a relatively high spatial resolution (70 m). However, cloud effects remain a challenge, especially during the monsoon, and data integration to provide daily high-resolution mapping of surface urban heat islands has been insufficiently explored. We used Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS2) and ERA5 reanalysis data to model hourly ECOSTRESS LST for two cities in western India. We used 183 ECOSTRESS images with low cloud cover in Ahmedabad and 185 in Surat spanning January 2019 to May 2025. The images were all visually checked and manually georeferenced if misaligned. We also used all cloud free HLS2 data to generate monthly composites of spectral indices including, normalized difference built-up index, normalized difference vegetation index, normalized difference moisture index, bare soil index, and albedo. For each city, we generated a 20 x 20 grid of spatial tiles within the 5 km bounding box around each city and randomly generated equal points in each grid cell, splitting the grids into separate training and testing sets. We used the XGBoost machine learning algorithm along with HLS2 spectral indices and ERA5 skin temperature to model hourly ECOSTRESS LST. The models were then applied to predict LST across the entire study period and extract daily minimum and maximum LST. In Ahmedabad and Surat, the models performed well across the diurnal cycle, with nighttime predictions showing slightly higher accuracy than daytime. The predicted maps showed more concentrated surface urban heat islands at night than during the day and also highlighted trends in the growth of these heat islands with urban expansion. These results provide insights into surface urban heat island trends in the context of daily and seasonal cycles and can be integrated with other sources of data to estimate heat exposure risk.

title: MosaIQ: An Open Web Portal for On-Demand Inference with NASA's Prithvi, Surya, and Lunar Foundation Models
authors: Othneil Drew, Slesa Adhikari, Abdelhak Marouane, Deepak Shah, Caden Helbling, Venkatesh Kolluru, Rajat Shinde, Iksha Gurung, Manil Maskey and Rahul Ramachandran
main_session: Open Earth System Science Data, Algorithms, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Advance Scientific Discovery and Applications III Poster
abstract: AI foundation models for Earth and space science, such as Prithvi-EO-2.0 for Earth observation, Surya for heliophysics, and LunarFM for planetary surfaces, have shown strong performance on tasks including flood mapping, burn scar delineation, crop classification, solar activity forecasting, and lunar crater detection. Yet, these capabilities remain out of reach for many potential users; running inference requires GPU resources, machine learning expertise, and familiarity with complex satellite data pipelines. This gap between released research models and operational use limits their scientific and societal impact. We present the MosaIQ Portal, a web application that makes foundation model inference accessible to anyone with a web browser. The system operationalizes fine-tuned models behind standard inference APIs and exposes them through an interactive map interface. Users select an event or draw a region of interest, trigger on-demand inference, and view results as image overlays on maps of the Earth, the Sun, and the Moon, with no code or data wrangling required. For Earth, Prithvi-EO-2.0 delineates flood extent, burn scars, and crop types. For the Sun, Surya forecasts upcoming solar conditions minutes to hours ahead. For the Moon, LunarFM detects craters, supporting surface science and landing site assessment. Beyond running inferences, the portal is a rich visualization environment for exploring model predictions. Users can explore curated event galleries of real floods, wildfires, and solar storms; drawing tools for defining custom study areas; side-by-side comparison views that place predictions next to observations; magnified inspection of fine spatial detail; animated playback of forecast sequences; and shareable URLs that make any analysis view reproducible. By turning foundation model outputs into open, interactive science products, MosaIQ enables domain scientists, decision makers, and students to explore model behavior across Earth, heliophysics, and planetary science.

title: Temporal-Gap-Aware Deep Learning for HLS NDVI Prediction
authors: Yifan Yang, Colorado State University, Fort Collins, United States, Zhengwei Yang, USDA, NASS, Washington DC, United States and Haonan Chen, Colorado State University and NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, United States
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat II Poster
abstract: Accurate prediction of Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) is important for monitoring crop growth, phenology, and vegetation condition at field scale. However, HLS NDVI time series are affected by cloud contamination, irregular revisit intervals, sensor differences between Landsat and Sentinel-2, and rapid seasonal changes during crop green-up and senescence. We developed a temporal-gap-aware deep learning framework to predict HLS NDVI at 30 m resolution over an agricultural region in the U.S. High Plains. The proposed work utilizes observations including most recent multispectral frames, recent NDVI-only temporal differences, target day-of-year encoding, and four previous-year NDVI frames near the same day of year to represent historical data. The prediction model encodes recent HLS observations with a time-aware ConvLSTM and spatial attention. Then a gated fusion module combines recent, historical, delta, and seasonal information to generate target-date HLS NDVI predictions. In the best-performing configuration, the model achieved a global RMSE of 0.079 NDVI and spatial correlation coefficient of 0.938 across matched prediction scenes. Performance analyses indicated that the biggest prediction errors occurred in rapid vegetation changing periods. Nevertheless, these results demonstrate that combining recent HLS spectral multispectral, historical data, NDVI change information, and explicit temporal-gap modeling can effectively improve field-scale HLS NDVI prediction for agricultural monitoring.

title: Fine-resolution Live and Dead Fuel Moisture Content Estimation from Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2
authors: Willa Egan, University at Buffalo, Civil, Structural and Environmental Engineering, Buffalo, NY, United States, Utkarsh Kumar, The University of Texas at San Antonio, College of AI, Cyber and Computing, San Antonio, United States and Negar Elhami Khorasani, University at Buffalo, Civil, Structural, and Environmental Engineering, Buffalo, United States
main_session: Vegetation-Fuel Mapping with Remote Sensing Poster
abstract: Fuel moisture content (FMC) is known to affect fire behavior, but is often considered in wildland fire spread models as a single scalar value encompassing live (L) and dead (D) fuels across the simulation domain. This simplification does not account for variation in FMC across different fuel types nor temporal patterns like seasonal growth and senescence or diurnal cycling, and can thus misrepresent spread and intensity. FMC proxies derived from Earth observation satellites are coarsely resolved and do not consider other variables affecting FMC, like weather conditions and soil moisture. Ground truth FMC measurements from the Fire Environment Mapping System (FEMS) are sparse and infrequent. They are separated from the nearest cloud-free satellite overpass by a potentially large range of hours to weeks, which introduces inconsistent data pairing. To overcome this, using NASA’s Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) product, our deep learning model encodes every HLS scene independently and attends over the resulting set, ensuring prediction capability is invariant to how many scenes are available at a given time. Dense records are randomly thinned so that every site is learned at every observation density. An independent model branch aggregates weather data from NOAA’s High-resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) and soil moisture data from NASA’s Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) over some fixed antecedent time window, which is learned and unique for each individual fuel class, following the 40 Scott and Burgan classification from LANDFIRE. The fuel-class-conditioned product can be queried for any time of interest, yielding L&D FMC estimates for each cell in the defined grid. The model is trained on FEMS measurements from 2015-2025 over the state of California and evaluated against historical day-of-year climatology under spatially-blocked leave-year-out validation. The product provides spatially and temporally resolved L&D FMC estimates for initializing fire spread simulations, and is integrated into an offline coupling of the Weather Research and Forecasting’s Community Fire Behavior Model for wildland and the Streamlined Wildland Urban Interface Fire Tracing (SWUIFT) model for community spread.

title: Improving Prithvi-EO-2.0 Burn-Scar Mapping with Full Fire-Event Trajectory Encoding and Target-Dominant Physical-Change Adaptation
authors: Soe Win Myint, Texas State University San Marcos, Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, San Marcos, United States and Yuanhui Zhu, Texas State University, Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, San Marcos, United States
main_session: Open Earth System Science Data, Algorithms, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Advance Scientific Discovery and Applications III Poster
abstract: The official Prithvi-EO-2.0 BurnScars checkpoint is based on a single target-date image. We evaluated whether it could be improved through direct multi-temporal encoding or target-dominant physical-change adaptation using explicit spectral-change variables. The dataset contained HLS S30 images at pre-event (T−1), target (T), and post-event (T+1) dates. All experiments used BurnScars normalization and three random seeds. We first evaluated the published checkpoints at full resolution and reproduced the official fine-tuning recipe in five independent runs. We then trained Single-T, pre/target and target/post 2T, and chronological 3T models end to end. In the change-guided models, the fine-tuned Single-T pathway remained frozen. A residual model and temporal adapter used dNBR, dNIR, dSWIR2, and dNDVI from T−1 to T; a bidirectional residual model used the same variables for T−1→T and T→T+1. D4 augmentation was also evaluated with 3T. The published checkpoints produced a burned-class intersection over union (IoU) of 0.848 in our full-resolution evaluation, and the official-recipe reproduction averaged 0.853±0.004. Chronological 3T reached 0.891±0.002, compared with 0.862±0.025 for Single-T, 0.877±0.015 for pre/target 2T, and 0.886±0.009 for target/post 2T. The post-event image contributed more than the pre-event image when each was paired with T, while produced the highest mean IoU and the smallest variation among seeds. The residual, temporal-adapter, and bidirectional-residual models reached 0.867–0.870, and 3T with D4 reached 0.879±0.008. In four held-out years and two UTM zones, models were retrained without the evaluation domain. The 3T model averaged 0.851±0.002, compared with 0.825 for the matched official-architecture baseline, and was higher in 17 of 18 seed-domain comparisons. Direct encoding of the full fire-event sequence provided the largest and most stable improvement over the official single-date model. Explicit spectral-change variables were less effective when used only as corrections to a frozen target-date pathway. Post-event observations provided the strongest additional signal, while the pre-event image supplied complementary context.

title: Leveraging NASA’s HLS for Scalable Within‑Season Monitoring of Agricultural Dynamics
authors: Feng Gao, U. S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service, Hydrology and Remote Sensing Laboratory, Beltsville, United States, Martha Anderson, USDA Agricultural Research Service, Hydrology and Remote Sensing Laboratory, Beltsville, United States, W D Hively, U.S. Geological Survey, Lower Mississippi-Gulf Water Science Center, Beltsville, United States and Haoteng Zhao, George Mason University, Center for Spatial Information Science and Systems, Fairfax, United States
main_session: Accelerating Impact: User‑Driven Earth Observation Solutions from the Satellite Needs Working Group II Oral
abstract: The Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel‑2 (HLS) dataset provides routine 30‑m surface reflectance with ~2-day revisit interval, enabling timely agricultural monitoring that was not possible before. This presentation highlights recent advancements in using HLS to characterize summer crop and winter cover crop (WCC) dynamics through phenology‑based, within‑season algorithms. We developed and evaluated four complementary approaches: the Within‑Season Emergence (WISE) algorithm for detecting summer crop green‑up using smoothed VI time series and MACD‑based trend transitions; an emergence‑adjusted crop condition monitoring method that aligns vegetation index anomalies with accumulated growing degree days; the Within‑Season Termination (WIST) algorithm, which identifies rapid VI declines associated with WCC termination; and a phenology‑driven WCC presence likelihood model that quantifies WCC performance in-season and post‑season. Assessments using field surveys, operational program records, and regional multi‑year analyses demonstrate that HLS temporal density and short latency enable accurate mapping of crop emergence, WCC termination, and WCC likelihood within the growing season. These methods support operational needs such as Maryland’s incentive programs and provide scalable, management‑relevant datasets for agroecosystem modeling and conservation assessment. Collectively, this work demonstrates how NASA’s HLS mission delivers critical observational capability for near‑real‑time agricultural monitoring across field‑to‑CONUS scales.

title: Accelerating Conservation Actions and Biodiversity Understanding by Creating Analysis-Ready HLS Vegetation Index Composite Products
authors: Madhu Sridhar, Africa Ixmucane Flores Anderson, Qiang Zhou, Junchang Ju, Pontus Olofsson, PhD, Christopher S R Neigh, Emil A Cherrington, Kelsey E Herndon, Phoebe Oduor, Amanda Hildt Armstrong, Colin A Quinn, Keiko Nomura, Dr. Shawn Serbin, BA, MS, PhD, Jacob Abramowitz, Yoseline Angel, Khuong H Tran, Weile Wang, Juan Luis Torres-Perez, Antonio Ferraz, Joseph Spruce, Amanda Clayton, Maggie Johnson, David Schimel, Tommy Le, Aatreyee Nath, Christopher Hain, K Fred Huemmrich, Petya K Campell and Janet Nackoney
main_session: Accelerating Impact: User‑Driven Earth Observation Solutions from the Satellite Needs Working Group III Oral
abstract: To continue serving the thriving community of users of NASA’s Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) suite of products, and in preparation for the decommissioning of MODIS sensors, NASA is developing high-level composite products derived from HLS. The high temporal (a global average 1.6 days) and spatial (30 m) resolution of HLS provide a unique opportunity for consistent, high-fidelity monitoring of Earth's land surface. Biodiversity and ecological applications, including phenology monitoring, flora and fauna habitat modeling, ecosystem disturbance, and surface change detection, rely heavily on Level 3 composite Vegetation Index products, such as monthly NDVI composites derived from MODIS or Landsat observations. Accordingly, NASA is creating a new data product: Monthly Vegetation Index composites derived from HLS datasets. We will present the new HLS composite product, including its characteristics, accessibility, and example applications. We expect this product to increase NASA's capabilities for long-term monitoring of the Earth's pulse and provide a valuable alternative in light of MODIS's imminent decommissioning.

title: HLS-GPT: A Foundation Model For Near-real-time Crop Monitoring Using Landsat and Sentinel-2 Time Series
authors: Hankui Zhang, Junjie Li, Santosh Subedi, Maitiniyazi Maimaitijiang and David Roy
main_session: Remote Sensing for Sustainable Agriculture II Oral
abstract: Satellite-based near-real-time agricultural monitoring provides timely information on crop conditions, soil moisture, and field-level changes, supporting rapid assessment and predictive modelling. Converting satellite observations into timely agricultural information remains challenging because observations are irregular and incomplete, while many algorithms require compositing or fixed temporal sampling, introducing weeks to months of additional latency beyond that imposed by satellite revisit frequency. Here, we present HLS-GPT, a phenology-aware Generative Pre-trained Transformer trained with more than 130 million harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) observations at 30 m resolution. HLS-GPT operates directly on arbitrary-length, cloud-free time series and reduces algorithm-induced latency to near zero by leveraging learned phenological dynamics to support retrieval even on dates without satellite observations. Three agricultural downstream applications are demonstrated: field-scale soil moisture retrieval, within-season crop-type mapping, and crop-damage detection. HLS-GPT consistently outperformed supervised baselines, existing foundation models such as NASA–IBM Prithvi, and operational products such as the NASA soil moisture product across the demonstrated applications. These results establish phenology-aware time-series foundation models as a scalable paradigm for timely agricultural monitoring, moving beyond foundation models designed primarily for static mapping. HLS-GPT provides a unified framework for crop monitoring, irrigation management, agricultural risk assessment, and food-security applications. Its phenology-modelling capability also enables extension to additional agricultural variables, including leaf area index, aboveground biomass, and crop yield, to support climate-resilient agricultural decision-making.

title: High-Resolution Harmonized Land Surface Temperature (LST) Products within HLS
authors: Christopher Hain, Forrest S Melton, Thomas R Holmes, Glynn C Hulley, Ryan A Wade and Trent Cowan
main_session: Science and Applications Enabled by Remote Sensing Data Fusion, Time Series Analysis, and AI I Oral
abstract: Land Surface Temperature (LST), measured from space using thermal infrared sensors, is a fundamental variable governing the exchange of heat, water, and carbon between the land surface and the atmosphere. Across all these applications, accuracy, spatial detail, and temporal frequency of LST are critical, yet all three remain challenging with current satellite systems. A persistent limitation is the coarse spatial resolution of thermal data. Thermal infrared sensors require larger detector elements and longer dwell times than optical sensors, resulting in lower resolution. For example, Landsat 8's optical bands provide 30 m resolution while its thermal bands deliver 100 m, meaning a single thermal pixel blends multiple surface types and cannot capture the fine-scale variability needed for field-level agricultural monitoring. To bridge this gap, thermal sharpening (downscaling) techniques exploit the correlation between LST and high-resolution optical land surface properties. The Sentinel-2 constellation provides surface reflectance at 10 to 20 m resolution with a 5-day revisit, and NASA's Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) project delivers a consistently calibrated 30 m product every 3 to 4 days. On the thermal side, VIIRS provides 375 m TIR data with near-daily coverage, and ECOSTRESS offers additional thermal observations. The goals are this effort include: (1) the need is for harmonized sub-weekly LST products derived from thermal infrared data at a spatial resolution of 30 m, especially for latency of 1 day or less; improving the temporal sampling capabilities of TIR-based evapotranspiration remote sensing systems will enhance agencies' ability to capture the impacts of high-frequency land management activities on water use, detect early signals of rapidly developing crop stress, and characterize daily to weekly water use in humid regions that have higher frequency of cloud cover; and the new harmonized product will accelerate the adoption of more frequent and more detailed new thermal products, shortening the time and government investment needed to integrate new thermal imaging assets into agencies' systems.

title: Gap-Free 30 m Surface Reflectance via Generative Multisensor Fusion of Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel, MODIS, and Sentinel-1 Observations.
authors: Bharath Irigireddy and Varaprasad Bandaru, USDA-ARS, U.S. Arid Land Agricultural Research Center, Maricopa, United States
main_session: Science and Applications Enabled by Remote Sensing Data Fusion, Time Series Analysis, and AI I Oral
abstract: High-resolution remote sensing imagery with high temporal frequency is crucial for agricultural and environmental monitoring, but cloud contamination and irregular revisit leave persistent gaps in the 30 m observations from the optical satellite missions, limiting their use for tracking rapid surface change such as vegetation growth and development. While coarser MODIS imagery provides near-daily spectral observations and Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar contributes all-weather structural information, combining these sources at 30 m resolution remains challenging due to differences in imaging physics, spatial resolution and acquisition timing, and any given date may be missing one or more of them. To address this, we present a conditional flow matching generative model with a vision transformer backbone that fuses 30 m surface reflectance observations with MODIS imagery and Sentinel-1 SAR to produce regular cloud-free reflectance estimates. The model is trained on a corpus of more than 75,000 locations across the contiguous United States, stratified by land cover and spanning 2000-2024. For dates preceding the Sentinel missions, the model leverages previously acquired Landsat images for structural context in place of SAR. Cloud removal is regarded as image inpainting, where the model treats cloud-covered areas as pixels with missing values and uses the learned generative process to fill these gaps from the available multisensor data. Predictions from our technique demonstrated lower spectral information divergence and higher Structural Similarity (SSIM) scores than baseline methods when evaluated across diverse regions of the USA. We applied the model over Nebraska for the 2023 growing season, generating gap-free 30 m surface reflectance at regular intervals, and NDVI trajectories derived from the reconstructed imagery are compared with actual cloud-affected HLS observations, highlighting the framework's capability to deliver consistent high-resolution data for continuous agricultural and environmental monitoring.

title: Retrieving the Full Annual Sequence of Field-Scale Rice Inundation Dynamics from Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 Time Series Using Long-Range Temporal Context
authors: Jiaqi Zou, Peng Zhu, Yanyu Lu, Youngryel Ryu, Ran Meng and Bo Huang
main_session: Advancing Climate-Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Through AI, Earth Observation, and Digital Twins I Oral
abstract: Accurate field-scale information on rice inundation dynamics is essential for assessing irrigation water use and methane emissions, and for informing improved water management strategies that promote water saving, emission reduction, and yield enhancement in sustainable rice production. However, previous studies have mainly focused on relatively coarse characterization of irrigation amount and regime, or on retrieval of one or a few predefined inundation dates, whereas continuous retrieval of rice inundation dynamics at the field scale remains largely unexplored. Here, we reformulate rice inundation monitoring as a dense classification problem and propose RID-Former (Rice Inundation Dynamics Transformer) to retrieve the full annual sequence of inundation states from Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) time series. RID-Former integrates time-series features from vegetation indices, water-sensitive indices, and SWIR2 reflectance, a local-enhanced tokenization module for preserving short-duration transitions, a Transformer encoder for modeling long-range temporal dependencies over the annual cycle, and a dual-masking strategy for robust learning from irregular observations and uncertain labels. This design enables joint characterization of the onset date, termination date, and duration of inundation events across diverse water-management regimes. We evaluated RID-Former on a multi-country dataset with daily inundation labels from 30 rice sites across China, the United States, South Korea, and Spain. Under five-fold cross-validation, RID-Former outperformed heuristic, conventional machine learning, and deep learning baselines, achieving mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 4.03, 10.05, and 10.95 days for inundation onset date, termination date, and duration, respectively. The model also showed strong cross-site and cross-year generalization. Overall, the proposed approach provides a scalable framework for monitoring field-scale rice inundation dynamics over the annual cycle, extending remote sensing from retrieving isolated inundation dates to retrieving continuous annual inundation trajectories, thereby supporting improved assessment of rice water use and greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Towards Crop Type Mapping Across Sub-Saharan Africa Using Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 Time Series
authors: Shuaijun Liu, Hankui Zhang and Junjie Li
main_session: Science and Applications Enabled by Remote Sensing Data Fusion, Time Series Analysis, and AI II Poster
abstract: Abstract : Food security in Africa remains a major global challenge, and satellite remote sensing provides a scalable means of monitoring agricultural land use at continental scales. However, continent-wide crop mapping remains difficult because of the high diversity of African cropping systems, spatially heterogeneous crop calendars, irregular satellite observations, and the limited and imbalanced availability of crop reference data. We previously introduced CRIT (Classifying Raw Irregular Time Series), a single-pixel, multi-year Transformer classification model trained on Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) 30-m surface reflectance to map 37 crop types across the conterminous United States (CONUS). Here, we extend CRIT to the African continent by combining WorldCereal crop labels and their corresponding HLS observations acquired between 2018 and 2024. For each reference label, the temporal observation window was aligned with the WorldCereal global crop calendar, ensuring that the input time series covered the complete crop growth cycle. A total of global 110,664,779 WorldCereal 30 m pixel locations were sampled and harmonized into 50 retained crop classes. To quantify the contribution of cross-region knowledge transfer, we evaluated three training strategies: (1) training CRIT from scratch using only African samples; (2) joint training using the complete global dataset; and (3) pretraining the CRIT encoder on non-African source-region samples, and subsequently fine-tuning the model using African samples. This study assesses whether and to what extent temporal–spectral representations learned from globally distributed crop samples can improve the classification of 50 crop classes across Africa’s diverse cropping systems and spatially variable crop calendars. The proposed framework provides a scalable basis for the future development of spatially continuous, 30-m crop-type maps across the African continent. Keywords: crop classification, irregular time series, Transformer, Landsat, Sentinel-2, HLS, transfer learning, Africa, phenology

title: Physics-Constrained 3D Deep Learning with HLS Time Series for Seasonal Forest Disturbance Monitoring in Northeast China
authors: Feng Zhao, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Northeast Institute of Geography and Agroecology, Beijing, China; Northeast Forestry University, Forest Resource Management, Harbin, China and Yuping Tian, Northeast Forestry University, Harbin, China
main_session: Science and Applications Enabled by Remote Sensing Data Fusion, Time Series Analysis, and AI II Poster
abstract: Temperate forests exhibit strong seasonal fluctuations, making it challenging to distinguish phenological variations from anomalous disturbance in optical time-series disturbance mapping, especially at the seasonal scale. This highlights the potential of combining 3D spatiotemporal modeling with forest prior knowledge for improving seasonal disturbance detection. This study developed a spatial-temporal deep learning framework integrating phenological priors that represent deviations in vegetation greenness and snow-background conditions from stable-forest baselines, for mapping seasonal forest disturbance in an 808,400 km² temperate forest using the Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 dataset. We further evaluated the contribution of the L-TAE temporal attention module, which can dynamically update temporal weighting, for seasonal disturbance mapping by comparing spatiotemporal models with and without explicit temporal attention. Model generalization was assessed through cross-region transfer. Results showed that phenological priors consistently improved disturbance detection accuracy across models by 2.91%–18.61% and 3.39%–13.99%, for F1 and IoU respectively. L-TAE module also provided stable gains, increasing F1 by 0.57%–12.92% over the original 3D TransUNet. Target-domain fine-tuning improved model’s regional adaptability, although gains were affected by patch morphology and terrain ruggedness. Results revealed that seasonal differences in disturbance occurrence, with Q1, Q2, Q3, and Q4 disturbances accounting for 85.36%, 4.31%, 0.91%, and 9.42% of the total detected disturbance area, respectively. These findings highlight the value of combining phenological priors and explicit temporal attention for seasonal disturbance mapping in temperate forests.

title: OPERA Dynamic Surface Water Mapping with NISAR: Development, Applications, and Synergy with DSWx-S1 and DSWx-HLS
authors: Jungkyo Jung, Bo Huang, Tyler Hudson, John W Jones, Bruce D Chapman, Charles Marshak, Steven Chan, Alexander L Handwerger, Luca Cinquini, Stirling Algermissen and Matthew Bonnema
main_session: Advancing Flood Science and Applications Using Earth Observations and Data-Driven Approaches II Oral
abstract: Surface water extent is a key indicator of flooding, drought, and wetland dynamics, yet no single observing system provides reliable coverage under all conditions. The NASA OPERA project is developing the Dynamic Surface Water Extent from NISAR (DSWx-NI) product to generate analysis-ready maps of open water and inundated vegetation from NISAR L-band Level-2 GCOV data. DSWx-NI combines filtering, adaptive thresholding, fuzzy classification, and region growing with ancillary information on topography, land cover, and historical water occurrence. The 30-m product follows the common OPERA MGRS tiling framework. This presentation summarizes the current DSWx-NI algorithm and presents dynamic surface water maps from several representative environments. The examples demonstrate open-water mapping in regions where low-backscatter land can be confused with water, wetland mapping under complex vegetation conditions, time-series monitoring of changing water extent, and detection of inundated vegetation. These cases illustrate the capabilities of L-band SAR for dynamic water monitoring and remaining challenges in distinguishing water from dark land and characterizing water beneath vegetation. We compare DSWx-NI with OPERA DSWx-S1 and DSWx-HLS. DSWx-HLS uses optical spectral information but can be limited by clouds and cloud shadows. DSWx-S1 uses C-band SAR for day-and-night, all-weather mapping and is particularly effective for open water. DSWx-NI offers similar all-weather capability while exploiting the longer L-band wavelength and polarimetric response to enhance sensitivity to inundation beneath vegetation. Their common 30-m MGRS framework supports direct comparison and combined analysis. Together, the products provide complementary spectral, temporal, and scattering information for monitoring dynamic surface water across diverse environments.

title: Evaluating Earth Observation Foundation Models: A Practical Guide for Flood Detection Using Prithvi and Clay
authors: Lillianne Thomas, Development Seed, San Francisco, United States, Wei Ji Leong, Development Seed, Washington D.C., United States, Daniel Wiesmann, Development Seed, Lisbon, Portugal and Soumya Ranjan, Development Seed, Ongole, India
main_session: Frontiers of Geospatial Artificial Intelligence and Capacity Building: Translating Research to Action III Oral
abstract: Earth Observation Foundation Models (EOFMs) represent a paradigm shift in geospatial machine learning, offering pre-trained representations that dramatically reduce the barriers to deploying AI for environmental monitoring. The chapter to be presented provides practitioners with hands-on guidance for evaluating and applying EOFMs to real-world disaster response scenarios. By leveraging self-supervised learning, these models extract meaningful representations from vast unlabeled datasets, eliminating the need for costly manual annotation. The chapter examines key considerations for EOFM adoption, including dataset sampling strategies to ensure generalization across diverse geographies, trade-offs between foundation models and task-specific approaches, and how EOFMs can reduce training costs and accelerate development cycles for resource-constrained organizations. To illustrate these concepts, we demonstrate practical workflows using two leading EOFMs—NASA/IBM's Prithvi and Clay—applied to the catastrophic 2022 Pakistan floods. Through interactive examples, readers learn to generate embeddings from satellite imagery that capture distinct hydrological states: pre-flood conditions, active inundation, and post-flood recovery patterns. These learned representations encode rich semantic information without requiring labeled training data, offering an alternative to traditional flood mapping workflows. The chapter shows how simple classifiers trained on these embeddings can achieve strong flood detection performance, dramatically accelerating the path from raw imagery to actionable insights. This capacity-building resource contributes to the broader goal of translating cutting-edge Geo-AI technologies into tools for environmental decision-making and climate adaptation worldwide.

title: Prithvi-Dust: Adapting a Weather and Climate Foundation Model for Global Dust Forecasting
authors: Yash Diggikar, University of Maryland Baltimore County, Department of Computer Science, Baltimore, United States, Milton Halem, University of Maryland Baltimore County, Computer Science, Baltimore, MD, United States, Aishwarya Raman, NASA Ames Research Center/Bay Area Environmental Research Institute, Earth Science Division, Moffett Field, CA, United States, Allison Collow, Global Modeling and Assimilation Office, Greenbelt, United States, Sujit Roy, University of Alabama in Huntsville, NASA IMPACT/ Earth System Science Center, Huntsville, United States and Jonathan Gee, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, United States
main_session: Advances in Global Aerosol Modeling: Representation, Assimilation, and Prediction II Oral
abstract: Mineral dust affects health, visibility, radiation, clouds, and biogeochemical cycles, yet remains difficult to forecast because emissions, transport, and removal depend on meteorology, surface conditions, and particle size. Satellite constraints are largely limited to column AOD, which remains uncertain over bright or cloudy regions. To our knowledge, no foundation model has been evaluated for global dust forecasting. We develop Prithvi-Dust by adapting the NASA-IBM Prithvi WxC foundation model for short-range global dust forecasting. Dust-specific training uses post-2000 MERRA-2 data with improved aerosol observations. The model retains the pretrained backbone while adding dust-specific input and output mappings for five size-resolved dust tracers, surface and column-integrated dust mass, aerosol optical properties, and emission, sedimentation, and wet/dry deposition diagnostics. The model will evaluate dust storms and transported dust from regional to intercontinental scales. We model MERRA-2-minus-observation residuals to diagnose bias. Using meteorological states and attention- and embedding-based attribution, we rank controls on surface and vertical residuals near sources and downwind: winds, PBL height, stability, mixing, precipitation, particle size, and deposition. We examine lofting height and the persistence of dust mass in the vertical column during trans-Atlantic transport, testing whether plume-height and downwind biases reflect meteorology or errors in emissions, size distribution, dry deposition, settling, or optics/speciation. These residuals identify priorities for GEOS aerosol improvements and future aerosol and meteorological observations. We reproduce Aurora’s one-day PM₁₀ forecast of the 13 June 2022 Iraq sandstorm and compare Aurora with Prithvi-Dust across events using harmonized diagnostics of plume occurrence, location, extent, transport, and spread. Evaluation uses error, bias, spatial correlation, Threat Score, and Fractions Skill Score by lead time, size, wind, precipitation, and altitude, against satellite products, AERONET, reanalyses, persistence, and climatology. These comparisons assess how meteorology, particle size, vertical transport, and removal drive regional and altitude-dependent dust biases and uncertainty.

title: Cloud-Gap Filling of Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel-2 Reflectance with the Prithvi-EO-2.0 Foundation Model and GeoNEX GOES-16/19 Data
authors: Rajat Shinde, Weile Wang, Africa Ixmucane Flores Anderson, Brian Freitag, Kelsey E Herndon, Emil A Cherrington, Keiko Nomura, Phoebe Oduor and Matthew S Johnson
main_session: Frontiers in Biogeochemical, Ecosystem, and Earth System Modeling: Integrating AI, Data-Driven, and Process-Based Approaches I Oral
abstract: Optical satellite records underpin ecosystem monitoring, but persistent gaps from clouds and shadows limit data availability, especially over tropics and coastal zones where land-surface change is fastest. These gaps break the continuity that vegetation indices, disturbance detection, and land-cover monitoring depend on. However, classical gap-filling techniques such as nearest-clear compositing, temporal interpolation, and seasonal climatologies borrow information from other dates without a learned prior of surface appearance. Consequently, these approaches degrade during long consecutive gaps and rapid surface changes that ecosystem studies prioritize. Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) pretrained on global archives offer a different route: they reconstruct masked regions from learned spatial and temporal contexts. We adapted the NASA-IBM Prithvi-EO-2.0 (300M-parameter) GeoFM to fill cloud and shadow gaps in Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel-2 (HLS-2) 30-m surface reflectance. A learnable adapter injects same-day geostationary composites from GeoNEX GOES-16/19 data at the target step while the Prithvi backbone remains largely frozen; clear pixels pass through unchanged, and only masked pixels are reconstructed.
