In preliminary experiments across 21 scene-donor pairs representing three cloud regimes (7-58% synthetic gap coverage), reconstruction was strongest in the visible bands (SSIM 0.79-0.89) and weaker in the shortwave infrared, where a GeoNEX-to-HLS bandpass mismatch adds a systematic bias. Error grew smoothly with gap fraction (overall RMSE ~300 to ~600 in digital numbers) rather than collapsing, demonstrating that the model degrades gracefully as conditions worsen. This predictable behavior is critical for ecosystem science, where knowing when a gap-filled value can be trusted is as vital as the value itself. This presentation covers: (1) An adapter architecture to transfer geostationary context into a GeoFM (2) Preliminary per-band and per-regime reconstruction performance across globally distributed biomes Our work shows that a pretrained foundation model turns cloud-gap filling from date-borrowing interpolation into learned reconstruction from spatial and temporal context. We present this as a step toward gap-free optical records for ecosystem science.

title: Global HLS-GPT: Extending a Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) for Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) Reflectance Time-Series Reconstruction to Global Scale
authors: Hankui Zhang, Junjie Li, Shuaijun Liu, David Roy and Jilin Men
main_session: Transfer Learning in Remote Sensing: Overcoming Data Scarcity and Domain Shift I Oral
abstract: We previously introduced HLS-GPT, a single-pixel self-supervised generative pretrained Transformer (GPT) developed to reconstruct NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) 30-m surface reflectance for arbitrary dates, pixel locations, and spectral bands across the conterminous United States (CONUS). The HLS-GPT operates directly on arbitrary-length, cloud-free HLS surface reflectance time series, and reduces algorithm-induced latency to near zero by leveraging learned phenological and surface temporal dynamics. Here, we extend HLS-GPT from the CONUS to global scale. The model retains its hierarchical Transformer architecture to accommodate spectral differences between Landsat and Sentinel-2 and is modified to reduce its sensitivity to residual cloud and atmospheric-correction errors incorrectly flagged in the NASA HLS data. To build and evaluate the global model, all available HLS observations from 2015 through 2025 were extracted every 128 30-m pixels across all 186,110 global HLS 109 × 109 km tiles. All cloud-free HLS observations were extracted for more than 11 million pixel locations, of which 80% were used for training and 20% were reserved for testing. During training, 12-month periods with randomly selected start dates were considered at each pixel location, 50% of valid observations were randomly masked, and the model was trained to reconstruct their reflectance from the remaining observations. For each pixel location and epoch, this procedure was repeated 10 times, using one randomly selected start date in each year from 2015 through 2024. The surface reflectance reconstruction is demonstrated over diverse conditions, including regions with complex crop phenology, persistent clouds, temporally irregular HLS observations, and regions with different phenology to the CONUS. The reconstruction accuracy is quantified using leave-one-observation-out and more stringent random-masking strategies. The results demonstrate robust global scale daily multispectral HLS surface reflectance reconstruction.

title: Evaluating Prithvi-EO-2.0 for Plot-Scale Corn Yield Prediction Using UAS Imagery
authors: Naiem Sheikh, Oklahoma State University, Department of Geography, Stillwater, United States, Yuting Zhou, Oklahoma State University, Geography, Stillwater, OK, United States, Huihui Zhang, USDA ARS, Fort Collins, United States and Pradeep Wagle, USDA-ARS, Grazinglands Research Laboratory, El Reno, United States
main_session: Transfer Learning in Remote Sensing: Overcoming Data Scarcity and Domain Shift II Poster
abstract: Whether geospatial foundation models trained on 30 m satellite imagery can provide useful representations for centimeter-scale unmanned aircraft system (UAS) applications remains an open question. We evaluated this question for corn ( Zea mays L.) yield prediction across an entire growing season by comparing Prithvi-EO-2.0, a geospatial foundation model designed for Earth Observation, with a task-specific Gradient Boosting model under identical imagery, spectral inputs, and train/test splits. Multispectral UAS imagery collected on eight flight dates during the 2023 growing season at a USDA-ARS field site in Greeley, Colorado, was used to predict corn yield under full and deficit irrigation. Both models used the same four spectral bands (Blue, Green, Red, and Near-infra-Red). Across all flight dates, Prithvi achieved a higher test R² than Gradient Boosting (0.71 vs. 0.63) and outperformed it at each flight date under both irrigation regimes. Prithvi's R² ranged from 0.61 to 0.74 across dates, compared with 0.51 to 0.70 for Gradient Boosting. Notably, Gradient Boosting produced negative R² under full irrigation on two dates, whereas Prithvi remained predictive throughout the season. These results demonstrate that a satellite-pretrained geospatial foundation model generates effective predictive features for UAS-based corn yield prediction without fine-tuning. This underscores the potential of foundation models for transferring information across spatial scales, while highlighting the need to further evaluate the individual contributions of pretrained representations, spatial heterogeneity, and model architecture to overall predictive power.

title: Domain Adaptation of the Prithvi-EO-2.0 Foundation Model for Inland Water Remote Sensing
authors: Naveen Kumar Purushothaman, Hongxing Liu, Yuehan Lu, Runlong Yu, Christopher A Impellitteri, Jilin Men, Dan Tian, Ekaterina Miliutina, Anindya Palaparthi and Amanjit Premsagar
main_session: From Satellites to Solutions: Advancing Water Management with Applied Earth Observations III Poster
abstract: Large-scale Earth observation foundation model NASA–IBM’s Prithvi-EO-2.0 has been pretrained on terabyte-scale archives of global Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery and have demonstrated strong generalization across a wide range of terrestrial remote-sensing tasks. However, their applicability to inland water-quality monitoring remains largely unexplored. The Prithvi-EO-2.0 pretrained model is dominated by terrestrial land-cover types and its input imagery is produced using an atmospheric-correction algorithm primarily optimized for land targets. Consequently, the learned encoder representations may not adequately characterize the weak, spectrally subtle, and optically complex water-leaving reflectance signals of inland lakes and reservoirs. We present a domain-adaptation framework that extends the self-supervised masked-autoencoder pretraining of Prithvi-EO-2.0 using water-dominated imagery, thereby shifting its learned representations toward the inland aquatic domain. The HLS image chips are extracted globally over lakes and reservoirs identified using the JRC Global Surface Water dataset. The imagery is then reprocessed with ACOLITE, an atmospheric-correction algorithm designed for optically complex Case-2 waters, to generate water-leaving reflectance inputs that more accurately represent aquatic optical signals. The resulting water-adapted encoder is evaluated against the original Prithvi-EO-2.0 encoder using reconstruction accuracy for held-out water scenes and embedding-space analyses such as cluster separability along trophic-state and turbidity gradients. These analyses serve as proxies for representation quality before the encoder is applied to downstream supervised retrieval tasks. We hypothesize that continued pretraining on ACOLITE-corrected, water-only imagery will produce representations that more effectively capture the spectral and temporal variability of inland waters than the original land-dominated encoder. The adapted model is therefore expected to provide a stronger and more reusable backbone for future multi-parameter water-quality retrieval applications. The domain-adapted encoder will be released publicly to support the broader development of foundation-model applications in inland water remote sensing.

title: Leveraging Temporal Prithvi-EO-2.0 Efficiently for Locating Fallow Fields Across Heterogeneous Agricultural Landscapes with True Multi-scale Features.
authors: Sk Muhammad Asif and Orhun Aydin, Saint Louis University, Earth, Environmental and Geospatial Science, Saint Louis, United States
main_session: Transfer Learning in Remote Sensing: Overcoming Data Scarcity and Domain Shift II Poster
abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of fallow land is important for optimizing the food-water (FW) nexus, given fallowing’s role in crop rotation and water conservation. Fallow is a low-accuracy class in the USDA Cropland Data Layer (CDL). Geospatial Foundation Model can be highly effective in detecting fallow objects, but existing approaches suffer from the absence of true multi-scale features required by object detection heads. We evaluate a fallow detection scenario using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), with temporal Prithvi-EO-2 as the backbone, deformable-detr as the detection head, and the introduction of true multi-scale features. Our results achieve a map@50 of 0.72 for Sentinel-2 imagery, revealing a 10% improvement over HLS imagery for the same band combination and demonstrating the superiority of higher resolution in fallow object detection. The results also demonstrate that lightweight spatial-prior fusion and temporal enrichment facilitate more effective capture of local fallow patterns across vast regions, outperforming approaches that rely on reshaped single-stride ViT tokens and a spatial-only approach. Our study shows that spatio-temporal foundation models with multi-scale feature introduction handle geographical differences effectively and locate fallow distribution crucial for understanding water-food tradeoffs.

title: Integrating WOFOST, HLS, and Crop Maps to Generate 30 m PACE Hyperspectral Time Series
authors: Leonid Shumilo, Sergii Skakun, Natacha Kalecinski and Mohammad Abdul Qadir Khan
main_session: Advances in Aquatic, Atmospheric, and Terrestrial Science with NASA's PACE Mission I Poster
abstract: Hyperspectral satellite observations provide detailed information on crop biochemical and biophysical conditions, but the relatively coarse spatial resolution of current sensors limits their application to field-scale agricultural monitoring. This study develops a neural network–based framework for generating PACE hyperspectral time-series data at 30 m spatial resolution and harmonizing them with Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) observations. The approach combines optical satellite data with crop-specific biophysical information derived from process-based crop-growth modeling. Daily crop-growth characteristics are generated using the geospatially interpolated World Food Studies (WOFOST) model implemented within the Crop Growth Monitoring System (CGMS). The model provides spatially and temporally explicit estimates of crop development and biophysical variables describing the condition and accumulation of dry and wet biomass. These WOFOST-derived variables are combined with cloud-free HLS multispectral observations, PACE hyperspectral measurements, and crop-type information. The different data sources are merged at the feature level within a neural network architecture. HLS reflectance and WOFOST-derived crop biophysical characteristics are used as explanatory input features, while coincident PACE observations provide the hyperspectral reference information required for model training. The trained network estimates PACE-like hyperspectral reflectance at the 30 m spatial resolution of HLS, producing spatially detailed and temporally consistent hyperspectral measurements harmonized with HLS data. Agricultural areas in Kansas, United States, were chosen as the test site for this framework with separate model simulations for winter wheat and maize. The resulting high-resolution hyperspectral time series are intended to support improved field-scale assessment of crop development, biomass condition, and stress, to expand the potential of PACE observations for agricultural monitoring, and harmonization of multimodal satellite data.

title: Multi-Sensor Machine Learning Classification of Tornado Damage Using HLS-2 and Sentinel-1 Data
authors: ABSTRACT WITHDRAWN
main_session: From Detection to Decision: Environmental and Societal Impacts of Disaster and Conflict in the Era of AI and New Earth Observation I Poster
abstract: A robust tornado climatology is an indispensable tool for understanding the mechanisms surrounding tornadogenesis and tornado dynamics. In the United States, the National Weather Service (NWS) maintains a tornado climatology based on ground surveys of tornado damage conducted by NWS personnel. Surveyors use the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale to rate tornado data in six classes, from EF0 (lowest) to EF5 (highest). The overall strength of the tornado is rated based on the highest classification within its path, and contours can be drawn along its path to give a more continuous representation of intensity. While the existing climatology is incredibly useful, staffing constraints, underreporting, land access issues, and other practical considerations mean that it is incomplete. Future climatologies could be improved by the development of remote sensing-based classification algorithms. Previous work has identified satellite remote sensing, including optical imagery as well as synthetic aperture radar (SAR), as being useful for the detection and classification of tornado damage but with highly variable results by land cover. Machine learning algorithms have also proven to be a useful tool for remotely sensed data towards classifying tornado damage. However, few studies have utilized a large sample of tornado events in their training and testing datasets, limiting performance and generalizability. The present study expanded upon previous literature by leveraging cloud computing resources (Google Earth Engine) to train a new random-forest based damage classification model on a large number of tornado occurrences (n > 2000) that occurred within CONUS between 2016-2025. These are the tornados that were entered into the NWS Damage Assessment Toolkit with nested contours of damage that distinguish within-track variation. The model used predictor variables from the Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) dataset for optical and infrared indices as well as Sentinel-1 SAR data. The nearest usable images from before and after the storm were differenced to best capture tornado induced change. Model performance was evaluated using an independent validation dataset. The results highlight the value of multi-sensor integration and suggest that future results can be improved by leveraging data from additional sensors.

title: Applying Autonomous Research Trajectory Optimizations for Science (ARTOS) to Climate Downscaling with NASA’s Prithvi-WxC Foundation Model
authors: Hugo Lee, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, CA, United States, Aashish Panta, University of Utah, computer science, Salt Lake City, United States and Sudhanshu Pandey, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, United States
main_session: Machine Learning, AI, and Emerging Methods to Advance Climate Science III Poster
abstract: Developing reliable regional climate downscaling with foundation models requires more than optimizing a stand-alone machine learning model. Performance depends on coupled choices in predictors, decoder architecture, loss functions, and evaluation. We present the application of Autonomous Research Trajectory Optimizations for Science (ARTOS) to downscaling with NASA’s Prithvi-WxC foundation model. Rather than automating a predetermined pipeline, ARTOS conducts a self-pruning search over hypotheses for mapping coarse atmospheric states to high-resolution precipitation and temperature. Under scientist-defined objectives, permitted data, validation demands, and scoring rubrics, a proposer agent chooses the next untested hypothesis. An execution agent runs a bounded, reproducible fine-tuning and inference experiment and produces metrics and plots; a quality-assurance reviewer checks data integrity, physical plausibility, and overclaiming; and an advisor agent scores novelty, correctness, and scientific significance. A ratcheting controller retains experiments that improve the research state and reverts failed or lower-value branches, while durable memory records configurations, outcomes, and next questions. We apply this loop to predictor subsets, high-resolution orography, selection of pretrained layers, decoder and loss-function design, and sampling strategies. Candidate trajectories are assessed using climate-relevant diagnostics, including climatology, extremes, spatial variability, distributions, and climate-change signals. The strongest evidence is assembled into figures and scientific narratives, challenged through adversarial review, and evaluated by researchers, who retain authority over interpretation and claims. By separating machine-led search from human-led scientific judgment, ARTOS can accelerate multistep hypothesis and scenario analysis while preserving reproducibility, provenance, and physical scrutiny. The framework moves beyond workflow automation toward evidence-driven development of reliable high-resolution climate information for risk assessment and resilience planning.

title: Evaluating the suitability of GDAS ancillary products for Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) atmospheric correction
authors: Eric Vermote, Trang Vo, Madhu Sridhar, Junchang Ju, Qiang Zhou, Christopher S R Neigh and Pontus Olofsson, PhD
main_session: Improving Science Data Processing Through Modern Science Data Systems II Poster
abstract: The Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) project produces global surface reflectance products from NASA’s Landsat-8/9 and ESA’s Sentinel-2A/B/C satellites at 30 m spatial resolution at a high temporal frequency of 2-3 days on a global average. A crucial processing step within the HLS processing flow is atmospheric correction, which converts top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance to surface reflectance. HLS uses the Land Surface Reflectance Code (LaSRC) algorithm to perform atmospheric correction on Level-1 input data from both Landsat and Sentinel-2 sensors. Currently, HLS processing relies on ancillary ozone and water vapor input data from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) Level-3 products; this dependence makes atmospheric correction the primary limiting factor in the current at-best HLS latency of 2-3 days. The HLS-Low Latency (HLS-LL) from the Satellite Needs Working Group (SNWG) Cycle 4 solutions aims to produce global HLS data with a six hour latency to benefit agricultural monitoring, wildfire, and flood response. A potential data source that could be utilized for HLS-LL data production is the Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) water vapor and ozone dataset . This study aims to report the feasibility of using these products for atmospheric correction with LaSRC and their effects on HLS L30 and S30 data quality using a diverse global evaluation dataset. A comprehensive comparison of the VIIRS- and GDAS-based surface reflectance outputs will be presented for all HLS spectral bands.

title: High-Frequency Global Ocean Surface Current Forecasting Using Prithvi-WxC and an Altimetry-Based SSH Emulator
authors: Luyu Sun, James Carton, Ligang Chen, Samuel Carton and Stephen G Penny
main_session: AI-Driven Ocean Modeling, Inverse Problems, and Data Assimilation: Advances in Data, Methods, and Applications IV Poster
abstract: Sub-daily ocean surface-current forecasts are critical for marine navigation and emergency response, yet the predictability of rapidly evolving currents remains poorly understood. Conventional forecasting systems are constrained by computational cost, data-assimilation latency, and temporal smoothing of mesoscale features. We ask whether a hybrid AI-physics framework can recover six-hourly surface-current variability and identify the dominant sources of forecast error across dynamical regimes and lead times. Our framework combines atmospheric forcing from NASA’s Prithvi-WxC Earth foundation model, an altimetry-based sea-surface-height (SSH) forecast emulator, physics-based estimates of geostrophic and wind-driven currents, and an explicit tidal-current component. The SSH emulator is trained on DASH1.0, a multidecadal 0.25° global daily SSH dataset derived from satellite altimeter observations. Forecast experiments target energetic regimes in the Gulf Stream and Agulhas Current at lead times from 6 to 48 h. Controlled replacement experiments isolate errors arising from SSH evolution, atmospheric forcing, and wind-stress estimation and trace their propagation into total surface-current forecasts. Preliminary results show that the SSH emulator preserves the evolution of large-scale SSH gradients and tracks mesoscale eddy displacement across forecast lead times. Forecast degradation varies strongly by dynamical regime, with the greatest sensitivity in energetic boundary currents and regions of rapid eddy propagation. Wind-driven and tidal components are included to represent sub-daily variability that cannot be recovered from geostrophic currents alone. The integrated system will produce global, six-hourly surface-current forecasts at lead times from 0 to 48 h. Forecast skill will be evaluated against gridded analyses, surface drifters, high-frequency radar, and routing-based metrics. This study provides a process-oriented assessment of where hybrid AI–physics forecasting adds skill, where predictability is lost, and how atmospheric foundation models and ocean emulators can be improved for decision-relevant ocean prediction.

title: Multi-Temporal Automated Mapping of Agricultural Hail and Wind Damage Swaths Using Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 Observations
authors: Andrew Molthan, Hannah G Pankratz, Alexander Melancon, Jordan R Bell and William Blaine Horn
main_session: From Detection to Decision: Environmental and Societal Impacts of Disaster and Conflict in the Era of AI and New Earth Observation III Oral
abstract: Mapping storm damage to agricultural areas is critical for disaster management and quantifying economic impacts. The Hail and Wind Damage Swath (HWDS) database consists of hand-drawn polygons generated from 20 years of Terra and Aqua MODIS optical imagery. These polygons outlined sudden surface changes in agricultural areas caused by thunderstorm-driven winds and hail, validated against National Weather Service warnings, public damage reports, and weather radar data. The original intent of the HWDS database was to document damage frequency, spatial distribution, and post-event detection latency to set the stage for automated processing. The availability of Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) at 30 m spatial resolution allows for more surface features to be discerned, enhancing the ability to map fine-scale elements across eight multispectral bands. From a subset of 72 MODIS HWDS events, cloud-free HLS imagery was acquired over a 14-day post-event window. Using the best HLS data within that window and ancillary data, over 30 additional swaths were identified , demonstrating the enhanced level of detail provided by 30 m observations. This work explores automated approaches to detect and assess HWDS impacts from HLS across varying temporal inputs and analytical methods: 1) localized anomaly thresholding using a single post-event image; 2) pre- and post-event composite differencing (+/- 14-day window); and 3) multi-feature random forest classification. The same HLS labels were then used to fine-tune geospatial foundation models (FMs), TerraMind and Prithvi, using a single post-event image to generate preliminary damage estimates. Accuracy metrics will be presented for each approach, with early results showing that composite differencing across longer temporal windows yielded higher agreement with ground truth labels. By comparing more traditional threshold and difference-based approaches against random forest and fine-tuned applications of FMs, this project highlights the strengths and limitations of each approach while identifying pathways for operational, near real-time deployment.

title: Progress on Integrating EMIT Spaceborne Imaging Spectroscopy Derived Snow Property Maps into Operational Workflows and Decision Making for Water Resources
authors: Brenton Wilder, Urs Bohn, Maggie Johnson, Joachim Meyer, Benjamin Roberts-Pierel, Ross Palomaki, Karl Rittger, Edward Bair, Niklas Griessbaum, Philip G Brodrick, David R Thompson, Robert O Green, Carrie Vuyovich, Thomas H Painter and Matthew Meadows
main_session: Interagency Session on Leveraging Geospatial Data for Integrated Water Risk and Water Resource Management in the American West Poster
abstract: The Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source InvesTigation (EMIT) spectrometer offers the capability to greatly reduce retrieval uncertainties in derived snow albedo maps compared to multispectral sensors due to hundreds of spectral channels and excellent signal-to-noise ratio. However, there are several technical challenges that impede immediate adoption in an operational context, including sparse temporal coverage, large data volumes, and implementations of current operational models. Our research sets out to bridge the gaps by incorporating these high-fidelity observations into established operational workflows and datasets. We present ongoing efforts to ingest fused snow products (e.g., VIIRS, HLS) improved by EMIT into the iSnobal energy balance model using the JPL-STARS data fusion algorithm. This project is facilitated by direct collaborations with the Kings River Water Association (KRWA), M3Works, and the Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO). Through co-developed workflows with our research partners, we are integrating EMIT data into production codes to ease operational adoption, yielding positive improvements in forecast skill within the Kings River watershed. Additionally, we discuss our collaboration with the SnowToday team at the Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research; their product serves a wide user base by supplying timely information on radiative forcing, impurity concentration, fractional snow cover, and snow albedo derived from daily VIIRS and MODIS observations. In this capacity, high-quality EMIT observations serve as a complementary dataset – similar to ASO imaging spectroscopy – for the verification and/or fusion of daily multispectral products. While future global imaging spectroscopy missions like EAGLE-VSWIR and CHIME will be more frequent than EMIT, they still may miss daily snow metamorphism and episodic dust events. Therefore, from an operational perspective, there will always be a strong need for advancing machine learning and data fusion methods to best represent snow surface properties at a timestep of interest by leveraging daily data (e.g., VIIRS). Our investigation supports this need, offering critical guidance and lessons learned for leveraging spaceborne imaging spectroscopy within operational workflows in the coming decades.

title: Spatial Structure of Disagreement Between Operational Fire Perimeters and Satellite Change Maps in 2026 California-Origin Wildfires
authors: Yeon-Jun Kim, University of Seoul, Department of Geoinformatics, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South); University of Seoul, Data Science Interdisciplinary Major, Seoul, South Korea and Hyung-Sup Jung, University of Seoul, Department of Geoinformatics, Seoul, South Korea
main_session: Wildfire Analysis Using Remote Sensing, Multisensor Fusion, Multisource Data Integration, and Artificial Intelligence I Poster
abstract: Operational fire perimeters define incident envelopes, whereas satellite change maps represent spatial variation in fire effects. Whether their differences occur mainly as isolated interior patches, narrow edge offsets, or spatially deep, boundary-connected zones is unresolved for recent events. We examined the complete cohort of eight 2026 fires with California points of origin meeting prespecified Wildland Fire Interagency Geospatial Services criteria at the 18 September data freeze: approved visible perimeters, at least 5,000 GIS acres, and 100% containment (942.6 km² total). Pre- and post-fire Sentinel-2 pairs followed training-consistent surface-reflectance scaling, HLS v2 bandpass adjustment, common-grid resampling, cloud and shadow masking, and checkpoint normalization. We applied a fixed three-seed Prithvi ensemble adapted from 30 m HLS pretraining to six-band Sentinel-2 inputs on a 10 m analysis grid and fine-tuned on 2024-2025 California data, without 2026 retraining, event-specific thresholds, or postprocessing. Neither WFIGS nor the model map was treated as pixel-level ground truth. Perimeter-map intersection over union ranged from 0.487 to 0.933. In six of eight events, boundary-connected components comprised most perimeter-only area; across all eight, their median contribution was 68.8%. Within those components, a median 44.3% of pixels lay more than 250 m inside the perimeter and 28.6% lay beyond 500 m, showing that the disagreement was not solely a thin perimeter fringe. Post-fire normalized burn ratio and its pre-to-post difference were scaled within each event between unchanged exterior pixels (0) and jointly mapped burned pixels (1). Deep boundary-connected zones had spectral signatures ranging from exterior-like to burned-like (event median 0.348); Rock's deep zone lay near the exterior anchor, whereas the deep zone in Lost exceeded the agreement-burned anchor. Thus, the same spatial form did not correspond to one spectral class, and the observed disagreement could not be represented as a uniform cartographic fringe. Across this complete cohort, the spatial depth and spectral variability of disagreement reveal two distinct records of fire extent: operational incident-envelope geometry and spectrally expressed surface change.

title: A Remote Sensing Framework for Improving Crop Residue Burning Emissions in Greenhouse Gas and Emissions Inventories
authors: Joanne Hall, Jessica McCarty, Michele L Reba, Nathan Torbick, Lindsay Barbieri and Louis Giglio
main_session: Integrated Approaches for Quantifying and Modeling Greenhouse Gas, Soil Carbon, and Trace Gas Fluxes Across Natural and Working Lands I Oral
abstract: Crop residue burning is a poorly quantified source of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Despite representing ~10% of annual global burned area (BA), cropland fires are underrepresented in GHG inventories. Limited crop-type information further complicates estimates because combustion characteristics, residue availability, and emission coefficients vary among agricultural systems. Further, recent growth in soil health programs and climate-smart initiatives are driving changes in management practices, such as no or reduced tillage, which amplifies uncertainty in cropland burning inventories. Improving both the spatial representation of crop residue burning and crop-specific emissions is therefore critical for developing more accurate, transparent, and reproducible emissions estimates. This study presents advances in the Global Cropland Area Burned (GloCAB) dataset, the first global remote sensing product for crop residue burning. GloCAB V1.0 provided monthly 0.25° BA estimates (2002–2022) by combining active fires with crop-specific BA conversion factors from >190,000 reference fields across five countries. Annual cropland BA averages ~81 Mha, more than double widely used global BA products, with implications for GHG emissions estimates. Building on this, we are collaborating with stakeholders, including the US EPA, California Air Resources Board, and GHGIA, to integrate updated crop-type BA and emissions estimates into modeling frameworks that support national inventories and international reporting. Ongoing research extends beyond BA mapping to characterize management practices that affect emissions, including post-burn tillage, sugarcane green harvesting, and orchard and vineyard pile burning. This includes fusing moderate- and high-resolution optical and SAR time-series observations, such as HLS, NISAR, and PlanetScope, using a suite of Geo-AI architectures and physical retrievals of cropland parameters (biomass, residue cover, calendar, tillage practices). Incorporating these land management practices into emissions estimation frameworks will improve representation of agricultural carbon dynamics, enhance spatio-temporal resolutions, and provide more policy-relevant information for GHG inventories, mitigation assessments, and sustainable land management.

title: Beyond Fair-Weather AI: AI and Foundation Model Based Approaches for Wildfire Chemistry and Air Quality Prediction
authors: Aishwarya Raman, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, CA, United States, Matthew S Johnson, Earth Science Division, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, CA, United States, Clayton Elder, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, United States, Jonathan Gee, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, United States, Yash Diggikar, Organization Not Listed, Washington, DC, United States, Sujit Roy, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, United States, Milton Halem, University of Maryland Baltimore County, Computer Science, Baltimore, MD, United States, Shobha Kondragunta, NOAA/NESDIS/Center for Satellite Applications and Research, College Park, United States, Amy K Huff, Pennsylvania State Univ, University Park, PA, United States, Hai Zhang, IMSG, College Park, MD, United States, Pubu Ciren, IMSG, College Park, United States and Patrick Richard Rea, Booz Allen Hamilton DC, Washington, United States
main_session: Practical AI for Wildfire Science I Oral
abstract: Accurate wildfire pollutant predictions near fires and downwind are vital for emergency responders and air-quality managers. Chemical transport models (CTMs) provide alerts but demand large runtimes, are not observationally constrained operationally, and cannot easily assimilate satellite air-quality data. Recent neural networks that predict smoke PM2.5 and ozone precursors run far faster than CTMs, but are not stress-tested across the varied conditions of different wildfires, and gaps persist in validating and automating them for state-agency use. Most neural networks and transformer-based models hold out scattered wildfire days, not entire events, measuring interpolation within a known regime rather than transfer to unseen fires; most target single events or subregions, not CONUS-wide variability. Some output PM2.5, others NO2 or O3. None has been benchmarked to output all wildfire-relevant chemistry and stress-tested under real-time fire conditions for runtime, skill, and the balance among species, chemistry, and meteorology. We address these gaps in two parts. First, using an event-holdout protocol across CONUS, we stress-test ML column-to-surface translation for aerosols (AOD to PM2.5), NO2, and O3 under wildfire versus non-fire conditions leveraging TEMPO against AERONET and surface networks to identify where column retrievals poorly constrain surface air quality across boundary-layer regimes and diurnal cycles, toward validated, automated tools for disaster response. Second, we introduce Prithvi-AQ: a regionally trained air-quality foundation model extending Prithvi-WxC via EPA EQUATES (12 km CMAQ/MCIP), predicting CO, O3, SO2, NO2, and elemental carbon. Because global foundation models can relax wildfire plumes toward background and lose photochemical consistency, we test whether Prithvi-AQ's fire chemistry is self-consistent and assess whether CO/EC and O3 covary coherently with observed PM2.5 and compare meteorological foundation models for fire-relevant meteorology. Together, these results map what AI can and cannot yet deliver for wildfire air quality: column-to-surface models degrade where smoke breaks their fair-weather assumptions, and a regional foundation model helps only insofar as its fire chemistry stays physically consistent.

title: Zooming In on Urban Heat: AI Downscaling Across Observational Modalities
authors: Maria J Molina, Jonathan Starfeldt, Ayman Sayed and Tiana Rabemanantsoa
main_session: Downscaling Weather and Climate: Development and Evaluation of Methods, Products, and Applications II Oral
abstract: Downscaling weather information to finer spatial scales is critical for making model and observational products actionable in real-world decision-making. However, developing reliable downscaling methods requires combining datasets with fundamentally different spatial and temporal sampling characteristics. Here, we present Urban Heat MiniCubes, an AI-ready dataset designed to support super-resolution and cross-modal learning for urban heat applications. The dataset integrates complementary satellite observations, including fine-spatial-resolution measurements from polar-orbiting Landsat and Sentinel-1 satellites and frequent, coarser-resolution observations from the geostationary GOES-R satellite series and passive microwave radiometers. We demonstrate how this harmonized dataset supports two approaches to translating coarse-resolution satellite observations into locally relevant information. The first estimates 2-m air temperature at weather-station locations from gridded GOES brightness temperatures. The second leverages the NASA–IBM Prithvi-EOv2 foundation model to learn mappings between coarse-resolution GOES observations and fine-resolution Landsat observations. The distinct challenges associated with point-based and gridded downscaling will be discussed, including mismatched spatiotemporal sampling. Together, these applications illustrate both the potential and limitations of multimodal AI for producing actionable urban heat information across spatial scales.

title: Parameter-Efficient Modality Extension of Geospatial Foundation Models via a Spectral Vision Adapter for SAR–Optical Flood and Forest Biomass Estimation
authors: Olivia Morgan Alexander, Sujit Roy, Ata Akbari Asanjan, Disha Shidham, Besart Mujeci, Soumya Ranjan, David Bell, Manil Maskey and Rahul Ramachandran
main_session: AI Foundation Models for Earth, Space, and Planetary Sciences I Oral
abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) have emerged in recent years as a powerful paradigm for Earth observation, pretrained on large satellite datasets and adapted to diverse downstream mapping tasks. Despite these rapid advancements, no single GFM is state-of-the-art across all tasks, and each is limited by its fixed set of pretrained input modalities. Extending a GFM to a new modality typically demands expensive multimodal pretraining from scratch, prompting interest in parameter-efficient ways to introduce new modalities for downstream fine-tuning. Here we introduce a parameter-efficient spectral vision adapter that injects multiscale convolutional SAR radar features into a frozen optical GFM through cross-attention and optional spectral (frequency-domain) gating. The adapter leaves the pretrained transformer backbone unchanged, training roughly 65M parameters, about one-fifth the size of the ~302M frozen backbone. We attach the adapter to Prithvi-EO 2.0 and compare against the frozen Prithvi backbone and TerraMind, a multimodally pretrained GFM. We evaluate two SAR-optical dense-prediction tasks: flood segmentation on UrbanSARFloods-Optical and above-ground forest biomass estimation on BioMassters. For flooding, the spectral vision adapter reaches 0.7459 IoU, compared to TerraMind's 0.6996. The frozen optical backbone (0.7043), a low-rank (LoRA) control (0.7068), and TerraMind (0.6996) cluster within 0.01 IoU of one another, while the adapter exceeds all three by 0.04 IoU. For biomass estimation, the spectral vision adapter lowers RMSE to 37.74 t/ha, versus 38.50 for TerraMind. Robustness and label-efficiency probes indicate that the adapter learns task-relevant SAR structure around the optical backbone. These results show that a vision adapter can extend a unimodal optical GFM to a new modality, matching or exceeding a multimodal model pretrained on that modality, without any multimodal pretraining, offering an efficient path to modality extension for operational Earth observation.

title: CORDEX-ML-Bench: First Results From a Community Benchmark for Data-Driven Regional Climate Downscaling
authors: Hugo Lee, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, CA, United States and Neelesh Rampal, Earth Sciences New Zealand, Auckland, New Zealand
main_session: Downscaling Weather and Climate: Development and Evaluation of Methods, Products, and Applications II Oral
abstract: Machine learning (ML) offers an efficient complement to dynamical downscaling, but comparisons remain difficult because studies use different datasets, domains, training protocols, and metrics. We present CORDEX-ML-Bench, the first coordinated multi-domain benchmark for data-driven regional climate downscaling. The benchmark maps 2° atmospheric predictors to daily maximum temperature and precipitation at approximately 10 km over the European Alps, New Zealand, and Southern Africa. We evaluate 40 configurations spanning traditional ML, U-Nets, vision transformers, graph neural networks, the Prithvi-WxC foundation model, and generative adversarial, diffusion, and flow-matching methods. A perfect-model design, with predictors coarsened from the target regional climate model, compares historical-only empirical-statistical downscaling with regional climate model emulation trained on historical and future climates. Evaluation covers daily error, climatology, extremes, spatial spectra, distributions, interannual variability, and climate-change signals. Across the benchmark, generative approaches generally achieve the strongest performance for precipitation, particularly in representing extremes and fine-scale spatial variability, whereas deterministic architectures remain competitive for maximum temperature. The results also demonstrate that daily RMSE alone is insufficient to characterize downscaling skill and that models trained exclusively on historical climates tend to underestimate future changes in temperature and precipitation extremes. We also briefly highlight results from Prithvi-UNet, the benchmark’s only foundation-model-based approach, which combines selective fine-tuning of NASA’s Prithvi-WxC model with a convolutional U-Net decoder. Prithvi-UNet reproduces the broad spatial patterns of temperature extremes, and its representation of mid-century temperature-change signals improves substantially when training includes both historical and future climate states. These findings illustrate the potential of weather and climate foundation models for regional downscaling while underscoring the importance of standardized, multi-metric, and extrapolation-focused evaluation for guiding future model development.

title: GeoFoundation model embeddings improve carbon fluxes modeling at heterogeneous FLUXNET sites
authors: Weijie Zhang, Climate and Ecosystem Sciences Division, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, United States; University of California Berkeley, Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management, Berkeley, CA, United States, Wantong Li, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, United States; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Climate and Ecosystem Sciences Division, Berkeley, United States, Vitus Benson, Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry, Jena, Germany, Ando Shah, University of California Berkeley, School of Information, Berkeley, CA, United States; Allen Institute for AI, Seattle, United States and Trevor Keenan, University of California, Berkeley, Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management, Berkeley, United States
main_session: AI Foundation Models for Earth, Space, and Planetary Sciences I Oral
abstract: Accurate ecosystem carbon-flux prediction requires land-surface representations that adequately capture ecosystem state. Current state-of-the-art systems rely primarily on variants of spectral vegetation indices, yet these are insufficient to fully capture the spatial variation of ecosystem states. This limitation can be especially important in heterogeneous landscapes (e.g., Savannas) or during periods when canopy conditions are not fully represented by greenness-based metrics alone. In order to unravel the potential of multi-spectral remote sensing images based geospatial foundation models (i.e., Prithvi-EO-2) in addressing this limitation, we here fuse geospatial foundation model embeddings for data-driven carbon-flux modelling for the period of 2017–2024. Specifically, we examine several feature combinations, including meteorological variables, vegetation indices, and foundation model embeddings, to predict ecosystem carbon fluxes (net ecosystem exchange, gross primary productivity, and ecosystem respiration). We find that geo-foundation model embeddings improve the carbon flux prediction mostly during growing seasons and at heterogeneous sites. However, embeddings only become effective when paired with meteorological forcing. These results establish geospatial foundation-model embeddings as promising predictors for ecosystem carbon flux modelling.

title: What’s in a pixel? Contextualizing observations for multimodal data reuse and interoperability in the tropics
authors: Kelsey Susanne Huelsman, Organization Not Listed, Washington, DC, United States, Natalia Leonor Quinteros Casaverde, City University of New York & The New York Botanical Garden, Biology, New York, United States, Yoseline Angel, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, United States, Dhruva Kathuria, Morgan State University/NASA GSFC, GESTAR II, Greenbelt, United States, Kit Lewers, University of Colorado Boulder, Loveland, COLORADO, UNITED STATES, Andres Baresch, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, United States and Dr. Shawn Serbin, BA, MS, PhD, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Environmental Science and Technologies Department, Upton, United States
main_session: Vegetation Detection, Characterization, and Monitoring Through Multisensor Remote Sensing and Data Fusion Techniques I Oral
abstract: The infrastructure devoted to long-term monitoring efforts in Panama provides a unique opportunity to leverage existing functional, structural, and spectral data in current analyses. Interoperability is possible when these multi-modal, multi-scale observations adhere to standards that capture their context in both a machine- and human-interpretable way. We demonstrate the process of contextualizing in situ measurements using the DarwinCore data standard, which is used broadly, including by the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF). Because the measurements include leaf spectroscopy, chemistry, and photosynthetic function, capturing the diurnal, seasonal, climatic, and phylogenetic context all serve to elucidate within-species trait and functional plasticity patterns. Using four different multi- and hyperspectral remote sensing products (EMIT, harmonized Landsat-Sentinel, and AVIRIS), we create a multimodal, multiscale timeseries of a seasonal dry forest canopy in Parque Natural Metropolitano in Panama City, Panama. Each product provides a complementary level of spatial (resolution of 1m, 30m, and 60m), temporal, or spectral detail to enable the detection of deciduousness; spatial resolutions range from 1m to 60m. Independent snapshots likely do not capture seasonal deciduousness dynamics, but the fusion of the snapshots into a time series unlocks spatiotemporal potential in modeling and monitoring efforts.

title: From Canopy Moisture Loss to Greenness Decline: Climatic Controls on Autumn Phenology in the West Midlands, UK
authors: Naya Desai, Emma Ferranti, Sarah Greenham, Joshua Vande Hey and Andrew Quinn
main_session: Vegetation Dynamics and Land-Atmosphere Interactions I Oral
abstract: Vegetation phenology is a key mediator of land-atmosphere coupling, regulating exchanges of water and energy that shape boundary-layer development and hydroclimate variability. However, the onset of autumn vegetation decline, a critical transition in this coupling, remains comparatively understudied, particularly how canopy moisture dynamics may signal shifts in evapotranspiration and surface-atmosphere exchange before visible senescence. Therefore, this study investigates autumn vegetation decline and its climatic controls across the West Midlands, UK, including Birmingham from 2018-2023. This study leverages harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 data to quantify vegetation greenness (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index; NDVI) and canopy moisture (Normalized Difference Moisture Index; NDMI). Phenological onset and maximum rate of decline (MRD) dates were extracted via Seasonal and Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) combined with hybrid derivative and threshold methods. Subsequently, these metrics were linked to HadUK-Grid climate observations and UK soil moisture maps using lagged and partial correlation analysis, linear models, and generalized additive modelling (GAM) to understand the controls for vegetation health decline. Results reveal NDMI decline onset preceded NDVI decline onset by 9-17 days, indicating that canopy moisture loss emerges before visible greenness decline, thereby demonstrating implications for land-surface energy partitioning. Monthly GAMs explained the majority of variance in onset timing (R² = 0.951 NDVI, 0.938 NDMI), with onset retaining climatic memory from temperature and vapour pressure conditions up to three months prior. Conversely, MRD GAMs (R² = 0.915 NDVI, 0.86 NDMI) were governed by near-term atmospheric conditions. These results reveal a shift from longer-term climatic memory to stronger near-term atmospheric control as decline accelerates. The Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is now being applied to resolve these sub-daily land-atmosphere interactions. Ultimately, by identifying canopy moisture decline as an early indicator and distinguishing antecedent from near-term climatic drivers, this study contributes to improved prediction and modelling of vegetation-atmosphere feedbacks under the changing climate.

title: Embedding-Guided Active Learning for Label-Efficient Mangrove Habitat Monitoring Across Space and Time
authors: Denys Godwin, Clark University, Clark Center for Geospatial Analytics, Worcester, United States and Hamed Alemohammad, Clark University, Clark Center for Geospatial Analytics, Worcester, MA, United States
main_session: Advancing Applications of Earth Observation Foundation Models and Embeddings for Biodiversity Monitoring: Methods, Challenges, and Insights Poster
abstract: Coastal mangrove systems are among the most biodiverse and threatened habitats on Earth, and their conversion to pond aquaculture is a leading direct driver of tropical coastal biodiversity loss. Monitoring this change at scale depends on expert-labeled reference data, which is slow and expensive to produce. Earth Observation (EO) foundation models could help experts scale this process, as their learned embeddings compress spectral, spatial, and temporal structure into representations that may let us map habitat from far fewer labels. However, it remains unclear which models yield useful embeddings, and how far that utility carries across ecosystems. We test whether active learning driven by EO foundation model embeddings (Prithvi-EO-2.0, AlphaEarth, OlmoEarth, and TerraMind) reduces the labeling effort to map mangrove and aquaculture extent versus random and uncertainty-based sampling. Using a publicly available, expert-labeled dataset spanning 17 tropical countries and multiple epochs, we hold out geographically and temporally disjoint regions to measure how label efficiency and classifier accuracy transfer across space and time, directly probing whether globally-trained embeddings encode transferable habitat signals. We then test whether task-agnostic markers of embedding structure (intrinsic dimension, effective rank) predict each model's downstream utility, providing a label-free proxy for selecting models before any ground-truth comparison. We report label-efficiency curves, spatial and temporal transfer for each model, and the degree to which embedding structure predicts applied utility. Findings offer practical guidance on operationalizing EO foundation model embeddings for label-efficient biodiversity monitoring and expose the spatial-temporal biases practitioners must anticipate when scaling foundation-model-based habitat mapping.

title: Integration of GEO-LEO Satellite Observations for Terrestrial Ecosystem Monitoring over Amazonia
authors: Weile Wang, NASA/AMES Research Center, Moffett Field, United States, Hirofumi Hashimoto, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, CA, United States, Taejin Park, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, United States, Keiko Nomura, Oregon State University, Corvallis, United States, Rajat Shinde, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Earth System Science Center, Huntsville, AL, United States, Africa Ixmucane Flores Anderson, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Earth System Science Center, Huntsville, United States, Junchang Ju, University of Maryland, Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center, College Park, MD, United States and Matthew S Johnson, Earth Science Division, NASA Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, CA, United States
main_session: Advances in Remote Sensing Capabilities Leading to a Better Understanding of Ecosystem and Natural Resource Management III Poster
abstract: Research and applications in monitoring terrestrial ecosystems demand satellite observations with increasingly high spatial, temporal, and spectral resolutions. Such demands cannot be fulfilled by any individual satellite but require an integrated multi-sensor approach. The third generation of operational meteorology geostationary satellites (GOES 16-19, Himawari 8/9, GK2A, MTG, etc.) feature advanced imagers with very high temporal resolution (~10 minutes for the full disk of Earth) as well as enhanced spectral bands and radiometric qualities that are closely comparable to MODIS/VIIRS. These features provide us opportunities to integrate the GEO observations with Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite data to enhance their spatiotemporal resolutions. Here, we present a prototype study that integrates GOES 16 ABI (Advanced Baseline Imager) observations with HLS (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel2) over Amazonia, where persistent cloudiness has been a challenge for land surface observations. We show that the GEO and the HLS observations contribute complementary information to address the cloud contamination issue. The high frequent GEO measurements help us detect the diurnal variations of clouds and identify the least cloudy conditions in the early morning or the late afternoon. The high spatial resolution of HLS provides us the capability to detect sub-pixel clouds and quantify their effects on the moderate-resolution GEO data. The integrated GEO-HLS datasets thus allow us to create daily time series of cloud-free images of the Amazon basin. We expect the integrated data products generated from this study to find broad interests in NASA Biosphere research and applications.

title: Enhancing SWOT River Discharge Estimates Through Multi-Satellite Data Integration with OPERA
authors: Thiago Lappicy, Renato P M Frasson, Luana Oliveira Sales, Daniel Beltrao, Alexandre Araujo, Saulo Aires De Souza, Tati Almeida and Rejane Ennes Cicerelli
main_session: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) Mission: New Frontiers in Hydrology IV Poster
abstract: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission provides global measurements of water surface elevation (WSE), width, and slope, enabling new opportunities for satellite-based discharge estimation. While SWOT accurately measures WSE, uncertainties in water classification limit the accuracy of width and cross-sectional area estimates required for many discharge algorithms. This study investigates whether the Observational Products for End-Users from Remote Sensing Analysis (OPERA) Project’s Dynamic Surface Water Extent (DSWx) product can complement SWOT measurements by improving river width and cross-sectional area observations, thus improving the discharge estimates. A case study was conducted for the Paraguay River in the Brazilian Pantanal using in situ stage and discharge observations together with DSWx-HLS products derived from Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery. Relationships between WSE and river width were evaluated using both in situ and SWOT observations and compared with widths derived from OPERA. Temporal aggregation windows ranging from 1 to 15 days were tested to assess the effects of cloud cover and revisit frequency on width estimation. Results show that SWOT accurately captures WSE but exhibits weak correspondence with observed river width. Incorporating OPERA-derived widths substantially strengthens the relationship between width and WSE, particularly for aggregation windows of up to seven days, after which width estimates become relatively stable. The combined SWOT–OPERA approach also improves the discharge estimations. These findings demonstrate that integrating OPERA with SWOT enhances river width and cross-sectional area estimates, providing a stronger foundation for satellite-based river discharge estimation worldwide.

title: Cost Analysis of Use of Foundation Models and Custom U-nets
authors: Erik Goeke, Georgia Institute of Technology, Marietta, Georgia, UNITED STATES, Iksha Gurung, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Earth System Science Center, Huntsville, AL, United States, Manil Maskey, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Office of Data Science and Informatics (ODSI), Huntsville, United States, Rahul Ramachandran, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, United States and Muthukumaran Ramasubramanian, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL, United States
main_session: AI Foundation Models for Earth, Space, and Planetary Sciences II Poster
abstract: Geospatial foundation models such as Prithvi-EO-2.0 promise strong performance across a multitude of Earth observation tasks; however, their upfront pretraining and engineering costs are significant in comparison to lighter-weight models such as U-net. This report represents a comprehensive analysis and review of foundation models and task-specific models and seeks to answer both when each is more accurate and when one is more economically advantageous. It evaluates model success, and also discusses the characteristics which make each model produce unique results. Furthermore, it also quantifies how many downstream tasks it will take to justify the upfront cost of a foundation model, and reveals model-specific advantages that arise in testing. Six architectures, U-net, DeepLabV3+, and both unfrozen and frozen Prithvi 300M and 600M models, will be compared across three task regimes: flood mapping, burn scar mapping, and crop segmentation. Results show that U-net is comparable to the Prithvi models at low data fractions; however, past the 25% mark, U-net loses its edge. Results also show that a foundation model is superior to U-net in generalization to previously unseen data.

title: Causal Estimation of Prescribed Burn Impacts on Wildfire Burn Severity Using Double Machine Learning with Spaceborne Lidar and Foundation Model Embeddings
authors: Josh Fuery, Madeleine Pascolini-Campbell, Caroline Juang, Antonio Ferraz, Gabriela Shirkey, Maggie Johnson, Adrian Pascual and Thomas Piechota
main_session: Practical AI for Wildfire Science II Poster
abstract: Fuel treatments (including prescribed burns) are a primary tool for reducing vegetation accumulations, improving ecosystem health, and mitigating destructive high severity wildfires . However, isolating treatment effects from confounding landscape factors (topography, weather, land cover) remains a central challenge. We use Double Machine Learning (DML), a causal inference framework, to estimate the effect of prescribed burns on wildfire burn severity (dNBR) across 17 California wildfires (2020-2024) at 30-meter pixel resolution. Our confounder set goes beyond prior observational studies by incorporating pre-fire vegetation structure from GEDI lidar and vegetation water stress from ECOSTRESS evapotranspiration, alongside topography, fire weather, climate normals, land cover, and ownership. Gradient-boosted trees predict burn severity while random forests estimate treatment probability, linked through a cross-fitting procedure that removes overfitting bias from the causal estimate. Prescribed burns reduce dNBR by 0.17 (95% CI: 0.08–0.23), roughly a 40% reduction in severity, with broadcast burns nearly twice as effective as mechanical pile burns. Adding ECOSTRESS evapotranspiration shifts the estimate by roughly 19%, indicating that vegetation water status is an important confounder. Effectiveness decays sharply beyond a five-year window, consistent with vegetation regrowth eroding fuel reduction benefits. Interpretability analysis (SHAP) shows that severity is predicted by ecological variables (evapotranspiration, canopy structure, fire weather) while treatment assignment is predicted by operational factors (community proximity, elevation), confirming the models adjust for confounding through distinct pathways. We further test whether a geospatial foundation model (Prithvi-EO-2.0) can substitute for specialized sensors. Embeddings from pre-fire Landsat imagery recover GEDI canopy structure and yield treatment effects indistinguishable from the lidar-based specification, but cannot recover ECOSTRESS evapotranspiration from reflectance alone. Pairing causal machine learning with multi-sensor observations offers a rigorous basis for evaluating fire management at scale.

title: Leveraging Remote Sensing Vegetation Indices and Machine Learning to Gap-Fill Ecosystem Fluxes in Wetland Ecosystems
authors: Katie Bossert, Ohio State University Main Campus, Columbus, OH, United States and Gil Bohrer, The Ohio State University, Department of Civil, Environmental and Geodetic Engineering, Columbus, United States
main_session: From Flux Measurements to Societal Benefits: Integrating Physics, Remote Sensing, and AI for Scaling Surface-Atmosphere Interactions Poster
abstract: Continuous eddy covariance records of ecosystem fluxes are routinely interrupted by instrument failures, power outages, and adverse weather, creating gaps that complicate annual budget estimates and model benchmarking. Standard gap-filling approaches rely on meteorological drivers that poorly capture the inundation dynamics and vegetation phenology that govern wetland methanogenesis. Here we present a remote sensing-driven framework to reconstruct missing CH₄ flux observations at wetland AmeriFlux sites. We processed Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery through the NASA AppEEARS platform to derive five vegetation indices, NDVI, EVI, SAVI, NDMI, and NDWI, at 30 m resolution across multiple site-years. Following cloud masking using the Fmask band, observations were smoothed with Savitzky-Golay filtering and interpolated to half-hourly resolution using AmeriFlux QC conventions (QC = 0 observed, 1 good fill, 2 poor fill), producing vegetation index timeseries directly compatible with BASE data products. Indices sensitive to surface water and canopy moisture content, particularly NDWI and NDMI, were hypothesized to serve as strong proxies for the hydrological and phenological conditions that drive CH₄ production and transport in wetland systems. These predictors were evaluated within Artificial Neural Network (ANN), XGBoost, and Conditional Score-based Diffusion Models (CSDI), using cross-validation to compare model performance across gap lengths and seasonal conditions. Model skill was assessed using RMSE, MAE, and R², with particular attention to performance during extended gaps where traditional meteorological gap-filling degrades most severely. This scalable, replicable pipeline offers the AmeriFlux community a practical pathway toward more complete wetland carbon records and improved integration of tower flux data with satellite-based ecosystem monitoring.

title: Transferability of Weather and Climate GeoFM for Regional Downscaling under Data Scarcity
authors: Anushka Narayanan and Karianne J Bergen, Brown University, Data Science Institute and Department of Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences, Providence, RI, United States
main_session: AI Foundation Models for Earth, Space, and Planetary Sciences II Poster
abstract: Geoscientific foundation models (GeoFMs) are large-scale models pretrained on global-scale weather and climate (WxC) data to learn representations of atmospheric and climate processes that can be adapted to various WxC downstream tasks, including regional downscaling. GeoFMs offer the capability to leverage global Earth system representations which is particularly important in data-sparse regions, where high-resolution observations are often limited, making it difficult to train reliable region-specific statistical downscaling models. A key motivation is to understand when GeoFMs provide meaningful advantages over independently trained regional models to enable the broader adoption of GeoFMs in observation-limited regional Earth-system applications. Accordingly, our work investigates the transferability of GeoFMs across distinct geographical regions using precipitation downscaling as a case study. We adapt the Prithvi WxC GeoFM model for downscaling using training data from data-rich source regions and evaluate its generalization to geographically distinct data-sparse target regions. We examine how source-region selection, source-region sample size and the incorporation of limited target region observations can improve high resolution precipitation mapping in target regions, and compare frozen and parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies for adapting the pretrained backbone. We also analyze how fine-tuning modifies the internal representations learned during pretraining and how these representation changes relate to successful regional transfer. Overall, we aim to determine whether pretrained GeoFMs can be effectively adapted across heterogeneous geographies with limited data and offer insights into when transfer from existing data-rich regions is sufficient and whether GeoFMs can improve data efficiency compared to independent region-specific models that conventionally require large amounts of regional training data.

title: Compound hazard, single vector: Can foundation model embeddings replace SPI, SPEI, and NDVI in predictive models of human displacement?
authors: Prakrut Haresh Kansara, Benjamin F Zaitchik, Chungmann Kim, Difu Shi, Gabrielle Prager, Sani Fatima, Chiara Altare and Paul Spiegel
main_session: Data-Driven Approaches to Quantifying Climate Impacts on Human Well-Being II Poster
abstract: Single-variable climate hazard metrics, such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), are inherently limited in their ability to capture compound and interacting extreme events. To address this limitation, we introduce Climate Hazard Embeddings (CHE): latent vectors derived from Earth Foundation Models (EFMs) that provide a complex, multi-scale characterization of climate extremes. Using the pre-trained Prithvi-WxC model, we extract high-dimensional latent features from hydrometeorological fields utilizing the MERRA-2 reanalysis dataset. These embeddings are generated for the African continent at a harmonized 0.5° resolution and a monthly temporal resolution for the period of 1980 to 2025. We benchmark the CHE vectors against standard hazard indices, including SPI, SPEI, soil moisture anomalies, and heatwave index, as well as vegetation health proxy such as MODIS NDVI. To evaluate the utility of these embeddings, we apply them to model human displacement in Mali, integrating the climate data with demographic, economic, and conflict records. We compare the predictive skill of machine learning models trained on conventional climate indices against models utilizing the CHE vectors as the sole climate input. This research aims to determine whether unified, deep-learning representations of climate stressors improve the modeling of multi-hazard societal impacts, providing a scalable approach for early warning systems and disaster risk assessment.

title: Examining Encoding of Land Cover Types and Vegetation Phenology in Earth Observation Foundation Models
authors: David L Miller, Marc Grimson, PhD, Courtney Davis, Daniel Fink, Shawn Ligocki and Tom Auer, Cornell University, Lab of Ornithology, Ithaca, United States
main_session: Advancing Applications of Earth Observation Foundation Models and Embeddings for Biodiversity Monitoring: Methods, Challenges, and Insights Poster
abstract: Earth observation (EO) foundation models (FMs) offer a promising way to represent the spatial, temporal, and spectral heterogeneity of remotely sensed imagery in compact feature embeddings, potentially simplifying the use of EO data for biodiversity modeling and applications. Biodiversity models commonly include correlates for species distributions using remote sensing products related to land cover and vegetation phenology. However, within a given study area, it remains unclear to what degree different EO FMs retain such ecological information that is known to predict species occurrence. Here, we examine how well land cover and vegetation phenology are encoded in two EO foundation models, Prithvi-EO-2.0 and TESSERA v1.0, focusing on New York State in 2025 as a test case. TESSERA provides rasterized embedding features, whereas Prithvi only provides the pretrained model weights and the user must generate the features themselves (e.g., from HLS imagery). For each EO FM, we use a CNN to train and test their ability to replicate existing remote sensing products, specifically land cover classifications (MODIS MCD12Q1, NLCD), vegetation phenology products (MODIS MCD12Q2, HLS land surface phenology), and temporal variability in vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI from HLS). Early analysis shows that TESSERA embeddings capture broad geographic features, such as water bodies, mountainous regions, and urban areas, but can show spatial discontinuities related to satellite image acquisitions. From this analysis, we can better constrain whether known ecological gradients are well-represented within different forms of EO FMs and if those representations are useful for species distribution modeling.

title: Invasion at Scale: Using high-resolution remote sensing to map the invasion front of Phragmites australis Across the U.S. East Coast
authors: Yuyang Wang, Cornell University, Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Ithaca, NY, United States, Emily S Bernhardt, Cornell University, Natural Resources and the Environment, Ithaca, United States and Justin Wright, Duke University, Biology, Durham, United States
main_session: Vegetation Detection, Characterization, and Monitoring Through Multisensor Remote Sensing and Data Fusion Techniques II Poster
abstract: Plant invasions are rapidly altering coastal wetland communities and their ecosystem functioning. Although satellites enable broad environmental monitoring, species-level change remains difficult to track. Classification models often fail across heterogeneous regions, seasonal growth patterns remain underused for species identification, and most studies map current distributions rather than quantify invasion over time. We use invasive Phragmites australis (Pa) to develop a scalable monitoring and forecasting framework for eastern U.S. coastal wetlands. Using NAIP imagery, our analysis quantified Pa invasion across 12 Atlantic coastal wetlands. Annual invasion rates ranged from −0.13 to 18.12% yr⁻¹, and canopy shading, soil pH, and microtopographic roughness together explained 70% of variation in invasion rate. 75% of mapped patches exceeded 900 m², suggesting that established stands may be detectable using the high-temporal-resolution Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) record. We are building geographically distributed training and validation datasets by compiling occurrence records from multiple sources and verifying them with high-resolution NAIP imagery. We then compare a deep-learning model using HLS imagery alone with a multisensor model that also incorporates elevation and NISAR radar data, and evaluate whether these models transfer to independent regions. Dense HLS time series will be used to identify the spectral and seasonal features that best distinguish Pa from native vegetation, including spring green-up, peak growth, autumn senescence, and maximum greenness. Finally, historical NAIP imagery extending to the early 2000s will be used to reconstruct changes in Pa extent and map the movement of invasion fronts through time. These regional invasion dynamics will be tested against canopy shading, microtopographic roughness, and hydroclimatic variables such as precipitation and flooding to determine whether relationships identified at the 12 pilot wetlands remain consistent at broader spatial scales.

title: Terra Transition: Alternative Data Sources and Access Options for MODIS and ASTER Users
authors: Alex Ketchpaw, Cole Krehbiel, Nathan Roberts and Mahsa Jami
main_session: Advances in Remote Sensing Capabilities Leading to a Better Understanding of Ecosystem and Natural Resource Management III Poster
abstract: Since its launch on December 18, 1999, NASA’s Terra satellite has collected more than 25 years of sustained Earth observations. Its instruments, including the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER), have produced imagery that has been indispensable to researchers, scientists, governments, and others across a broad range of applications. As Terra approaches its end of life, users of MODIS and ASTER data are seeking guidance as they transition to new data sources to meet their research and application needs. Fortunately, there are a number of available alternative data products from other projects and sensors. For MODIS, this includes the NASA-produced Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) products, the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, and ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission products, and others. Data source alternatives for ASTER include the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) project, USGS Landsat data, and NASA’s Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT) and ECOsystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (ECOSTRESS) missions, among others. Also, guides, tutorials, scripts, and Jupyter notebooks are available to help users make the transition from MODIS and ASTER to new data alternatives. NASA Earthdata’s Application for Extracting and Exploring Analysis Ready Samples (AppEEARS) is another useful resource that supports data access transitions as well. Here we present commonly used MODIS and ASTER datasets, potential alternative data sources, and resources designed to assist users transition their existing workflows.

title: An Integrated Framework for Estimating Winter Wheat Crop Growth Stages at Regional Scale using Remote Sensing and APSIM Phenology Model
authors: Swati Singh Sikarwar, University of Arizona, School of Plant Sciences-Ext, Tucson, AZ, United States and Varaprasad Bandaru, USDA-ARS, U.S. Arid Land Agricultural Research Center, Maricopa, United States
main_session: Vegetation Detection, Characterization, and Monitoring Through Multisensor Remote Sensing and Data Fusion Techniques II Poster
abstract: Winter Wheat is one of the world’s most important cereal crops. Accurate estimation of crop phenological stages is needed for effective crop management, in-season crop monitoring and yield forecasting. Remote sensing data provides continuous observations of seasonal vegetation dynamics and enables the identification of crop phenological transitions. However, these spectral indicators do not always correspond to physiological development stages because crop phenology is also influenced by environmental conditions, management practices, and biotic and abiotic stresses. Crop simulation models for winter wheat simulate phenological development using thermal time and environmental drivers such as photoperiod and vernalization. However, their accuracy is often limited by uncertainties in model inputs and parameters. Integrating process based phenology models with remote sensing-derived phenological indicators offer the potential to improve the estimation of crop growth stages. In this study, the phenology sub-routine of Agricultural Production Systems sIMulator (APSIM) model was integrated with Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) NDVI-derived canopy transitions to develop a hybrid framework for estimating key winter wheat growth stages, including emergence, jointing, heading, coloring, and maturity. The hybrid approach was evaluated across the state of Kansas for 2017-2024 growing seasons by using field observations and state-level USDA Crop Progress Reports (CPRs). The estimated growth stages captured the typical spatial and inter-annual variability associated with regional weather patterns and crop management dynamics. The framework showed close agreement with observations, resulting in biases of -6.00, -1.71, 1.43, 0.71 and 0.14 days for emergence, jointing, heading, coloring and maturity, respectively. Overall, the results demonstrated that integrating the APSIM phenology model with high resolution HLS observations improves the estimation of winter wheat phenological stages across heterogeneous landscapes. The framework provides a scalable and robust approach for regional crop monitoring and agricultural applications.

title: Hydrology constrained high resolution downscaling of Solar-Induced Fluorescence (SIF) across tidal Wetlands
authors: Ajay Devda, Peter Hawman, Kyle Runion, Deepak R Mishra and Jessica L O'Connell
main_session: Carbon Cycling in Global Wetlands and Peatlands III Poster
abstract: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is a fundamental measure of terrestrial carbon assimilation. However tidal wetland GPP models are influenced by rapid inundation cycles and mixed land–water pixels, which distort the reflectance signals in traditional GPP models. Solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), emitted during photosynthesis following absorption of photosynthetically active radiation, provides a direct observational constraint on vegetation photosynthetic activity and is strongly correlated with GPP. However, SIF-GPP relationships have not been tested in a hydrodynamic environment. Further, current satellite SIF observations have spatial footprints of several square kilometers, limiting their application in spatially heterogeneous salt-marsh landscapes. Consequently, the environmental controls on the SIF–GPP relationship and its transferability across tidal wetland ecosystems remain poorly understood. This study develops a hydrology-constrained framework to downscale OCO-2 SIF observations to 30 m in tidal salt marshes of the southeastern United States.
