For this, coarse-resolution SIF retrievals and associated uncertainties were temporally matched with Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel (HLS) reflectance, vegetation indices, and environmental drivers including photosynthetically active radiation, ERA5 meteorology, and tidal conditions. A machine-learning model was trained to generate spatial SIF weighting factors from the predictor variables. The physical consistency of the model was evaluated via coarse-resolution products from PACE, MODIS, and Sentinel-3. Finally, downscaled SIF was corrected using an independently developed inundation model. Retrieval, model, and hydrologic classification uncertainties were propagated into the final product. The downscaled SIF could be useful for evaluating SIF-GPP relationships in hydrologically variable ecosystems and improve understanding of photosynthetic carbon uptake across heterogeneous coastal wetlands

title: LAI4EO: A Global In Situ Leaf Area Index Database for Earth Observation Validation and Applications
authors: Yuval Sadeh, Mirco Boschetti, Nikhil Sasi Rajan, Josef Wagner, Francesco Nutini, Xavier Bailleau, Sheila Baber, Gabriele Candiani, Manav Gupta and Inbal Becker-Reshef
main_session: Data, Methods, and Applications for Understanding Climate Impacts on Global Agriculture II Poster
abstract: Leaf Area Index (LAI) is a key biophysical variable for monitoring vegetation dynamics and supports applications including crop condition assessment, yield forecasting, evapotranspiration estimation, carbon accounting, and land-surface modelling. Although LAI is routinely retrieved from decametric Earth observation data, the in-situ measurements needed for calibration and validation remain fragmented across research groups, measurement protocols, spatial scales, and metadata conventions. The LAI4EO Consortium, led by NASA Harvest and CNR-IREA, is addressing this limitation by developing a harmonized, quality-controlled, openly available global database of field-measured LAI suitable for evaluating Sentinel-2, Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS), PlanetScope, and related products. The database also supports algorithm testing with current imaging spectroscopy missions, including PRISMA, EnMAP, and NASA PACE/OCI, in preparation for Copernicus CHIME and NASA SBG. The consortium has developed a common database schema, data-governance approach, and harmonization workflow. The schema captures geolocation, measurement date and time, elementary sampling unit characteristics, crop type or plant species, phenology, LAI statistics, instrument and sampling information, measurement conditions and quality-control information, and the intended satellite product and pixel resolution. The current database contains approximately 2,485 measurements from France, Australia, and Italy, spanning 11 crop types and multiple instruments, including AccuPAR LP-80, LI-COR LAI-2000 and LAI-2200C, digital hemispherical photography, and PocketLAI, with a subset featuring multitemporal acquisitions at the same sites and/or characterizing within-field variability at decametric scale. Contributors retain ownership of their datasets, receive a harmonized version and persistent citation, and share data through open repositories under standard licenses. By expanding geographic, crop, seasonal, and methodological coverage, LAI4EO provides a consistent reference resource for benchmarking LAI retrievals, diagnosing product uncertainty, and improving the reproducibility and transferability of agricultural Earth observation applications.

title: Do geospatial foundation model embeddings encode land use? A distance-based evaluation against dimension-matched spectral features
authors: Mrs. K M Ashraful Islam, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, United States, Myscon Truong, Spatial Informatics Group, LLC, Alameda, United States and Robert E Kennedy, Oregon State University, Corvallis, United States
main_session: AI Foundation Models for Earth, Space, and Planetary Sciences II Poster
abstract: A satellite measures reflectance. It does not measure purpose. A warehouse and a big-box store return nearly the same spectrum, yet one moves freight and the other sells shoes. Land use is a human function, and it is largely invisible to the physics a multispectral sensor records. Geospatial foundation models are now widely assumed to have absorbed abstraction of such human functions from imagery alone. That assumption is rarely tested against a spectral baseline granted equal dimensions, which is the only comparison that separates what the model learned from what the pixels already held. We put the assumption on trial across Oregon, Washington and Idaho. OpenStreetMap polygons are refined into 24 land-use classes and intersected with a grid matched to the native patch footprint of Prithvi EO V2. We keep only cells the map describes well, cluster them by land-use composition, and ask one question of every cluster pair. Are two land uses further apart in the model's embedding space than in a dimension-matched tasseled-cap space built from the same Harmonized Landsat Sentinel imagery? We answer with multivariate Wasserstein and cosine distances. The comparison proved harder to make than it looks. Measuring distance across a learned space and an engineered one introduces a bias that has nothing to do with land use, and that bias can be the same size as the effect being measured. We show where it comes from and how to remove it. We present the class-pair comparison, the falsification test, and the correction that emerged from it. The findings speak to anyone using a foundation model as a feature extractor and assuming its embeddings carry more than the pixels did.

title: Integration of SWOT & OPERA for Lake Area-Elevation-Volume Change
authors: Shruti Soman, Alireza Farahmand, Jingjing Li, Daniel Beltrao and Renato P M Frasson
main_session: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) Mission: New Frontiers in Hydrology IV Poster
abstract: SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography), NASA’s collaboration with the French Space Agency CNES (Centre National d’Études Spatiales ) has immense hydrological capabilities allowing measurements of water-surface area and water-surface elevation (WSE) using the Ka-band Radar Interferometer ( KaRIn ) . However, the SWOT mission has a low temporal resolution of 21 days . When SWOT data is integrated with that of the Observational Products for End-Users from Remote Sensing Analysis (OPERA) project , the number of available lake-area observations increases, and the WSEs and the lake volume can be estimated for a given period with a higher temporal resolution. OPERA’s Dynamic Surface Water extent products – DSWx-S1 and DSWx -HLS – only provide water extent, whereas SWOT provides both water surface elevation and extent. These 30m OPERA rasters have a combined temporal resolution of 3 days. The rasters will be reclassified, where strengths of both OPERA products will be leveraged to capture maximum open water extent. SWOT’s Prior Lake Database (PLD) is a static foundational database implemented in generating SWOT’s products. The PLD is utilized with a 1 km buffer to extract the lake area from the reclassified OPERA rasters . This process was conducted for a 7-day, 15-day, and 30-day interval. SWOT’s vector dataset, LakeSP Prior Product, can be paired with OPERA-derived lake areas to develop hypsometric maps. The integration method consists of assigning SWOT WSE values for the days where SWOT LakeSP data overlaps with the dates of the reclassified OPERA rasters . Then, hypsometric plots are created to observe the trends in area-elevation-volume relationships and estimate changes in lake volume . The study lakes are – Eagle Lake, Clear Lake, Mono Lake, and Lake Shasta – which are a combination of natural lakes with dams, saline lakes, and reservoirs. This method has two major implications where SWOT’s capabilities are further explored through integration with OPERA, and supports applications in hydrologic modeling and water management, especially under changing climate conditions.

title: Preliminary Analysis of Desert Bloom Event Detection Using Remote Sensing Imagery and Meteorological Predictors in Picacho Peak State Park
authors: Katherine McDaniel, University of Arizona, Tucson, United States, Kyung Yoon Kim, Boston College, Earth and Environmental Sciences, Chestnut Hill, United States and Dominick Michael Ciruzzi, William & Mary, Department of Geology, Williamsburg, United States
main_session: Vegetation Detection, Characterization, and Monitoring Through Multisensor Remote Sensing and Data Fusion Techniques II Poster
abstract: Desert blooms are a rare natural phenomenon of increased vegetational coverage that predominately consist of wildflowers, driving tourism and providing a habitat for important pollinators. Remote sensing technology provides an opportunity to expand current knowledge on the contributing conditions towards bloom events due to its extended spatial and temporal capacity. Desert blooms can be detected as anomaly events with MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) and distinguished from regular vegetation greening events with crowd-sourced imagery (i.e. iNaturalist). For enhanced identification, HLS (Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2) and hyperspectral imagery from EMIT (Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation) were used to further classify events with additional spectral wavelengths. Five of these events were identified in Picacho Peak State Park from the years 2000 to 2025 using this method, all occurring in the spring months of their respective year, whereas ten vegetative greening events occurred in other months. Blooms were then compared to climate variables from the DAYMET product to better understand controls and to create a predictive model. Preliminary results reveal that these blooms were preceded by months of low average vapor pressure deficits, which correlate to the higher number of preceding rain days in a 90-day window. Cohen’s d effect sizes distinguish the bloom versus greening periods as well, with blooming events having a value of ~2 for the number of frost days in a preceding 60 day window, and greening events having a value of 2+ for growing degree days in a 90 day window. Overall, this research advances the understanding of desert ecohydrological responses to changing weather conditions and increasing temperatures by examining a highly responsive system.

title: Benchmarking Geospatial Foundation Models for Dynamic Irrigation Mapping with High-Quality State-Level Labels
authors: Ehsan Jalilvand, PhD, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Hydrological Sciences Laboratory, Greenbelt, MD, United States, Sujay V Kumar, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, United States, Parth Patel, University of Maryland, Computer Science, College park, United States, Hamed Alemohammad, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Civil and Environmental Engineering, Cambridge, MA, United States, Sam Khallaghi, Clark University, Clark Center for Geospatial Analytics, Worcester, MA, United States and David Ketchum, University of Montana, Missoula, United States
main_session: AI Foundation Models for Earth, Space, and Planetary Sciences II Poster
abstract: Irrigation consumes ~70% of global freshwater withdrawals, yet maps of actually irrigated area remain static and infrastructure-based, limiting their value for water management and hydrologic modeling. Building on our earlier work fine-tuning NASA's Prithvi EO v2.0 for irrigated/rainfed classification, we extend the framework along two axes: a substantially improved label dataset and a broader benchmark of pretrained Earth representations. Labels are built from state-level, human-verified irrigation records at submeter resolution, fused with complementary vector and raster references (USGS/NLCD built-up, JRC and Dynamic World water, ACPF/CSB/CDL rainfed cropland) into five-class maps (water, natural, irrigated, rainfed, built-up) at 30 m, with per-pixel confidence derived from source agreement and QA against NAIP imagery. Core states are selected to span dry-to-humid climates, warm-to-cool growing regions, and both groundwater- and river-fed irrigation systems, so that foundation-model pretraining can carry the learned signal into regions where high-quality labels are rare or unavailable. Using multi-temporal (May to August) HLS, Sentinel-2 L2A, and Sentinel-1 RTC inputs, we benchmark three geospatial foundation models (Prithvi EO 2.0, TerraMind, and Clay v1.5) alongside Google AlphaEarth annual embeddings, all trained through a shared TerraTorch pipeline with non-overlapping geographic splits. Planned analyses include cross-state transfer with frozen decoders to quantify geographic generalization, the contribution of radar versus optical inputs, sensitivity to label confidence and training-set size, and frozen-embedding versus fine-tuned backbone performance. We will present benchmark results and annual irrigation maps for the study states.

title: Principles and a Measurable Instrument for Operationalizing Geospatial Foundation Models: The Operational Readiness Profile
authors: Rajat Shinde, Venkatesh Kolluru, Abdelhak Marouane, Caden Helbling, Deepak Shah, Othneil Drew, Slesa Adhikari, Iksha Gurung, Manil Maskey and Rahul Ramachandran
main_session: AI Foundation Models for Earth, Space, and Planetary Sciences II Poster
abstract: Operational Earth observation (EO) services for disaster response, agricultural monitoring, and environmental accounting are increasingly adopting geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) pretrained on petabyte-scale multi-sensor archives. However, the majority of these GeoFMs are evaluated solely on benchmark accuracy, which does not assess their operational efficacy. Typically, these evaluations characterize the GeoFM artifact in silos, while the deployed pipeline, the data services feeding it, the preprocessing steps that bind inference inputs to the training data distribution, the validation reference products, and the serving infrastructure remain uncharacterized. Hence, the deployed GeoFMs can fail silently at the data, model, and deployment interfaces. Building on our earlier operationalization of NASA-IBM Prithvi-EO-2.0 for near-real-time monitoring (Kolluru et al., AGU 2025, IN52B-03), we formalize the principles behind it into a systems framework that decomposes a deployed GeoFM pipeline into three pillars (data, model, deployment) plus a governance layer, and convert it into a measurable instrument: the operational readiness profile, with eight axes (P1-P8) covering system-level documentation, operational scaling, preprocessing methods, modality disclosure, validation with reference products, observability, user interaction, and performance of GeoFM inference under missing or corrupted data. We apply the instrument to production pipelines for burn-scar detection, flood inundation mapping, and crop classification across 17 global events (See Figure 1). We validate ~200 inference results for these events against up to four independent reference products. This presentation focuses on- (1) The P1-P8 principles for operationalizing a GeoFM, (2) How to compute the profile to measure the operational capability of a deployed pipeline, and (3) The tested use cases and how the profile supports reliable AI-powered decision support systems. Our measurements show that operational failure modes emerge at pipeline interfaces that accuracy benchmarks do not probe. We propose the operational readiness profile as an instrument for GeoFM deployments.

title: Enhancing Brazilian Reservoir Monitoring Using Remote Sensing Data from Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission and the Observational Products for End-Users from Remote Sensing Analysis (OPERA) Project
authors: Daniel Beltrao, Renato P M Frasson, Thiago Lappicy, Luana Oliveira Sales, Rejane Ennes Cicerelli, Alexandre De Amorim Teixeira, Alexandre Araujo, Saulo Aires De Souza and Tati Almeida
main_session: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) Mission: New Frontiers in Hydrology IV Poster
abstract: Reservoirs and lakes play a pivotal role in water management, particularly in areas vulnerable to hydrological cycle extremes and water use changes. They enhance water availability by storing water during wet periods and releasing it gradually during dry periods and play a critical role in mitigating extreme events, acting as flood control and flow regulation, thus attenuating the impacts of both precipitation and drought events. However, monitoring these water bodies represents a significant challenge, since the high costs associated with in situ measurements make large-scale monitoring largely unfeasible. In this context, remote sensing emerges as a promising solution, enabling water monitoring in a broader, simpler and cheaper way than traditional field-based techniques. This work aims to enhance lake and reservoir monitoring by integrating multiple state-of-the-art remote sensing tools. We combined Water Surface Elevation (WSE) measurements from the SWOT satellite (launched in 2022) and Water Surface Area (WSA) computed from the Dynamic Surface Water Extent suite of products, including DSWx HLS (Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel 2) and S1 (Sentinel 1) datasets, with measurements dating back to April 2023. By combining these datasets, we derived hypsometric curves for approximately 20 Brazilian reservoirs with more consistent results than relying on a single data source. Our results were compared against in situ data from the Brazilian National Water and Sanitation Agency (ANA) and Brazilian National Electric System Operator (ONS). The comparison showed strong agreement. For WSE, the median correlation coefficient was 0.90, and the median Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) was 0.73 cm. For WSA, the median correlation coefficient was 0.75, and the median percentage RMSE was 11.90%. Consequently, hypsometric curves were derived with high precision and accuracy for most of the reservoirs. These findings suggest that our developed methodology is suitable for monitoring reservoir parameters and can be potentially scaled to unmonitored water bodies, particularly across the vast, dispersed, and remote lake and reservoir networks of Brazil.

title: Annual Mapping of Vascular Plant Species Richness in Australia from 2000 to 2025 Using Earth Observation Embeddings
authors: Wenyuan Li, Organization Not Listed, Washington, DC, United States, Junpeng Li, the University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Junpeng Li, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, United States, Han Ma, The University of Hong Kong, Department of Geography, Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Jin Wu, University of Arizona, Tucson, United States and Shunlin Liang, University of Hong Kong, Department of Geography, Hong Kong, Hong Kong
main_session: Advancing Applications of Earth Observation Foundation Models and Embeddings for Biodiversity Monitoring: Methods, Challenges, and Insights Poster
abstract: Vascular plant species richness (VPSR), a fundamental measure of local α-diversity, indicates ecosystem functioning, stability, resilience, and conservation value. Despite advances in species distribution models and spectral variability methods, analyzing continental-scale VPSR dynamics remains challenging because of (1) the lack of annual products capturing long-term and interannual changes, (2) the limited ecological specificity and robustness of conventional spectral proxies across heterogeneous landscapes, and (3) insufficient transferability across sites, regions, and years. We selected Australia (approximately 7.69 million km²) as a representative region, with its diverse climatic gradients, for continental-scale analysis. Landsat time-series imagery and remote-sensing-derived Essential Biodiversity Variables (RS-EBVs) were integrated into analysis-ready data cubes. Using 75,559 vegetation-plot records from 2000–2020, we compared three remote sensing foundation models (Prithvi, AgriFM, and SkySense++) and two Earth observation embedding products (AlphaEarth Foundations, AEF; Embedded Seamless Data, ESD) through random, spatially independent, and temporally independent cross-validation. Earth observation embeddings outperformed the foundation models. We combined ESD estimates for 2000–2024 with AEF estimates for 2017–2025, calibrated over their 2017–2024 overlap, to generate annual Australian VPSR maps for 2000–2025. The product showed three advantages: (1) good predictive performance (ESD: R² = 0.63, RMSE = 10.58; AEF: R² = 0.72, RMSE = 9.98); (2) robust spatial and temporal transferability (spatial R² = 0.42 for ESD and 0.63 for AEF; temporal R² = 0.32 and 0.61, respectively); and (3) sensitivity to extreme climatic disturbances, including a marked VPSR decline in areas burned during the 2019–2020 Black Summer bushfires. This continuous annual product supports continental-scale investigations of long-term biodiversity dynamics and their drivers.

title: Advancing Crown Fire Modeling in California with EMIT-Derived Canopy Water Content
authors: Natalie Queally, Hudson Billock, Xiulin Gao, Philip G. Brodrick, Lara M Kueppers, Pablo Saide, Sreyashi Debnath and Elsa Ordway
main_session: Advancing Global Imaging Spectroscopy and Thermal Infrared Measurements: ECOSTRESS, EMIT, and EAGLE II Oral
abstract: As severe fire weather conditions become more prevalent and drive extreme wildfire events, the ability to model crown fire behavior is increasingly important. Canopy water content (CWC) is a key metric that informs plant water status and is an important factor in assessing canopy fuel status and likelihood of crown fire. However, the lack of spatially and temporally continuous observations of CWC limits our ability to evaluate and improve process-based models that require characterization of vegetation moisture and its response to environmental change. To address this, we developed a statewide CWC dataset for California using a deep learning framework that bridges imaging spectroscopy and satellite monitoring by leveraging EMIT-derived CWC, Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 reflectance, and topographic variables. Using this CWC dataset, we assessed whether a novel implementation of the Functionally Assembled Terrestrial Ecosystem Simulator (FATES) crown fire model captures observed canopy moisture dynamics. We compared monthly CWC from our remote sensing-derived estimates and initialized FATES simulations from 2014-2019 at the Blodgett Forest Research Station in El Dorado County and elsewhere in California mixed conifer forests. Satellite imaging spectroscopy and FATES yielded similar seasonal patterns in CWC, following winter peaks and summer troughs consistent with seasonal weather patterns in the region. However, remotely sensed CWC captured substantial interannual variability while FATES exhibited minimal interannual fluctuations. Since the study period was marked by extreme interannual climate fluctuations, including years of both exceptional drought and higher-than-normal precipitation, our results suggest that the FATES crown fire model may underestimate vegetation moisture sensitivity to anomalous climate conditions. Capturing these responses is critical for understanding crown fire behavior under climate extremes. Remotely sensed CWC derived from satellite imaging spectroscopy provides an important spatially explicit and temporally continuous observational constraint for refining model parameterizations and improving predictions of crown fire risk under increasingly variable climate conditions.

title: Water Volume Dynamics in Central Asian Reservoirs Observed by the SWOT LakeSP Product
authors: Xiaoran Han, Jean-Francois Cretaux, Dr. Jida Wang, Claire Pottier, Adrien Selles, Ben Jarihani and Guoqing Zhang
main_session: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) Mission: New Frontiers in Hydrology III Oral
abstract: Reservoirs in Central Asia provide critical water supplies and irrigation for tens of millions of people, sustained by glacial meltwater, snowmelt, and precipitation and baseflow runoff. With rapid climate change and increased water consumption in this arid region, monitoring reservoir volume changes has become critical to water management and security. However, limited by the spatial resolution and wide ground-track spacing of traditional satellite altimeters, comprehensive monitoring faces unsolved challenges, especially for small-sized reservoirs. The SWOT mission, launched in late 2022, promises to overcome this limitation. In this study, we propose a processing framework for the LakeSP (Version D) data product to acquire reliable water surface elevation (WSE) time series. Volume changes are derived by integrating SWOT WSE with area time series obtained from OPERA DSWx-HLS data. Our study reveals that using the combination of ‘ wse_std ’, ‘ area_total ’, and IQR filtering renders a reasonable compromise between retained observations and accuracy for LakeSP WSE time series of the studied 33 reservoirs. Applying the framework proposed in this study, we found that water management within the individual basins, namely the Ili, Syr Darya, and Amu Darya basins, exhibits diverse patterns. At the basin scale, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya show inverse cumulative volume changes across seasons. The proposed framework contributes to future data processing by facilitating effective WSE retrieval from LakeSP data. Furthermore, the identified reservoir patterns across different basins in Central Asia advance the understanding of transboundary water management.

title: Integrating Earth Foundation Models and Diffusion for Global, Fine-Scale Land Surface Temperature Reconstruction
authors: Zihui Ma, Peishi Jiang, Yiheng Chen, Qikai Hu, Yilong Dai, Xinyue Ye, Lingyao Li, Rita Sousa and Runlong Yu
main_session: GeoAI and Integrative AI Modeling for Earth System Informatics and Infrastructure Resilience II Oral
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) varies substantially across urban areas, vegetation, water bodies, and other heterogeneous landscapes, yet satellite thermal observations often lack the spatial detail needed to characterize these local patterns. Reconstructing fine-resolution LST from coarse measurements is therefore highly underdetermined, particularly under extreme spatial degradation. We present a GeoAI framework that integrates multi-resolution Earth observations with pretrained geospatial representations and diffusion-based modeling. The framework combines coarse thermal inputs with colocated Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 reflectance. Rather than directly concatenating multispectral bands with thermal data, Prithvi-EO-2.0 encodes land-surface structure into geospatial embeddings that guide the diffusion process through cross-attention. We evaluate the approach for 32× LST reconstruction using 242,416 paired thermal and reflectance patches across 3,094 globally distributed tiles. Results show that foundation-model guidance improves reconstruction relative to raw multispectral conditioning, with the largest gains occurring in spatially heterogeneous scenes and along land-cover boundaries where coarse pixels contain multiple surface and thermal regimes. Two diffusion formulations provide complementary outcomes: one achieves stronger pixel-level accuracy and structural agreement, while the other better preserves realistic fine-scale thermal textures. These findings demonstrate that Earth foundation models can support generative integration of multi-modal observations across spatial scales and provide a transferable pathway for improving fine-scale environmental monitoring when direct high-resolution thermal observations are limited.

title: Beyond Downstream Accuracy: Exploring Latent Observation Spaces in Earth Foundation Models with GELOS
authors: Hamed Alemohammad, Denys Godwin, Rufai Balogun, Eli Simonson, Yao-Ting Yao and Sam Khallaghi
main_session: GeoAI and Integrative AI Modeling for Earth System Informatics and Infrastructure Resilience II Oral
abstract: Earth foundation models are rapidly becoming core infrastructure for Earth system science, supporting applications ranging from environmental monitoring and hazard assessment to Earth system modeling. Yet most evaluation approaches focus on downstream task performance after fine-tuning, providing limited insight into how environmental information is represented within latent spaces learned during pretraining. As a result, models with similar benchmark performance may encode fundamentally different representations of Earth system processes. We present Geospatial Exploration of Latent Observation Space (GELOS), an embedding-centric framework for systematically characterizing latent representations produced by Earth foundation models. Rather than evaluating only end-task accuracy, GELOS examines the structure, separability, robustness, and environmental sensitivity of learned embeddings across sensors, modalities, and geographic phenomena. The framework integrates benchmark datasets, standardized embedding extraction workflows, representation analysis techniques, and perturbation experiments to investigate how models organize Earth observation information. We demonstrate GELOS across three complementary environmental challenges: global land cover classification, crop type classification, and wildfire-driven landscape change detection. We apply the framework to multiple state-of-the-art Earth foundation models, including Prithvi, TerraMind, OlmoEarth, and AlphaEarth. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in latent representation behavior across models, including variations in class separability, modality utilization, robustness to perturbations, and sensitivity to environmental transitions. In several cases, models exhibiting similar downstream performance produce markedly different embedding structures, highlighting limitations of task-based evaluation alone. These findings demonstrate that latent-space analysis provides complementary insights into model capabilities that are invisible to conventional benchmarking approaches.

title: Wildfire Severity Reshapes Remotely Sensed Surface Temperature and Vegetation Phenology in a Western Cascades Forest Ecosystem
authors: Daniel M Griffith, Christopher J Still, David M Bell, Matthew Betts, Amelia Fitch, Hannah Sachs and Mark Schulze
main_session: Advancing Global Imaging Spectroscopy and Thermal Infrared Measurements: ECOSTRESS, EMIT, and EAGLE II Oral
abstract: Wildfire reorganizes forests by altering canopy structure, surface energy balance, vegetation activity, and microclimate. However, these effects remain difficult to quantify across seasons, times of day, burn severities, and complex terrain. We used the 2023 Lookout Fire at the H.J. Andrews Experimental Forest, Oregon, to test how fire severity altered coupling between surface temperature and vegetation phenology. We integrated ECOSTRESS land surface temperature (LST), HLS-2 near-infrared reflectance of vegetation (NIRv), RAVG burn severity, Daymet climate, airborne LiDAR, and phenology observations. ECOSTRESS observations were standardized by harmonic regression for seasonal and diurnal acquisition timing. Post-fire warming was strongest in summer and increased with burn severity (1.5 °C increase for severe). High-severity areas warmed more than unburned areas, especially under high shortwave radiation, low rainfall, and high vapor pressure. Open vegetation cover was associated with warmer LST, whereas higher elevations were cooler. At phenology plots, ECOSTRESS LST generally exceeded instantaneous air temperature (ΔT = 0.55), and burn severity steepened this relationship after fire (1 to 1.15 slope). HLS NIRv captured seasonal and disturbance-driven vegetation activity and was associated with Douglas-fir budbreak and summer temperature. Across the landscape, post-fire declines in NIRv were associated with warmer noon-standardized LST, and structural equation modeling indicated that reduced evapotranspiration largely mediated this relationship. Among the first to use ECOSTRESS observations, our study resolved seasonal and diurnal post-fire warming while linking thermal responses to satellite vegetation activity, LiDAR-derived structure, and field phenology. Together, these results show that wildfire severity reorganized thermal regimes across seasons and times of day, while vegetation phenology provided biological context for post-fire climate change.

title: Harvest Date Detection Using Synthetic Aperture Radar
authors: Divya Kumawat, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, SSAI, Silver Spring, Maryland, UNITED STATES, Rajat Bindlish, NASA GSFC, Greenbelt, United States, Jeonghwan Park, Ohio State University, Electroscience Lab, Columbus, United States and Joel T Johnson, The Ohio State University, ElectroScience Laboratory, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Columbus, United States
main_session: The NASA-ISRO SAR (NISAR) Mission: Early Results in Geodesy, Cryosphere, Ecosystems II Oral
abstract: Although accurate, timely and field-scale mapping of crop harvest dates is critical for agricultural monitoring, yield forecasting, and crop model parameterization, obtaining spatially continuous harvest information from conventional ground-based reporting systems remains a challenge. The 3–10 m resolution L-band radar backscatter observations provided at 12-day global repeat cycle by the NASA-ISRO SAR (NISAR) mission offer a unique opportunity to map harvest dates operationally across major agricultural regions. The proposed approach relies on the contrast in radar backscatter between vegetated and bare soil surfaces. Dense vegetation causes rapid temporal decorrelation in the SAR signal leading to low coherence and increased VH backscatter during the growing cycle. Agricultural harvest removes the vegetation canopy and exposes bare soil, producing a sharp, sustained rise in coherence as well as a decrease in VH backscatter. Building on this physical framework, time series observations of VH backscatter and coherence are used to train a deep learning model. The model is initially trained using Sentinel-1 observations and applied to NISAR measurements. Harvest date validation is performed using observations from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) and Planetscope optical constellations over the US Midwest. Predicted harvest dates are also compared with crop progress survey reports from the United States Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Statistics Service (USDA NASS).

title: Discovery through Data Stewardship: Curating, Preserving, and Connecting a 3-meter Resolution Offline Satellite Imagery Data Archive in support of Peak Greenness Predictions used in Scientific Aerial Surveys
authors: John Adler, John Musinsky and Matthew Saxton
main_session: Connections Foster Evolution in Science and in Science Data Stewardship II Oral
abstract: The National Science Foundation's NEON Project (National Ecological Observatory Network) is a 30-year effort to monitor 20 unique biomes across the United States. It utilizes field-based physical sampling by ground crews, and aerial-based remote sensing by air crews. We demonstrate the utility of using space-based imagery to support NEON's flight operations, and discuss the possibilities of further supporting NEON data products utilizing this data archive. The SuperDove satellite constellation (from planet.com) produces 8-band images in the visible and into the near-infrared spectrum. We selected imagery temporally spanning from 20March to 15October, which encompasses the normal seasonality for vegetation growth in these ecological domains. A high-quality data curation process was then employed to select 57 distinct NEON ground sites across the United States, each consisting of a circular 75 square km area of 95% cloud free days, spanning the past six years. A large 1.2Tb offline data archive was then created, to assist with peak greenness scheduling for the low-altitude NEON hyperspectral & lidar survey aircraft. This offline imagery archive also ensures data accessibility and integrity, regardless of service denial periods, or inadvertent cloud computing data loss. Historically, other satellite imagery, including MODIS and Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel data, were used to calculate peak greenness – a key variable used in scheduling both airborne and field-based ecological sampling campaigns. Each of these data sources has a considerably reduced spatial and temporal resolution (10-625 meters, and 2-3 days or greater revisit times) when compared to Planet's SuperDove 3-meter daily imagery. Our findings show the SuperDove imagery does effectively calculate peak greenness in the traditional manner at a much higher spatial resolution. Beyond the EVI vegetation index used to calculate peak greenness, this data archive could be used for other NEON products measuring fine-scale vegetation health and productivity, canopy dynamics, and monitoring of invasives. Further research could also be done in the realm of peak greenness micro-calculations, specifically targeting small areas of interest (~2 square km).

title: Frequent burning fuels new extremes in Amazon forest fire behavior
authors: Douglas C Morton, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, United States, Ane Alencar, IPAM Amazon Environmental Research Institute, Brasilia, Brazil, Dr. Shane Coffield, University of Chicago, Chicago, United States, Paulo M Brando, Yale University, School of the Environment, New Haven, United States, James Tremper Randerson, University of California Irvine, Earth System Science, Irvine, United States, Yang Chen, University of California Irvine, Earth System Science, Irvine, CA, United States and Marcia Macedo, Columbia University, New York, United States
main_session: Fire-Ecosystem Interactions Under Global Environmental Changes I Oral
abstract: Fires in tropical forests substantially alter ecosystem structure and composition. Drought conditions that spur widespread fire activity in tropical forests and peatlands are becoming more frequent, a pattern that may strengthen fire feedbacks via canopy tree mortality and fuel accumulation. Notably, the 2023-2024 El Niño led to record fire activity in the Amazon and surrounding biomes, and the return of El Niño conditions in 2026 increases the threat of more widespread drought and fire impacts, including repeated burning in areas that burned in 2023-2024. Here, we leverage new satellite-based monitoring tools developed to track fire risk and fire activity in near real-time to assess the patterns and impacts of repeated burning on Amazon forests. Our analysis draws on field, airborne, and satellite data to characterize the impact of frequent fires and the potential for a disturbance-driven tipping point in Amazon forests from repeated burning. We leverage new tailored fire detection data from VIIRS and the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel (HLS) data records to reduce the impact of canopy cover and cloud obscuration on fire detection. These additional detections guide burned area mapping to better quantify the full extent of Amazon forest fire damages and enable sub-daily fire tracking of individual fire spread and intensity. We utilize the overlapping records of updated burned area (1985-2026), fire tracking (2012-2026), and soil water deficits from GRACE (2002-2026) and SMAP (2015-2026) to isolate the influence of fire history on individual fire behavior. Combined, these lines of analysis capture differences in fire behavior as a function of fire frequency and pre-fire forest structure. In addition, the updated burned area time series provides new insights regarding the duration of elevated vulnerability to reburning in the absence of drought conditions—a critical indicator of a fire-driven tipping point in Amazon forests.

title: Near-real-time crop phenology monitoring by harmonizing satellite time series from multiple sources
authors: Yongchang Ye, South Dakota State University, Geospatial Sciences Center of Excellence (GSCE), Department of Geography & Geospatial Sciences, Brookings, SD, United States, Xiaoyang Zhang, South Dakota State University, Geospatial Sciences Center of Excellence (GSCE), Department of Geography & Geospatial Sciences, Brookings, United States, Yu Shen, Duke University, Nichoals School of the Environment, Durham, United States, Weile Wang, NASA/AMES Research Center, Moffett Field, United States and Zhengwei Yang, USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service, Research and Development Division, Washington, United States
main_session: Advances in Monitoring of Land Changes Using Remote Sensing, Quality Assessment, and Statistical Inference: Methods, Applications, and Challenges I Poster
abstract: Crop phenology has been widely investigated from historical satellite observations. The historical phenology information is useful in modeling crop growth and yield. However, delayed crop phenology information is of limited value for guiding real-time agricultural practices. Predicting crop phenology in near-real-time (NRT) is challenging due to the lack of timely available high-quality cloud-free satellite observations. Recently, NRT crop phenology prediction has been explored in the Midwestern agricultural region of the United States by fusing Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) data and Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) data. It leverages the advantages of the fine spatial resolution (30 m) of HLS observations and the high frequency (10 min) of ABI observations to generate 30 m cloud-free time series. However, a well-known limitation of ABI data is that large view zenith angles may result in inaccurate temporal variations. In this study, we incorporated VIIRS data to calibrate the temporal shape of ABI time series and then used it to fuse with HLS data. Specifically, we first fused ABI two-band Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI2) time series with VIIRS EVI2 values using a Spatiotemporal Shape-Matching Model (SSMM). Second, the fused ABI-VIIRS time series was used to further fuse with HLS EVI2 values. Then, the HLS-ABI-VIIRS EV2 time series was used to build the NRT crop phenology model. The model was constructed by SSMM using two successive years of EVI2 time series just before the date at which timely data were available. It was then applied to predict the potential EVI2 values for the remaining portion of the growing season that had not yet occurred. Finally, phenology of crop growth was predicted on a weekly basis. We implemented this algorithm to predict NRT crop phenology at the 30-m field scale for 10 crop types in nine states of the Midwest US. We evaluated the results using the weekly Crop Progress Reports (CPRs) released from the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) of the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA).

title: Evaluation of Multispectral Imagery for Remote Sensing of Microplastics in the Sacramento River and San Francisco Bay Area
authors: Leart Jahaj, Providence College, Providence, United States, Mashalle Olomi, University of California Davis, Davis, United States and Mehmet Kurum, University of Georgia, Athens, United States
main_session: Advancements in the Fate, Transport, Transformation, and Remediation of Contaminants in the Environment V Poster
abstract: Microplastics have become a prevalent and concerning source of pollution in modern society. They have been linked to carcinogenic, cardiovascular, and reproductive pathologies. These polymers exhibit extreme environmental persistence and bioaccumulate across many different species, including humans. Microplastics aggregate and travel in the environment primarily through industrial and wastewater effluent, urban stormwater, and agricultural runoff. Attempts to remotely sense the presence and aggregation of microplastics in the environment have been limited and are typically restrained to terrestrial sensing. Remote sensing of microplastics in aquatic environments, like lakes, bays, or rivers, has been rarely attempted, creating a noticeable gap of knowledge in the current global study of microplastics. This study aims to develop and apply novel strategies to remotely sense microplastics in the San Francisco Bay and Sacramento River in California using 2017 data to find areas of high microplastic aggregation. Through a robust validation of overlapping San Francisco Estuary Institute in-situ, HyspIRI airborne campaign, CYGNSS, SWOT, Worldview-3, and Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 satellite datasets, hotspots of microplastics and their movement through the aquatic environment were detected and catalogued. Near-infrared channels at ~940 nm and short-wave infrared channels at ~2200 nm were interrogated across the datasets for microplastic identification and yielded moderate negative correlations between microplastic concentration and surface reflectance (R=-0.38 and R=-0.49). Bodies of water near wastewater treatment plants, agricultural fields, population dense areas, and marinas saw high levels of aggregation. River forks, and larger water masses in the San Francisco Bay-Delta also exhibited higher aggregation. Future work should aim to incorporate a larger volume of in-situ validation datasets, examine multi-year seasonal transport dynamics, and scale this method to other highly populated areas in a more recent timeframe.

title: Uncovering patterns and drivers of forest loss in the western Congo Basin
authors: Hannah Stouter, Alysson Bery, Sumalika Biswas, Fanny Djomkam, Benis Egoh, Wesner Epie, Mody Lacour and Elsa Ordway
main_session: Tropical Variability and Interbasin Interactions Across Scales: Earth Observations, Processes, Modeling, and Global Impacts I Poster
abstract: Forest loss has accelerated in the Congo Basin, the world’s second-largest tropical forest, over the last decade. Disturbance in tropical forests impacts carbon emissions and the strength of the carbon sink, threatens biodiversity, jeopardizes key ecosystem services, and at large scales, can disrupt land-atmosphere interactions. However, land is also needed to meet growing demand for food, fuel, fiber, and other development goals. In the Congo Basin, forest loss is primarily driven by small-scale rotational agriculture to meet household food needs. However, the landscape-scale patterns of accelerating forest loss and its local drivers remain underexplored. We develop a machine learning model using satellite-based optical and radar data from Landsat, the Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel-2 (HLS) dataset, and Sentinel-1 to map land cover from 2000-2025 over a 482,500 km 2 region in the western Congo Basin, centered around the Dja Biosphere Reserve in Cameroon. In addition, to understand the community and household factors driving land use change and small-scale agricultural expansion, we conducted household surveys (n=312) in 32 villages around the Dja in 2024. At a landscape scale, our findings align with previous work confirming that small-scale agriculture is the primary driver of forest loss in this region. At a local scale, preliminary results from the household surveys reveal that more than 80% of agricultural fields are created from primary or secondary forest. Moreover, while household demand for food and income is the primary driver of field creation, these factors interact with land tenure security and domestic and international market pressures to influence farmer decisions around crop planting. Our results highlight that to effectively curb deforestation in the Congo Basin efforts must address the locally specific, underlying, and intertwined drivers of deforestation. For example, in regions like the Dja, reducing deforestation may rely on efforts that support household food and livelihood security, such as supporting solutions that increase yields of staple crops on existing agricultural fields and or programs such as payments for ecosystem services (PES) that incentivise farmers to conserve forest.

title: Healing Across a Continent: Energy–Water Co-Limitation of Forest Disturbance Recovery Across the NEON Network
authors: Bozheng Jiao, Organization Not Listed, Shenyang, China and Di Yang, University of Florida, Department of Geography, Ft Walton Beach, United States
main_session: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Forest Disturbance and Recovery I Poster
abstract: The rate at which a forest regains canopy function after disturbance is a direct, measurable signature of ecological resilience, but whether recovery is governed primarily by energy or by water availability remains unresolved at continental scale because existing studies are often single‑biome and methodologically inconsistent. Here we present a network‑consistent synthesis of forest disturbance and recovery across 28 forested National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) sites, from tropical (~18°N) to boreal (~65°N) forests. Using a harmonized Landsat 5/7/8/9 record (1985–2024) and the LandTrendr temporal‑segmentation algorithm, we quantify site‑level disturbance magnitude, spectral recovery ratio, post‑2000 disturbance fraction, and data density, and relate site‑level recovery to mean annual temperature, precipitation, elevation, and disturbance severity. Recovery did not increase monotonically with mean annual temperature, and a quadratic temperature model did not support a hump‑shaped response. Instead, recovery differences were better explained by a multivariate model including precipitation, elevation, and disturbance magnitude. Precipitation significantly improved the climate‑only model, whereas elevation was negatively associated with recovery in the full model. Contrary to the severity‑dependent resilience hypothesis, recovery was positively associated with mean disturbance magnitude at the site scale and the magnitude × temperature interaction was not significant. These results refine the energy‑water co‑limitation hypothesis by showing that recovery is not controlled by temperature alone. The framework provides a continental baseline that NEON’s airborne and in‑situ observations can mechanistically validate.

title: Does BRDF Correction Matter for PROSAIL Leaf Area Index Retrieval? An Evaluation Across Three Sentinel-2 Derived Products for Corn and Soybean
authors: Nitish Singh and Soumyashree Kar, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Centre of Studies in Resources Engineering, Mumbai, India
main_session: Remote Sensing for Sustainable Agriculture I Poster
abstract: Satellite retrievals of leaf area index (LAI) from radiative transfer models such as PROSAIL assume nadir-viewing reflectance, yet the Sentinel-2 MultiSpectral Instrument (MSI) images across a 290 km swath at view zenith angles up to about 12 degrees, introducing bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) effects that grow with wavelength and are largest in the near-infrared and shortwave-infrared bands. The extent to which these directional effects degrade operational LAI retrieval, and whether analysis-ready products already remove them, remains unquantified for row crops. To date, no study isolates the reflectance-product effect on PROSAIL LAI retrieval by holding the inversion machinery fixed across raw, BRDF-corrected, and harmonized Sentinel-2 inputs for row crops. This work compares three Sentinel-2-derived surface reflectance products as input to an identical PROSAIL inversion: (1) raw Level-2A (Sen2Cor, no angular normalization); (2) native L2A normalized to nadir BRDF-adjusted reflectance using the c-factor method via the sen2nbar Python package; and (3) Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) S30 v2.0, already nadir-BRDF- and bandpass-adjusted at 30 m. Corn (Zea mays) and soybean (Glycine max) are analyzed separately with crop-specific priors (leaf-angle distribution, hot-spot, chlorophyll) using PROSPECT-D coupled with 4SAIL and a hybrid feed-forward neural-network inversion, holding the look-up table, priors, architecture, and six common bands (B2, B3, B4, B8A, B11, B12, all area-averaged to 30 m) fixed across treatments to isolate the reflectance-product effect. The study spans two growing seasons (2023, 2024) over a full corn-soybean rotation at flux-tower sites near Ames, Iowa and Mead, Nebraska, with per-pixel crop labels from the USDA Cropland Data Layer. The retrievals are evaluated against MODIS MCD15A3H LAI and, where available, in-situ AmeriFlux LAI, using RMSE, bias, R-squared, temporal smoothness, and view-zenith-angle dependence of error as performance metrics. The comparison substantiates whether explicit BRDF correction of native Sentinel-2 and the harmonization already applied in HLS S30 yield equivalent PROSAIL LAI, informing product choice for operational Corn Belt crop monitoring.

title: Cover Crop Mapping in the Southern High Plains of Texas
authors: Dorothy Janick, Oliver Matus-Bond, Shawronna Sengupta and Jaya Hafner
main_session: Remote Sensing for Sustainable Agriculture I Poster
abstract: The Southern High Plains of Texas is a semi-arid agricultural region that is vulnerable to soil erosion and water scarcity. Winter cover cropping, the practice of sowing crops during the winter season specifically for ecological benefits rather than for harvest, is a potential strategy for reducing erosion. However, trends in cover crop adoption and their effects on water dynamics in the region are insufficiently understood. In partnership with the Sandhills Area Research Association, Bamert Seed Company, and Texas A&M AgriLife, we used field data from farmers and Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery to test the feasibility of mapping winter cover cropping in the region, characterize spatial patterns in winter cover crop adoption, and explore evapotranspiration and soil moisture trends on winter cover cropped fields using a research site as a case study. We developed a random forest model to detect winter cover-cropped fields. The model results indicated that cover crop mapping in the region was improved by incorporating diverse vegetation and soil indices, termination detection, and field data from farmers. Preliminary results from satellite-derived evapotranspiration and soil moisture data showed that cover crops impact water availability, but further validation is needed. These results supported the partners in evaluating cover crop adoption, assessing cover crop impacts on water supply, and informing future research in the region.

title: Operational Field-Scale Management Products for Cropland GHG Inventories and Projections
authors: Sarah Kanee, Charlotte Malmborg, Katherine Rein, Mrinalee Reddy, Xinyuan Ji, Matthew Kim, Akash Boraraja Varavu, Alexey Shiklomanov, Chris Black, David LeBauer and Michael Dietze
main_session: Remote Sensing for Sustainable Agriculture I Poster
abstract: Remote sensing provides scalable observations of crop type, phenology, and disturbance, but agricultural greenhouse gas (GHG) inventories and projections require a broader set of field-scale, temporally resolved management inputs. Existing data are fragmented and rarely resolve event timing, intensity, or sequencing. We present an operational, open-source system within the Predictive Ecosystem Analyzer (PEcAn) multi-model workflow that integrates satellite, meteorological, soil, and agronomic data into model-ready events for process-based models. We demonstrate the system across California croplands using LandIQ parcels and crop classifications. Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) time series are processed with the Multi-Source Land Surface Phenology (MSLSP) algorithm to estimate seasonal phenology, while Normalized Difference Tillage Index (NDTI) time series derived from HLS are used to infer tillage during fallow periods. Crop identity and phenological timing condition downstream products: crop-specific traits are used to initialize carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) pools at planting and estimate biomass removal and residue inputs at harvest; phenological development informs irrigation demand modeled from precipitation, reference evapotranspiration, and soil water-holding capacity; and crop identity conditions fertilizer and organic-amendment rates, timing, and C properties. These products are aligned into coordinated parcel-level events for planting, leaf-on, leaf-off, harvest, tillage, irrigation, fertilization, and organic amendments, with documented provenance, quality-control flags, and observational gaps. The events initialize and drive simulations with the Simplified Photosynthesis and Evapotranspiration Model (SIPNET), which estimates how cropland C and N budgets vary with parcel-specific management timing and intensity under historical and alternative management scenarios. The code and documentation are openly available through PEcAn’s GitHub. Although implemented in California, the workflow is transferable to regions with analogous parcel, crop, satellite, meteorological, soil, and agronomic data.

title: Evaluating Legacy and Regionally Tuned Burned-Area Indices for Canadian Wildfires
authors: Emraul Islam Emon, Afia Mubassira Islam, Christopher Ball, Ajay Kumar Patel, Vasit Sagan, Sahin Ozdemir, Tugce Baser, Dr. Go Iwahana, PhD and Joel T Johnson
main_session: Wildfire Analysis Using Remote Sensing, Multisensor Fusion, Multisource Data Integration, and Artificial Intelligence III GeoBurst Poster
abstract: Canada’s record-breaking 2023 wildfire season, widespread burning in 2025, and renewed wildfire activity during the ongoing 2026 season highlight the need for timely and regionally appropriate burned-area mapping. In 2023, more than 18.5 million ha burned nationally, more than twice the previous Canadian record. For burned area detection, remote sensing studies continue to rely largely on established spectral indices such as the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR). Indices developed for broad global applications, however, may not be optimal for vegetation, surface water conditions, soils, and disturbance patterns of Canada’s boreal landscapes. We investigate whether a regionally tuned index can improve burned–unburned discrimination regionally. We develop pixel-level labels using a triple-confirmation framework requiring spatial and temporal agreement among National Burned Area Composite perimeters and MODIS burned-area and active-fire products. Each confirmed burned pixel is assigned an independently supported burn date rather than a fire-wide ignition date, allowing post-fire observations to be aligned across fires and regions. The analysis emphasizes the 2023 and 2025 Canadian fire seasons and extends to 2026 fires using observations and agency perimeters available through a current-season cutoff. A broad library of candidate indices is evaluated using MODIS and Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel (HLS) imagery. The search spans two- to four-band linear and nonlinear combinations of visible, near-infrared, and shortwave-infrared reflectances. Candidates are compared with NBR and other established indices using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, Bhattacharyya distance, F1 score, and Cohen’s d. Performance is assessed across fires, years, sensors, ecological zones, and post-fire periods to identify effective formulations transferable between sensor systems. Independent evaluation is performed using provenance-screened provincial and territorial fire-agency perimeters compiled in the Canadian National Fire Database, emphasizing GPS, infrared, and field-derived boundaries where source information is available. The presentation will compare regionally tuned and legacy formulations across Canada’s boreal environments and between MODIS and HLS observations.

title: Toward Fully Probabilistic Atmospheric Correction and Harmonization of the Landsat Record
authors: Nimrod Carmon, Organization Not Listed, Washington, DC, United States
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat I Oral
abstract: Landsat provides the foundational calibrated record for monitoring Earth’s surface, but its growing use in multi-sensor time series and operational decisions requires uncertainty information not routinely available in surface-reflectance products. Atmospheric variability, instrument noise, auxiliary-data limitations, topography, bidirectional reflectance effects, and radiative-transfer approximations introduce errors that vary across pixels, bands, sensors, and acquisition geometries. Without explicit uncertainty characterization, these effects can be misinterpreted as surface change and limit harmonization across Earth-observation missions. We present a framework for adapting ISOFIT, an open-source optimal-estimation atmospheric-correction system, to the Landsat archive and upcoming Landsat missions. The approach retrieves surface reflectance and, where supported, atmospheric properties while incorporating uncertainties from measurements, auxiliary inputs, and forward-model assumptions. The products provide pixel-level, band-specific uncertainty estimates. The framework accounts for sensor-specific spectral response functions, calibration, noise, and auxiliary-data availability. Optional topography- and BRDF-aware formulations can reduce illumination-dependent biases or represent their unresolved effects within the uncertainty budget. This probabilistic framework provides a physically traceable basis for harmonization across the historical Landsat record, Landsat 8 and 9, Sentinel-2 and HLS, upcoming Landsat missions, and hyperspectral missions including EMIT, EAGLE, and CHIME. Scalable cloud implementation will support archive-scale processing. Uncertainty-aware products can help distinguish geophysical change from retrieval variability, strengthening applications in vegetation monitoring, agriculture, water resources, snow and ice, land-use change, carbon accounting, and disaster response.

title: Tailored Active Fire Data for Tropical Forests and Peatlands using Landsat and Sentinel-2: First Insights from Indonesia
authors: Shi Jun Wee, Dr. Shane Coffield, Xiao-Peng Song and Douglas C Morton
main_session: Tropical Forests Under a Changing Environment II Oral
abstract: Tropical forests are experiencing a surge in fire activity, driven by intensifying droughts and land-use change. Recent events, particularly during El Niño years, have caused substantial carbon emissions, biodiversity loss, and widespread public health impacts, underscoring the urgency to prevent future occurrences of similar scale. However, our understanding of tropical fire dynamics remains severely limited by data availability. Current operational active fire products (e.g., MODIS and VIIRS-based) are designed for global fire monitoring and are therefore intentionally conservative. With their coarse spatial resolutions, these products chronically underestimate fires in tropical forests and peatlands due to persistent cloud cover, small fire sizes, and canopy obscuration. While moderate-resolution sensors (e.g., Landsat) can improve detection of smaller fires, they are limited by long revisit intervals (i.e., 8 days with Landsat 8 and 9), and current products are not yet routinely available across the tropics. To bridge these gaps, we developed an active fire algorithm tailored specifically for tropical forests and peatlands using Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) data, achieving a 2–3 day revisit interval at 30-m resolution. We demonstrate the algorithm’s capabilities across Indonesia’s forests and peatlands, which are actively threatened by large-scale land conversion and are currently experiencing a surge in early-season fires from the ongoing 2026 El Niño event. In 2023, our algorithm using only L30 data detected nearly 5 times more active fire pixels across forests and peat swamp forests than NASA’s Landsat-based algorithm, and approximately 12 times more active fire pixels with the inclusion of S30 data. Using this dataset, we also provide updated estimates of fire activity across managed and unmanaged lands to better characterize contemporary patterns of fire behavior, including fire size, spread rates, and persistence in forests and peatlands. We also compare fire activity in El Niño and non-El Niño years to evaluate changes in fire behavior and persistence during drought years. In the near term, our algorithm will be scaled across forests and peatlands in Amazonia and the Congo Basin, advancing fire monitoring across threatened tropical ecosystems.

title: Spatiotemporal Fusion of Landsat and VIIRS Imagery for Monitoring Daily Reservoir Storage Variations
authors: Chi Hsiang Huang, Shuai Zhang and Huilin Gao
main_session: Remote Sensing of Rivers, Lakes, and Wetlands II Oral
abstract: The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) provides high temporal resolution satellite observations, offering strong potential for detecting rapid changes in water storage caused by human-induced regulations, such as reservoir sediment flushing, flood control and hydropower generation. Capturing these rapid dynamics is essential for optimizing sustainable water management, mitigating downstream environmental impacts, and enhancing regional water security. However, its coarse spatial resolution (375m) leads to large errors for small- and medium-sized water bodies (<100km2). Mixed shoreline pixels further increase uncertainty and reduce the stability of water-extent estimation. To improve the accuracy and spatiotemporal resolution of the reservoir area and storage estimations, we develop an image-fusion framework built on a U-Net architecture and diffusion-based generative models. The framework pairs hundreds of harmonized Landsat 8/9 (HLSL30) and VIIRS imageries acquired at similar dates from over a dozen locations to train the spatial/radiometric relationship between the two sensors and to generate 30-m -resolution reflectance images at visible and NIR bands from daily VIIRS observations. As the high uncertainties usually occur near the shorelines, only mixed shoreline pixels are used to train the fusion model to avoid overfitting. Lastly, cloud-contaminated areas are reconstructed using historical water-occurrence maps and shoreline information from previous cloud-free observations. Compared with the HLSL30 image acquired on a similar date, the testing results demonstrate a 30% improvement in VIIRS reflectance accuracy, with median R² rising from 0.64 to 0.83 across 11 representative reservoirs across a range of sizes and locations. We further apply this framework across 164 global reservoirs from 2014 to 2025 . Then, the fused surface area estimates are applied to the area-storage curves from the 3D-LAKES dataset converted into water-storage time series and validated against in situ measurements. This framework leverages Landsat’s high spatial resolution and VIIRS daily frequency to support reservoir management, flood monitoring, and assessments of human impacts on surface-water dynamics.

title: From California to Central Africa: leveraging satellite remote sensing to inform adaptive forest management under compound stressors
authors: Elsa Ordway, Hudson Billock, Carissa DeRanek, Anna Ongjoco, Natalie Queally and Hannah Stouter
main_session: Sustainable Forest Management Under Compounding Stressors: Wildfire, Insects, and Climate Impacts I Oral
abstract: Forests worldwide face increasing pressure from interacting stressors including wildfire, drought, and deforestation. Improving forest resilience requires coordinated observations that link ecosystem processes, disturbance dynamics, and ecosystem condition. We present three case studies demonstrating how remote sensing can support adaptive forest management across California and Central Africa. Although these regions differ markedly in climate and ecology, both face mounting pressures on their forests. First, we use long-term satellite archives to quantify post-fire vegetation recovery following 1,116 California wildfires (1999–2020). Recovery has slowed over the past two decades, with post-fire hot drought compounding the additive effects of heat and drought, particularly in mid-elevation forests and large, high-severity burn areas, highlighting priority sites for restoration and fuel management. Second, we develop a scalable, open-source framework to produce spatially explicit, temporally continuous estimates of canopy water content (CWC), a key indicator of vegetation health and wildfire risk. By combining NASA EMIT hyperspectral observations, Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel (HLS) imagery, and deep learning, we extend CWC monitoring across the HLS archive at high spatial and temporal resolution. The resulting time series reveals persistent vegetation water deficits following California's megadrought despite episodic wet years, demonstrating the value of continuous CWC monitoring for identifying drought legacies and anticipating fire risk. Finally, we examine increasing fire activity in the Congo Basin, where climate change, agricultural expansion, and widespread under-detection of understory fires limit assessments of ecosystem vulnerability. We show how satellite observations, integrated with local expertise and in situ ecological studies, can improve detection of understory fires, quantify ecosystem impacts, and support adaptive management in tropical forests. Together, these case studies demonstrate how integrated remote sensing can reduce uncertainty surrounding compound disturbances while informing forest management, fire risk assessment, and climate resilience.

title: From Modular Hydroinformatics to Foundation Models: Probing Reusable Representations Across Space, Time, and Tasks
authors: Gerald Corzo Perez, IHE Delft Institute for Water Education, Delft, Netherlands
main_session: Geospatial Foundation Model and Remote Sensing for Hydrologic Prediction Across the Terrestrial Water Cycle II Oral
abstract: Hydroinformatics has long addressed complex systems by dividing them into regimes, processes, and specialized models, then recombining their outputs through committee and hybrid architectures. Deep learning moved part of this decomposition inside the model: LSTMs learned temporal memory, CNNs learned spatial structure, and ConvLSTMs learned their joint evolution. Foundation models extend this trajectory by learning reusable representations from broad data, but their hydrological value depends on whether those representations transfer across space, time, and tasks. We examine TerraMind, Clay, Prithvi, and Hydro FM as alternative Earth-observation backbones within a backbone-agnostic Hydrological Foundation Architecture (HFA). A controlled Hydro FM probe showed that frozen early-layer features with a 0.01-second logistic-regression classifier achieved IoU 0.991 and boundary F1 0.992 on a synthetic 12-band coastal scene, compared with IoU 0.529 and 0.518 for NDWI and MNDWI. A nonlinear multiscale probe did not improve accuracy, showing that task information was readily accessible, while also confirming that a simple within-scene benchmark cannot establish geographic transfer. Two bridge experiments tested how distributed cell states connect to hydrological prediction. Spatial neighbors did not improve one-step soil-moisture prediction because persistence saturated the task (R2=0.9997). In contrast, nonlinear processing of distributed soil-moisture cells improved next-step discharge prediction from R2=0.702 to 0.827, whereas a linear formulation deteriorated. These results support nonlinear state fusion, but not yet temporal, topological, or cross-task generalization. Grounded in earlier Amazon space-time and Magdalena network- and operation-aware modelling, the proposed HFA maps alternative or complementary EO backbones through model-specific adapters into a common hydrological state core with temporal evolution, river and reservoir connectivity, local adaptation, physical constraints, and task-conditioned outputs. Foundation models are thus reusable perceptual cores, not universal replacements for hydrological models.

title: Knowing Where vs. Knowing What: Geography-Aware Evaluation of Geospatial Foundation Models
authors: Jichao Fang, Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL, United States and Wei Luo, Northern Illinois Univeristy, DeKalb, United States
main_session: Open Earth System Science Data, Algorithms, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Advance Scientific Discovery and Applications III Poster
abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are becoming a common representation layer for Earth observation. However, Earth data are not independent as most attributes are spatially autocorrelated. A model can perform well on a conventional random split because it recognizes where a sample is, instead of having learned a relationship that will hold in a new region. We compare four widely used representations -- AlphaEarth, OlmoEarth, Clay, and Prithvi -- on the same ten thousand near-global set of locations and ten targets spanning climate, topography, vegetation, human activity, and land cover. For each case, we evaluate the embeddings alongside a coordinate-only model. For every task evaluation, we progressively separate training and test data, from random splits to continent holdout. We introduce GeoRecovery to describe how an embedding performs once the coordinate model can no longer rely on local spatial interpolation, and we interpret it together with the raw scores in each held-out region. All four representations look stronger under random splitting. The degradation in performance when evaluated on geographic and continent hold-out depends on the representation and the task. For example, AlphaEarth has a clear advantage for elevation, consistent with its broad environmental training context. The other encoders maintain useful signals for canopy height, terrain texture, land cover, and built environments. Sometimes a good pooled score can mask failure on a given continent. Using the four-season input instead of the single annual composite generally results in better performance in new regions, but it also makes it easier to recover latitude from the embeddings, showing that better predictions and stronger geographic structure can increase together. As a result, we argue that geography-aware evaluation against an explicit coordinate baseline is needed to read GFM benchmarks correctly.

title: Differentiable modeling for corn yield prediction by unifying machine learning and crop growth model
authors: Zhen Zhao and Yanghui Kang, Virginia Tech, Department of Biological Systems Engineering, Blacksburg, Virginia, United States
main_session: Crop Modeling, Data Assimilation, and Machine Learning for Agricultural Decision Support III Poster
abstract: Timely and accurate crop yield prediction is essential for agricultural management and food security. Crop growth models mechanistically simulate crop development and are well developed at plot or field scales, but their large-scale application is constrained by limited calibration observations, incomplete management inputs, and challenges in efficiently leveraging large and heterogeneous data. Machine learning approaches can flexibly learn from satellite and environmental observations, yet scarce training data and unobserved drivers limit their robustness and generalization. Recent advances in differentiable modeling address these limitations by embedding physical processes within end-to-end trainable machine learning frameworks that can be directly constrained by sparse, heterogeneous, or multiscale observations. In this study, we develop DiffSAFY, a differentiable implementation of the Simple Algorithm For Yield estimates (SAFY) crop model, and apply it to predict corn yield from field to county levels across the U.S. Corn Belt. DiffSAFY is trained with county-level crop yield data and 30m Leaf area index (LAI) time series derived from Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery. The predictions are validated against independent yield observations at field and county levels. We benchmark DiffSAFY with the original SAFY model and pure machine learning approaches in prediction accuracy, extrapolation capability, and computational efficiency. DiffSAFY provides a unified framework integrating mechanistic models, machine learning, and heterogeneous observations for large-scale, high-resolution yield prediction. The proposed framework has the potential to advance robust, physically consistent, and scalable crop monitoring and modeling to support agricultural decision-making.

title: Do Geospatial Foundation Models Beat Task-Specific U-Nets for Flood Mapping Under Label Scarcity? A Split-Design Study on Sen1Floods11.
authors: ABSTRACT WITHDRAWN
main_session: Open Earth System Science Data, Algorithms, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Advance Scientific Discovery and Applications III Poster
abstract: Flood mapping from satellite imagery requires hand labels that are expensive and scarce, and when used in the real world, deployment asks a model to analyze regions it never saw in its training dataset. Geospatial foundation models, or GFM’s for short, promise a label-efficient alternative to this issue. However, they are typically validated on random train/test splits that place chips from the same flood event on training and testing sides, leading to often inaccurate results and generalization. This study asks whether frozen-encoder GFMs, Prithvi-EO-2.0 and Clay in this experiment, beat a fully-trained U-Net when labels are scarce and the test region is truly unseen. Using the Sen1Floods11 hand-labeled subset (446 chips, 11 events), we run a controlled 90-evaluation matrix -- three models by five label budgets {5,10,25,50,100}% by three seeds -- under a fair-comparison protocol: one shared 6-band Sentinel-2 input, one optimizer, loss, and early-stopping rule. Every model is scored on two held-out sets: an in-region test (same events, optimistic) and an out-of-region test (three entirely separate events: arid Somalia, monsoon Sri-Lanka, temperate Spain). We find the GFM advantage is concentrated on hard, unseen regions at low label budgets ununiformly: at 10% labels, Clay beats the U-Net on all three held-out events across all three seeds (Somalia +0.21 water-IoU), while on easy scenes such as Spain, both results are equivalent. Prithvi-EO-2.0 lacks the U-Net at most budgets and is weakest at full labels, meaning that the blanket term of “foundation model” isn’t inherently superior to U-Nets.

title: Effects of Nadir View Assumption on the Atmospheric Correction of Landsat Data
authors: Junchang Ju, University of Maryland College Park, College Park, MD, United States, Eric Vermote, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Terrestrial Information Systems Laboratory, Greenbelt, MD, United States, Trang Vo, NASA IMPACT, Huntsville, United States, Madhu Sridhar, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL, United States, Weile Wang, NASA/AMES Research Center, Moffett Field, United States, Qiang Zhou, Science Systems and Applications, Inc., Maryland, United States, Christopher S R Neigh, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Biospheric Sciences Laboratory, Greenbelt, MD, United States and Eric Vermote
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat II Poster
abstract: Landsat sensors, with ±7.5° off-nadir scan, have traditionally been treated as narrow field-of-view instruments. Despite the modest scan angle range, the angular dependence of Landsat surface reflectance has long been recognized, and BRDF normalization methods have been developed over the past two decades. Yet atmospheric correction of Landsat imagery continues to assume nadir viewing in general, most notably in the USGS adaptation of the original Land Surface Reflectance Code (LaSRC) to reduce runtime costs.
