The adapted version is used for USGS Landsat Collection 2 surface reflectance and the NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) products. Specifically, the view zenith angle is hardcoded to zero, and consequently the variation in the Rayleigh scattering phase function across the swath is not accounted for. This nadir=view assumption introduces a systematic, geometry-dependent error in Rayleigh path reflectance. At the forward-looking swath edge, Rayleigh scatter intensity is approximately 4–5% weaker than at nadir; at the backward-looking swath edge it is 3–4% stronger — a directional pattern analogous to land surface BRDF behavior. When pixels from the sidelaps of adjacent swaths are considered together, the combined error in Rayleigh path reflectance can reach 6–8%. Although this error affects all spectral bands, it is most consequential in the blue band, where Rayleigh path reflectance typically exceeds surface reflectance for most land cover types. Because LaSRC uses the blue band to retrieve aerosol optical thickness (AOT), errors in blue-band Rayleigh correction propagate into AOT estimation and cascade into surface reflectance retrieval across all bands, and ultimately compromise BRDF correction and multi-temporal consistency. Using annual time series of Landsat 8 and 9 observations over sites spanning a range of latitudes, we quantify the magnitude and seasonal variation of this error and evaluate how accounting for per-pixel view angle variation in the Rayleigh scattering phase function — and potentially in the aerosol scattering phase function and upward path length — improves the accuracy and angular consistency of LaSRC surface reflectance retrievals.

title: Physics-Guided Neural Networks for Remote Sensing-based Evapotranspiration Modeling
authors: Ananya Sharma and Di Tian, Auburn University, Department of Crop, Soil & Environmental Sciences, Auburn, United States
main_session: Evapotranspiration (ET): Advances in In Situ ET Measurements and Remote Sensing–Based ET Estimation, Mapping, and Evaluation IV Poster
abstract: Evapotranspiration (ET) regulates land-atmosphere water, energy, and carbon exchange. It remains a challenge to estimate across heterogeneous, observation-sparse regions. Here, we develop physics-guided neural networks (PGNNs) to estimate latent heat flux (LE), the energy equivalent of ET, based on harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, and land data assimilation meteorological forcings by incorporating surface energy balance and energy partitioning through physics layers. Model estimates are evaluated against AmeriFlux eddy covariance flux observations across the contiguous United States. We designed and tested three physics-integration strategies: surface energy balance constraints (PGNN-SEB), neural network-learned biophysical constraints coupled with a Priestley-Taylor Jet Propulsion Laboratory (PT-JPL) based physics layer (PGNN-PT-JPL), and neural-network-learned biophysical constraints coupled with a two-source energy balance (TSEB) based physics layer (PGNN-TSEB) that partitions fluxes between soil and canopy components. PGNN models are benchmarked against a purely data-driven neural network and the conventional process-based PT-JPL model. Model generalizability is assessed across random, temporal, spatial, and extreme-condition holdouts. PGNN-SEB matched the data-driven neural network in overall LE accuracy while improving physical consistency and reducing extreme-condition RMSE by 20.5 W m⁻² under cold, low-LE conditions and 99.1 W m⁻² under hot, high-LE conditions. PGNN-PT-JPL performed best, reducing RMSE from 116.7 to 71.4 W m⁻² and increasing R² from 0.39 to 0.77 relative to PT-JPL. Compared with the data-driven neural network, it reduced RMSE from 77.4 to 71.4 W m⁻² while achieving near-zero internal surface energy balance closure error. Ongoing experiments extend the framework to PGNN-TSEB to assess whether explicit soil-canopy flux partitioning provides additional benefits. Results demonstrate that coupling neural network learned empirical terms with physical equations enables robust and physically consistent LE estimation under extrapolative extreme and data-sparse conditions, outperforming both process-based and data-driven machine learning models.

title: Cloud-Supported and Sensor-Agnostic: Re-Engineering the SPIReS Algorithm into an Operationally Ready Open Pipeline for Landsat Product Generation
authors: Niklas Griessbaum, Ross Palomaki, Brent Wilder, Karl Rittger, Christopher J Crawford and Ned Bair
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat II Poster
abstract: Snow supplies water to nearly two billion people, yet the USGS's operational Landsat snow products are constrained less by physics than by their underlying software. Fractional snow-covered area (fSCA) comes from a closed-source spectral-unmixing algorithm, while the leading open, physically based alternative, Snow Property Inversion from Remote Sensing (SPIReS), existed only as legacy MATLAB research software bound to a specific computing host, directory layout, and on-disk file conventions. That architecture is not portable, reproducible, or scalable to the ~3.3 terabytes the forthcoming Landsat 10 mission will add daily. We present a ground-up re-engineering of SPIReS into a modular, open-source (MIT) pipeline for cloud-scale product generation. Independent packages (sensor input/output, lookup tables, a hybrid Python/C++ inversion core, and post-processing) are joined by executable xarray data contracts that fix the data schema at every boundary, so each stage is tested in isolation and new sensors plug in through a common adapter, spanning MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat, Sentinel-2, and the Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) product. A Dask/SLURM layer parallelizes retrieval over image stacks and space-time data cubes. The result: a documented, tested, reproducible, cloud-ready engine built for open science. This modernization advances snow remote sensing and next-generation Landsat fSCA products that also report snow grain size and light-absorbing-particle concentration. We also address the reflectance "hooking" artifact, recently identified in imaging-spectrometer data, that mimics dirty snow. Retrievals will be validated at and near the Jeff Dozier Snow Study Site (Mammoth Mountain, 2940 m), a mid-latitude site with deep, seasonally polluted snow. Following the USGS's established Science-Algorithms-to-Operations pathway, we will demonstrate end-to-end Landsat and HLS retrievals, bringing SPIReS to operational readiness for Landsat and Landsat 10.

title: Construct Shift as an Axis of Geographic Transfer Failure in Climate GeoAI: Cross-Climate Divergence of Borrowed Vulnerability Priorities
authors: Md Shahriar Sharif, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, United States and Insoo Kim, Arizona State University, School of Geographical Sciences and Urban Planning, Tempe, AZ, United States
main_session: Advancing AI for Environmental Sustainability: Data, Methods, and Applications II Poster
abstract: Climate GeoAI models are increasingly trained in one city and transferred to another. Transfer failure is usually explained by covariate shift and relationship shift, an explanation that is complete only when the target is measured. Heat vulnerability indices are not directly observed but constructed from measured indicators, and their construction rule is defined locally. We identify a third mechanism, construct shift: error arising purely because the target's construction rule differs between places, a spatial analogue of measurement non-invariance. Across six US cities in two climate regimes (140 to 1,068 tracts), we build three targets over one predictor set: land surface temperature, a physical control with zero construct shift, a fixed weight index, and a city-specific PCA index, both standardized within each city. RF and XGBoost are trained on tabular predictors and on frozen Prithvi EO 2.0 embeddings, with ridge probes separating representation from learner, yielding 360 models across 30 directed zero-retraining transfers. Rather than differencing two indices' errors, which is confounded by scale, we transport the rule itself: source fitted PCA weights applied to target tracts, compared with the native rule by rank, top-k and kappa agreement. Common support collapses from 54% within the arid group to under 2% across climates. Global rankings still transport almost perfectly (ρ = 0.98), but priority neighborhoods do not: a borrowed rule recovers 85% of top decile tracts overall, 81% across climates and 67% at worst, missing 7 of Atlanta's 21 highest-priority tracts. Agreement rises with overlap (ρ = 0.75), yet divergence triples between arid and humid pairs at matched covariate distance (0.04 versus 0.11). Embedding-only models fail on the indices (R²= 0.40 to 0.47) but succeed on temperature, showing the ceiling is the feature set, not the learner. Construct shift therefore belongs in the diagnostic vocabulary wherever constructed targets are transported. This opens a new direction for transferable Climate GeoAI, with implications for composite indices beyond heat vulnerability. Future work should validate the concept against observed heat morbidity and test whether local adaptation repairs what better features cannot.

title: Impacts of Urban Green Space on Ground-Level Ozone Concentrations: Focusing on Nonlinearities under Varying Summer Meteorological Conditions
authors: Eunji Kim and Heeyeun Yoon, Seoul National University, Department of Landscape Architecture and Rural Systems Engineering, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South)
main_session: Urban Air Pollution: Interaction with Weather/Climate and Impact on Health I Poster
abstract: Rising summer temperatures due to climate change have contributed to a long-term increase in ground-level ozone concentrations and heightened the risk of high-ozone episodes. This trend is associated with intensified solar radiation, atmospheric stagnation, and increased emissions of ozone precursors under high-temperature conditions. Ground-level ozone can impose socioeconomic burdens by causing symptoms such as coughing, shortness of breath, and impaired lung function, as well as by limiting outdoor activities and work capacity. Urban green space (UGS) has been recognized as a nature-based solution for lowering atmospheric ozone concentrations through deposition onto leaf surfaces and uptake through stomata. However, the ozone-regulating effects of UGS exhibit nonlinear patterns that vary with meteorological conditions and vegetation greenness, vitality, and moisture status. In particular, during heatwaves, increased water stress and biogenic volatile organic compound emissions may further aggravate ozone pollution. Previous studies have largely examined climate change-induced declines in vegetation activity and the air pollution mitigation effects of UGS separately. Consequently, how the ozone-reduction capacity of UGS changes under high summer temperatures remains insufficiently understood. Against this backdrop, this study aims to investigate how UGS affects ground-level ozone concentrations under different summer meteorological conditions. The analysis uses daily data from 2018 to 2025 for approximately 500 urban air quality monitoring stations across South Korea. We employ XGBoost to estimate complex nonlinear relationships and interactions between meteorological conditions and UGS characteristics within buffers around each station. Next, we interpret the contributions of the key variables and directions of their effects through Shapley additive explanations and accumulated local effects. The dependent variable is the daily maximum 8-hour average ozone concentration. The main input data include UGS conditions derived from Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery and meteorological factors, such as temperature, humidity, and drought. Our findings can provide a scientific basis for UGS planning and management in response to increasingly severe climate change.

title: Severe Drought Reveals Hidden Vulnerabilities of Intensively Managed European Forests
authors: ABSTRACT WITHDRAWN
main_session: Advance in Remote Sensing and Modeling of Trees and Forest Ecosystems I Poster
abstract: Forest management is crucial for sustaining forest functioning under increasingly severe drought. While previous research indicates significant differences in drought resistance and recovery between managed and unmanaged forests, the effects of various management strategies on drought vulnerability within managed forests remain unclear. We used HLS NIRv time series, SPEI-3-based drought exposure, European forest-management map and canopy structural-diversity data to assess peak canopy impact and recovery time during the 2022 European drought. Management types showed modest average differences, but diverged significantly with increased drought exposure. Under high drought exposure, 68.8% of very intensively managed forests entered a high-impact, slow-recovery state, compared to 38.3–39.5% for other management strategies. This pattern persisted across different drought exposure and risk definitions, even after considering spatial dependence. Intensive management greatly reduced canopy structural diversity. In contrast, forests with complex structures suffered less damage and recovered faster from drought, highlighting the protective role of canopy structure. These findings indicate that while intensive management's vulnerability may be hidden during mild droughts, it becomes evident during severe drought. The research also highlights canopy structural complexity as crucial for forest drought resilience and emphasizes considering management intensity in climate-adaptive forest strategies.

title: A multiscale framework for wheat tiller density estimation from UAS and satellite multispectral imagery using deep learning
authors: Santosh Subedi, Maitiniyazi Maimaitijiang, Kushal Poudel, Swas Kaushal, Mr. Ubaid Janjua, Mohammad Maruf Billah, Subash Thapa, Hillson Ghimire, Dante Jerome Koupal, Muhammad Ali Irshad, Sunish K. Sehgal, Mandeep Singh and Jyotirmoy Halder
main_session: Advancing AI for Environmental Sustainability: Data, Methods, and Applications II Poster
abstract: Tiller density is an important determinant of wheat yield potential because it influences canopy structure, grain number, and biomass accumulation. Conventional field-based counting is labor-intensive and generally limited to small sampling areas, restricting the spatially comprehensive characterization needed for precision management and yield forecasting. Satellite observations offer the required spatial coverage but lack reference data at a resolution suitable for calibrating tiller-level canopy properties. Here, we present a multiscale framework that transfers ground-measured wheat tiller density to satellite observations through an intermediate Uncrewed Aircraft System (UAS) layer. Ground-count data collected from 2023 to 2025 at field sites near Brookings, Hayes, and Winner, South Dakota, USA, during tillering to jointing growth stages, were combined with high-resolution UAS multispectral imagery to train deep learning models, including transformer-based architectures. The trained UAS models were applied to generate spatially continuous, field-scale tiller-density maps. These maps were subsequently aggregated to satellite pixel footprints, to produce pixel-level reference labels for training and validating separate models based on Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 (HLS) and PlanetScope multispectral imagery. The two sensors were evaluated independently to assess the trade-off between the finer spatial detail of PlanetScope and the radiometric consistency and open availability of HLS. Both satellite-based models estimated wheat tiller density and reproduced the major spatial patterns observed in the UAS-derived reference maps, although their ability to preserve fine-scale within-field variability differed because of differences in spatial resolution. The results demonstrate the potential of a hierarchical ground-to-UAS-to-satellite framework to extend plot-level measurements to broader spatial scales, while noting that satellite-model accuracy remains bound by the UAS model from which its training labels derive. This approach may support early-season assessment of wheat stand development, site-specific nitrogen management, and in-season yield forecasting.

title: Tidal Aliasing and the Absence of Morphodynamic Memory on a Macro-Tidal Delta Margin
authors: Golam Nur Nabi Miraz, Institute of Forestry and Environmental Sciences, Chittagong University, Chittagong, Bangladesh
main_session: River Deltas: Observing, Modeling, and Predicting Natural and Anthropogenic Changes III Poster
abstract: Blind benchmarking has recently shown that the best-performing shoreline prediction models reproduce sandy-beach evolution to roughly 10 m, comparable to the accuracy of satellite observation itself. The same models are applied to the macro-tidal deltaic margins where coastal risk is concentrated, and reported as acceptable on RMSE against withheld observations - a metric that cannot establish whether a forecast beats simply assuming no change. We make that comparison using 7,021 transect-epoch Landsat/HLS shoreline positions spanning 1999-2023 across a 140 km margin of the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta. Sentinel-1 inundation-frequency retrieval yields intertidal slopes near 0.001 m/m, one to two orders of magnitude below sandy beaches, and TPXO9-predicted tidal aliasing explains 81% of the epoch-to-epoch variance in apparent coast-wide shoreline position (r = -0.90). A planar model nonetheless overpredicts displacement fivefold, indicating that the optical waterline pins at morphological breaks rather than migrating freely across the flat. Critically, this represents a common-mode error: a coast-wide offset of 165-290 m between epochs, comparable to the morphodynamic signal it contaminates. Common-mode error destroys temporal inference while sparing cross-sectional inference, and both consequences are confirmed. Under rolling-origin validation, persistence outperforms every trend-based forecast in all three folds, and no fold shows useful positive correlation between predicted and observed change. A disjoint-window design further shows that the change envelope is reliably measured within a period (r = +0.67) yet carries no forward information across periods (r = -0.03). The coast is morphodynamically memoryless, so history-based prediction fails in principle rather than merely in practice; subsequent movement is governed instead by intertidal gradient. Two specifications in current use - climatology-referenced skill scores and shared-window predictor-response pairs - produced an apparent predictability threshold and an apparent geomorphic control respectively in our own analysis; neither survives a corrected design.

title: Fmask 5: A new physics-informed machine learning cloud detection algorithm
authors: Shi Qiu, Zhe Zhu, Xiucheng Yang, Junchang Ju, Qiang Zhou and Christopher S R Neigh
main_session: Evolving Science and Applications of Landsat II Poster
abstract: Accurate cloud detection is a critical preprocessing step for analyzing optical remote sensing data, such as from Landsat and Sentinel-2. Here, we introduce Fmask 5 (Version 5 of Function of mask) for cloud detection in Landsats 4-9 and Sentinel-2 imagery, based on a novel physics-informed machine learning (PIML) framework. This framework synergistically integrates physical rules with machine learning (ML) models (i.e., UNet and LightGBM), overcoming their respective limitations. Specifically, a base ML model first generates a preliminary cloud mask to adapt to the application of physical rules, determining the optimal combination of spectral tests and thresholds for that image. The resulting physical-rule-adapted mask serves as additional “localized” training data to fine-tune the ML model. For a global, independent validation dataset combining simple random and disagreement-stratified samples from over 600 images per sensor, Fmask 5 achieved design-weighted overall accuracies of 93.46% [95% Confidence Interval (CI): ±0.96%] for Landsats 8-9, 92.50% [95% CI: ±1.02%] for Landsats 4-7, and 95.38% [95% CI: ±0.90%] for Sentinel-2, representing improvements of 1.6-6.0 percentage points over Fmask 4. The Fmask 5 algorithm is computationally efficient on CPUs, making it well suited for large-scale operational processing, such as generating the quality assessment (QA) band for NASA’s Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) product.

title: The Role of Satellite Data Characteristics in Dryland Smallholder Crop Type Discrimination
authors: Margaret Wooten, William Wagner, Qiang Zhou, Woubet G. Alemu, Rodrigo Vieira Leite, Jordan Caraballo-Vega, Mark Carroll and Christopher S R Neigh
main_session: Crop Modeling, Data Assimilation, and Machine Learning for Agricultural Decision Support III Poster
abstract: Accurate crop type information is essential for monitoring agricultural production, improving food security, and guiding adaptation in climate-vulnerable systems. This is especially difficult in sub-Saharan African drylands, where rainfed smallholder agriculture, strong interannual rainfall variability, small (<3 ha) and often intercropped fields, persistent cloud cover, and heterogeneous landscapes challenge conventional remote sensing approaches. In these settings, it is unclear whether spatial detail, spectral richness, temporal frequency, or radiometric stability matters most for distinguishing crops. We address this question through a controlled, ablation-style comparison of two optical data streams over a pilot site in southwest Niger: a 10m prototype of the Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) product, and Planet's SuperDove constellation, which offers finer spatial resolution and eight spectral bands at a near-daily revisit but with different radiometric characteristics. Both are evaluated against a rich in-situ reference archive of crop-cuts that span multiple dry and rainy seasons and include both staple and cash crops such as millet, sorghum, cowpeas, maize, anise, tomatoes, and onions. Using tree-based machine learning models trained on phenological, spectral, and temporal feature sets, we design matched experiments that hold reference data and study area constant while varying sensor characteristics via date-matched, band-matched, and joint date-plus-band-matched configurations, together with spectral, temporal-window, and spatial ablation tests. Model performance and feature attribution (SHAP) are used to identify which characteristics carry the strongest signal for which crops. Preliminary results suggest that the relative importance of each data attribute is not fixed but shifts by crop, season, and landscape context, offering actionable guidance on sensor selection and data design for smallholder agricultural monitoring under a changing climate.

title: Expanding Availability, Visualization, and Application of Openly Available Analysis Ready Data on Surface Water Dynamics.
authors: John W Jones, U.S. Geological Survey, Hydrologic Remote Sensing Branch, Kearneysville, United States
main_session: Accelerating Impact: User‑Driven Earth Observation Solutions from the Satellite Needs Working Group II Oral
abstract: Satellite remote sensing of surface water extent fills knowledge gaps regarding timing, frequency, and amount of surface inundation. Openly available Analysis Ready Data (ARD) on surface water extent derived from satellite imagery allow anyone with internet access to: monitor changes in water and habitat availability; prepare for/respond to natural hazards (i.e. flood and drought); plan scientific and restoration activities more effectively; train, drive, or evaluate models; and develop other applications. USGS Dynamic Surface Water Extent (DSWE) ARD have been automatically generated for every Landsat scene collected over the US to yield a 42-year and growing record. DSWE became the seed for a more expansive ARD undertaking by NASA. The OPERA Dynamic Surface Water eXtent (DSWx) product suite provides high-frequency observations at near-global scale through complementary use of harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (DSWx-HLS), Sentinel-1 (DSWx-S1) and very recently, NISAR (DSWx-NI) inputs. Importantly, DSWE/DSWx-HLS target sub-pixel mixtures of water, soil, and vegetation, termed partial surface water (PSW), to more comprehensively map water extent and wetlands than is possible using products solely focused on open water pixels. While the radar-based DSWx-S1 and DSWx-NI haven’t the sub-pixel PSW capability of DSWx-HLS, the radar-based products target inundation under vegetation canopies that are too dense for DSWx-HLS PSW detection. DSWx-S1 and DSWx-NI also detect inundation regardless of cloud cover. Although DSWx-S1 and DSWx-NI products are forward processed, starting in 2024 and 2026, respectively, back processing of DSWx-HLS data to 2016 has been completed. Data from periods before 2023 will soon be available. Tools within the NASA Earthdata GIS platform, inclusion in the Google Earth Engine public catalog, QGIS plugins, and ArcGIS PRO toolboxes all facilitate DSWx application for users with GIS and coding experience. Public facing visualization and query dashboards provide entry points for ARD exploration and basic applications, regardless of user experience. USGS application to terminal lake and waterbird habitat monitoring illustrates different relative strengths and weaknesses of the various products in the DSWx suite, as well as the synergy provided by their combined use.

title: Using Near-Real-Time Disturbance Alerts to Identify Clean Water Act Violations in U.S. EPA Region 1
authors: Eleanor Horvath, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Boston, United States
main_session: Accelerating Impact: User‑Driven Earth Observation Solutions from the Satellite Needs Working Group II Oral
abstract: In 2018, NASA’s Satellite Needs Working Group identified a need for continuous monitoring of Earth’s surface by land management agencies. The resulting data product, called “DIST-ALERT,” is based on Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 data, giving it the ability to map global changes in vegetation cover every 2 to 4 days at 30-meter resolution. Today, the DIST-ALERT data are freely available and continuously updated, allowing users to track landscape change around the world in near-real-time, as well as the events, such as fires, floods, landslides, droughts, development, and mining, that cause them. In New England, Region 1 of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is using DIST-ALERT to detect land clearing activities that may violate the Clean Water Act with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution to support intervention. Each week, we extract the most intense, ongoing disturbances from the DIST-ALERT data and process them further to isolate alerts that are most likely to represent unauthorized activities. Disturbances are then fed to a web-based application and analyzed in conjunction with publicly available ancillary datasets and moderate-resolution imagery before being verified in the field by EPA experts. An unprecedented rate of violations identified using the DIST-ALERT data have resulted in immediate actions to return these sites to compliance with the Clean Water Act. Within the Agency, this initiative has increased performance metrics, improved efficiency in the use of limited staff resources, and expanded compliance assistance for the regulated community, but its impacts reach beyond internal outcomes. Using DIST-ALERT, we have increased our capability to remediate sites with the greatest potential for negative environmental consequences across New England. We demonstrate a straightforward and cost-free strategy for monitoring landscape change and open doors for further collaboration to protect public goods.

title: Municipality-Level Forest Disaster Characterization Using Hazard-Specific Spatial Units for Wildfire and Landslide Susceptibility Assessment
authors: Seunghyun Hong, Kookmin University, Department of Forest Resources, Seoul, Korea, Republic of (South), Heejung NAM, Kookmin University, Department of Forest Resources, Seoul, South Korea and Wanmo Kang, Kookmin University, Department of Forest Environment and Systems, Seoul, South Korea
main_session: Compound, Consecutive, and Cascading Hazards: From Geospatial AI and Physical Understanding to Risk Management II Oral
abstract: Wildfires and landslides exhibit distinct spatial patterns governed by different environmental and topographic drivers, making hazard-specific spatial assessments essential for effective municipality-level forest disaster management. This study assessed wildfire and landslide susceptibility using different spatial units and classified municipality-level forest disaster characteristics in Gyeonggi Province, South Korea. Wildfire and landslide occurrence data from 2011 to 2023 were combined with GEDI L4A-derived aboveground biomass density, HLS-derived vegetation indices, forest type, topographic, and anthropogenic variables. To account for hazard-specific processes, wildfire susceptibility was assessed using 30 m grid cells, whereas landslide susceptibility was evaluated using DEM-derived slope units generated with the GRASS GIS r.slopeunits algorithm. Separate susceptibility models were developed using the BIOMOD2 ensemble framework with cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to evaluate variable importance. High-susceptibility areas were subsequently aggregated by municipality to classify forest disaster characteristics. Both susceptibility models demonstrated reasonable predictive performance. The integrated analysis classified municipalities into wildfire-dominant, landslide-dominant, compound, and low-susceptibility types. Wildfire susceptibility was primarily influenced by anthropogenic variables, whereas landslide susceptibility was primarily associated with topographic variables. This hazard-specific spatial framework enhances the precision of vulnerability mapping and provides a scalable decision-support tool for integrated regional forest disaster mitigation. * This study was conducted with support from the R&D Program for Forest Science Technology provided by Korea Forest Service (Korea Forestry Promotion Institute) (Project No. RS-2024-00404816).

title: Rapid monitoring of global vegetation disturbance - updates of the OPERA DIST-ALERT product
authors: Matthew Hansen, Amy Hudson Pickens, Zhen Song and Xinyuan Li
main_session: Advances in Monitoring of Land Changes Using Remote Sensing, Quality Assessment, and Statistical Inference: Methods, Applications, and Challenges II Oral
abstract: OPERA DIST-ALERT employs the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) time-series dataset to deliver low latency updates of vegetation disturbance globally, available 2023 to present. The product is thematically simple, using vegetation fraction as the target variable and tracking anomalously low values compared to a 3-year history of percent vegetation estimates within a +/- 15-day window of the time of observation. Alert magnitude and repeat detections are used to build confidence in per pixel alerts. This talk will highlight use cases and next steps in evolving the product. Current operational applications include verifying timber sourcing, identifying unauthorized construction, and protecting forest habitat. Attribution of drivers is a key goal, as the current product relies on users to apply context - for example antecedent forest cover in a protected area - in order to support decision-making. Current attribution work is being developed in a hierarchical framework, differentiating at the top level natural versus mechanical proximate causes, with both subsets planned for further division, for example logging versus commercial development. Preliminary results on mechanical versus natural DIST-ALERT attribution will be detailed. Other aspirational improvements of the product include expanding alert coverage backward to include the entire HLS record and tracking positive anomalies, detecting, for example, expansion of irrigated agriculture in drylands.

title: A Generalizable Satellite-Based Framework for Field-Level Cover Crop Mapping Across the Contiguous United States
authors: Saibo Li, Kaiyu Guan, Sheng Wang, Qu Zhou, Yide Xu, Zhixian Lin and Dr. Bin Peng
main_session: Remote Sensing for Sustainable Agriculture II Oral
abstract: Cover crops provide multifaceted agroecosystem benefits, yet their spatial distribution and growth dynamics remain poorly characterized at the field scale across the contiguous United States (CONUS). Existing satellite-based approaches commonly rely on vegetation signals during the non-growing season. Still, these signals are influenced by climate, cropping systems, and soil background, limiting the transferability of cover crop detection approaches across diverse agricultural landscapes. Here, we develop a generalizable framework for field-level cover crop mapping across CONUS using Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) time series. The framework separates cover crop growth from other components of seasonal satellite signals. Specifically, we first characterize field-specific bare-soil spectral conditions from multi-temporal observations and derive a soil NDVI baseline to account for spatial variations in soil background. We then identify and remove winter cash crop signals based on their distinct phenological characteristics. Finally, satellite-derived features are integrated with environmental information to account for regional variations in cover crop growth and enable consistent detection across diverse cropping systems and environmental conditions. We apply the framework across major U.S. cropping systems and evaluate its performance across regions, years, and environmental conditions. The framework is designed to provide a scalable approach for field-level cover crop monitoring, including adoption, phenological timing, and seasonal vegetation growth. The resulting maps and growth metrics will support large-scale monitoring of field-level cover crop adoption and provide spatially explicit information for assessing the environmental benefits of cover cropping for sustainable agriculture.

title: Monitoring Land Disturbance and Sediment Dynamics with NASA Earth Observations to Improve Water Quality Management in the Missouri River Basin
authors: Vicky Espinoza and Renato P M Frasson
main_session: Accelerating Impact: User‑Driven Earth Observation Solutions from the Satellite Needs Working Group III Oral
abstract: Extreme runoff, flooding, and land disturbances can rapidly increase sediment transport to rivers, degrading water quality and disrupting drinking water treatment. Recent high-turbidity events in the Missouri River Basin, including the October 2025 event near Williston, North Dakota, which left the community without a reliable drinking water supply for approximately one week, highlight the need for timely monitoring tools capable of identifying vulnerable river reaches before water quality impacts occur. We present a multi-sensor Earth observation framework that integrates NASA's OPERA Surface Disturbance (DIST) product with Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery processed using ACOLITE to monitor land disturbance, sediment dynamics, and river conditions across the Missouri River Basin. The framework combines satellite observations with field measurements and stakeholder knowledge to improve the characterization and validation of river dynamics while addressing operational water management needs. Initial case studies include (1) flooding on the Yellowstone River near Billings, Montana (2022), where extreme turbidity disrupted municipal drinking water treatment; (2) recurring spring runoff in the Missouri River near Bismarck, North Dakota (2024), where sediment pulses degraded source-water quality; and (3) the high-sediment event near Williston, North Dakota (2025), where elevated turbidity reduced treatment capacity and interrupted drinking water services to the community. These events provide a testbed for evaluating the capability of integrated remote sensing products to detect watershed disturbances and sediment accumulation prior to water quality degradation and treatment disruptions. The resulting methodology supports scalable, near-real-time monitoring of vulnerable river reaches and demonstrates how operational NASA Earth observations can enhance decision support for sediment management, source-water protection, and the resilience of drinking water systems across large river basins.

title: Multi-Sector Applications of Products Generated by the SNWG OPERA (Observational Products for End-Users from Remote Sensing Analysis) Solutions
authors: Luca Cinquini, Steven Chan, Alexander L Handwerger, Marin Govorcin, David Bekaert, Stirling Algermissen, Mary Grace Bato, Matthew Bonnema, Ines Fenni, Renato P M Frasson, Matthew Hansen, Emre Havazli, Seongsu Jeong, John W Jones, Jungkyo Jung, Riley Kuttruff, Hyun Lee, Steven Lewis, Gerald Manipon, Kevin M Marlis, Charles Marshak, Sara Mirzaee, Dinuke Munasinghe, Talib Oliver-Cabrera, Lala Pashaian, Amy Hudson Pickens, Christopher Rivas, Simran Sangha, Gustavo H.X. Shiroma, Cole M Speed, Rosanna Sumagaysay, Rishi Verma, Richard D West and OPERA (Observational Products for End-Users from Remote Sensing Analysis)
main_session: Accelerating Impact: User‑Driven Earth Observation Solutions from the Satellite Needs Working Group III Oral
abstract: The Observational Products for End-Users from Remote Sensing Analysis (OPERA) project, funded by NASA’s Satellite Needs Working Group Implementation Team (NSITE) and led by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in collaboration with federal, academic, and DAAC partners, produces higher-level analysis-ready satellite products designed to meet diverse stakeholders’ needs. OPERA generates four product suites requested by federal users: Dynamic Surface Water Extent (DSWx), Surface Disturbance (DIST), Surface Displacement (DISP), and Vertical Land Motion (VLM). These products enable a wide array of multi-sector applications across environmental management, hazard mitigation, resource planning, and civil infrastructure: Dynamic Surface Water Extent (DSWx): Derived from HLS, Sentinel-1, and NISAR observations, DSWx delivers surface water maps that empower decision-makers to track water resources, map floods, protect critical habitats, and drive smarter environmental stewardship. Surface Disturbance (DIST): Derived from HLS and Sentinel-1 observations, DIST detects changes in vegetation and land surfaces resulting from wildfires, logging, mining, and urban expansion, enabling land managers to assess conditions, prioritize areas of concern, and plan mitigation or recovery actions. Surface Displacement (DISP): Derived from Sentinel-1 and NISAR observations, DISP tracks ground movement from diverse natural and human-driven processes—such as land subsidence, landslides, earthquakes, and volcanic activity—to inform hazard assessment and emergency planning. Vertical Land Motion (VLM): Derived from Sentinel-1 and NISAR observations, VLM measures long-term vertical (and horizontal, wherever satellite geometry allows) ground uplift and subsidence to inform decisions regarding relative sea-level rise, oil and gas extraction, infrastructure safety, community planning, and land-change management. This presentation will highlight examples that demonstrate how, by delivering accessible remote sensing data, OPERA translates satellite observations into actionable data for diverse users from federal, state, municipal, commercial and nonprofit sectors.

title: Urban Pulse: A Satellite Time-Series Framework for Diagnosing Dynamic Urbanization Processes
authors: Zhe Zhu, Michail Fragkias, Kexin Song, Ji Won Suh, Karen C Seto, Ella McCoshan, Lelin Chen, Juwon Kong and Tian Li
main_session: Advances in Monitoring of Land Changes Using Remote Sensing, Quality Assessment, and Statistical Inference: Methods, Applications, and Challenges II Oral
abstract: Urbanization has traditionally been quantified using static indicators, such as the extent of built-up land or annual rates of urban expansion, which capture the outcomes of development but overlook its underlying dynamics. Recent advances in dense satellite time series now enable continuous monitoring of land surface changes at unprecedented temporal resolution, creating new opportunities to characterize urbanization as an evolving process rather than a static state. In this presentation, I introduce the Urban Pulse framework, a new remote sensing approach that transforms dense satellite observations into dynamic diagnostics of urban development. Using Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery and dense time-series analysis, Urban Pulse quantifies construction dynamics through time and space across six globally distributed metropolitan areas representing diverse socioeconomic and geographic contexts. Rather than treating urban growth as a monotonic trend, the framework identifies temporal "pulses" of development and characterizes their intensity, timing, duration, and spatial synchronization. Results reveal three universal properties of urbanization. First, urban growth is spiky, consisting of episodic bursts rather than gradual change. Second, it is cyclical, transitioning through alternating phases of expansion, stabilization, and decline. Third, it is asynchronous, with neighborhoods within the same city exhibiting distinct and often uncoordinated development trajectories. Analysis of the COVID-19 period further demonstrates that disruptions to urbanization varied substantially among cities, with some rapidly returning to pre-pandemic dynamics while others experienced persistent shifts in development patterns. The Urban Pulse framework illustrates how dense satellite time series can move beyond mapping land cover change toward diagnosing the dynamic processes that shape cities. More broadly, it highlights the potential of near real-time Earth observation to provide process-based indicators, support early detection of urban transitions, and inform timely planning and sustainability decisions.

title: Multi-source data assessment of extreme fire behavior during South Korea's first pyrocumulonimbus event
authors: Minho Kim, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States, Marc Castellnou, GRAF, Catalan Fire and Rescue Service, Cerdanyola del Vallès,, Spain and Marta Gonzalez, University of California Berkeley, City and Regional Planning, Berkeley, United States
main_session: Wildfire Analysis Using Remote Sensing, Multisensor Fusion, Multisource Data Integration, and Artificial Intelligence VI Oral
abstract: In March 2025, South Korea experienced an unprecedented wildfire characterized by an extreme fire growth rate and large burned area, resulting in numerous casualties and over a billion US dollars in damages. The convergence of severe fire weather conditions and intense surface heat led to Korea's first-ever documented pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) that coincided with the fire's most rapid growth phase. To investigate the wildfire's extraordinary behavior, we analyze surface and atmospheric conditions using ERA5 reanalysis and Geo-KOMPSAT-2A geostationary satellite time series data, cross-validated against Himawari-9 imagery. We also compare the fire's progression with burn severity using harmonized Sentinel-2/Landsat-8 imagery. We benchmark the wildfire event against four different global datasets of wildfire activity and pyroCb observations. Our findings demonstrate that this wildfire far exceeded the regional statistical norms. The wildfire ranked in the extreme tail of global distributions, especially in terms of maximum daily fire growth rate, placing it alongside some of the most extreme and fastest fires in recent history. We also observe that the wildfire's pyroCb did not occur under severe atmospheric instability. Rather, the intense fire at the surface provided sufficient heat flux to trigger pyroconvection. These findings emphasize that extreme fire behavior like pyroCb can occur in unexpected regions. In an era of climate extremes, understanding fire-atmosphere dynamics and anticipating potential extreme fire behavior is critical to mitigating risk and avoiding catastrophic disaster.

title: Operational Near-Real-Time Monitoring of Crop Progress Through the Fusion of Multiple Satellite Observations
authors: Xiaoyang Zhang, Geographic Information Science Center of Excellence, Brookings, SD, United States, Yongchang Ye, South Dakota State University, Geospatial Sciences Center of Excellence (GSCE), Department of Geography & Geospatial Sciences, Brookings, SD, United States, Yu Shen, Duke University, Nichoals School of the Environment, Durham, United States and Naeem Abbas Malik, South Dakota State University, Geospatial Sciences Center of Excellence (GSCE), Department of Geography and Geospatial Sciences, Brookings, SD, United States
main_session: Farm-Scale Integrated Assessment for Regenerative Agriculture: Monitoring, Modeling, and AI/ML Innovations II Oral
abstract: A crop progress (CP) report provides information regarding crop development during a growing season, which is crucial for farmers, grain buyers, food companies, policymakers, and investors to make informed decisions. The crop progress is routinely reported weekly at a state level by the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) of United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) according to ground-based crop progress monitoring systems. Recently, crop progress has been closely linked to phenological metrics (phenometrics) derived from satellite time series, which offers spatially distributed crop development stages. This study presents an operational system that fuses multiple satellite observations for monitoring crop phenometrics and crop progress in near real time on a weekly basis. The first part of this system is to establish time series of cloud-free observations by fusing time series of geostationary satellite observations with temporal polar-orbiting satellite data for crop phenology detections. The Advanced Baseline Imagery (ABI) onboard the GOES-R (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite - R) series observes earth surface every 10 minutes for 0.5~1 km pixels, which offers much high opportunities to capture cloud-free observations, while observations from polar-orbiting satellite sensors, which are daily VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) in 500-m pixels and ~3-day HLS (harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2) in 30-m pixels, are frequently contaminated by clouds. Thus, this system first uses a Spatiotemporal Shape-Matching Model (SSMM) to fuses ABI EVI2 (two-band Enhanced Vegetation Index) with VIIRS (or HLS) EVI2 for a two-year period before the date for near real time crop monitoring, which generates fused EVI2 time series for 500-m or 30-m pixels. Then, this system compares the latest one-year fused EVI2 time series for a give pixel with a set of preceding one-year fused EVI2 time series at surrounding pixels to generate a SSMM that is applied to predict the future EVI2 time series for the given pixel. Finally, the timely available fused EVI2 time series and the predicted EVI2 values are combined to extract crop phenometrics in near real time. This system updates the process weekly as new satellite observations become available, allowing the phenometrics to be progressively improved throughout the crop-growing season. The second part of this system is to calibrate the satellite-derived phenometrics using field-observed USDA NASS crop progress report, which leads pixel-based crop progress weekly that is biophysically equivalent to field observations. This system has been tested for monitoring 500-m crop progress across the US corn belt using VIIRS-ABI observations and 30-m crop progress in central western US using HLS-ABI observations.

title: A New Radar Disturbance Product (DIST-S1) Using Sentinel-1 Observations and a Machine Learning Approach
authors: Richard D West, Charles Marshak, Talib Oliver-Cabrera, Jungkyo Jung, Amy Hudson Pickens, David Bekaert, Steven Chan, Alexander L Handwerger, Stirling Algermissen, Mary Grace Bato, Luca Cinquini, Matthew Hansen, Theo Kerr, Anna Komarova, Hyun Lee, Riley Kutruff, Jake Lee, Steven Lewis, Andre Lima, Kevin M Marlis, Aleksandra Mikus, Andrew J. Poulson, Diego Martinez, Christopher Rivas and Zhen Song
main_session: Advances in Monitoring of Land Changes Using Remote Sensing, Quality Assessment, and Statistical Inference: Methods, Applications, and Challenges II Oral
abstract: The NASA Satellite Needs Working Group (SNWG) has identified land surface disturbance as an important measurement type for remote sensing data sets. Surface disturbances cover natural changes such as wildfires, and anthropogenic processes such as urban development and agriculture changes. The Observational Products for End-Users from Remote Sensing Analysis (OPERA) project has released a series of remote sensing data products designed to make analysis-ready satellite products for the Earth science community. In mid-2026, OPERA’s newest Surface Disturbance product was put into production. The product marks land surface disturbances globally using C-band SAR data from the Sentinel-1 satellites and has the short name DIST-S1. The SAR-based products have a resolution of 30 meters, an update cadence of 6 - 12 days, and are designed to complement the OPERA Surface Disturbance from Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (DIST-HLS) product – developed by the University of Maryland, which was put into production in 2023. The algorithm employs deep learning to produce a self-supervised vision transformer which is then used to estimate per pixel normal parameters from a baseline of OPERA Radiometric Terrain Corrected SAR backscatter data to compare against recent data. A metric threshold approach is applied uniformly to all backscatter data available over land, and a wide range of disturbance types are detected such as forest loss due to wildfires or logging activities, land use change such as urban expansion, and persistent changes of water bodies. The algorithm was validated by comparing detections with human-labelled disturbance data over a validation data set stratified over landcover types and disturbance types. Validation analysis was also done for a set of known disturbance events. This presentation will summarize the development and details of the disturbance detection algorithm. We will also discuss the validation analysis applied in partnership with the University of Maryland which showed a total accuracy of 95.1% over all types of change and provide some examples of potential applications. This work is supported by the NASA OPERA project at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology.

title: From Planting Dates to Conservation Practice Mapping: Scaling the Farm Action Toolkit for Agricultural Resilience in the United States
authors: Aparna Phalke, PhD, Sarah Cox, Dwane Roth, TJ Flax, Lee Ellenburg, Vikalp Mishra, Lena Pransky, Reetwika Basu, PhD, Vanesa Martin, David Haliczer and sarah cox
main_session: Farm-Scale Integrated Assessment for Regenerative Agriculture: Monitoring, Modeling, and AI/ML Innovations II Oral
abstract: Farm Action Toolkit (FAcT) is a scalable, openly available framework that integrates NASA and partner satellite data, agronomic knowledge and GeoAI to generate actionable agricultural information delivered through interactive dashboards. FAcT translates stakeholder-defined questions into locally-tuned decision support for farm-to-national-scale decisions. We present two scalable FAcT capabilities. The first, FAcT-Tillage capability is co-developed with the farmer-led Agricultural Producers Data Exchange (APDE) in Kansas. FAcT-Tillage creates two novel tillage-sensitive metrics: an optical residue score and a SAR-derived structure score. These scores are derived using harmonized Landsat/Sentinel-2 (HLS) and Sentinel-1 VV/VH temporal data metrics responsive to soil roughness, structure, moisture, residue, crop rows, and cover crops. Together, they support an advanced field-level tillage product that classifies conventional tillage, no-till, strip-till, and no-till after cover crops. Farmers can use tillage maps as evidence to complement field records, field visits, and conservation reporting. The second, FAcT-Planting Date capability is co-developed with the Alabama Office of the State Climatologist. FAcT-Planting Date uses HLS data, crop type masks, vegetation-index trajectories and phenology-based inference from canopy growth to generate a tailored statewide corn planting date product. These planting calendars reveal field variability not captured by county-scale crop progress summaries or frost-based estimates and support crop-model workflows for yield sensitivity, irrigation need, and flash-drought resilience. A linked economic value assessment evaluates how FAcT data relates to yield risk, water and energy demand, avoided losses, and targeted resilience or conservation investments. Together, these capabilities show how satellite monitoring, GeoAI and trusted pathways produce local agricultural intelligence from field to national scales.

title: Virtual Replication of Eddy Covariance Measurements Using Regional Mesonet Observations, Remote Sensing, and Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks.
authors: Cole Walton, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, United States and Nuria Gomez-Casanovas, Texas A&M AgriLife Research, Vernon, Texas, USA, Vernon, United States
main_session: Advances for Measuring and Modeling Food System Resilience IV Poster
abstract: Eddy covariance (EC) towers measure ecosystem carbon and water exchange, but their cost limits replication across treatments and landscapes. We developed a virtual sensing framework combining neighboring EC towers, regional mesonet observations, tower meteorology, and Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel 2 imagery. Each field is represented as a multivariate environmental time series. Temporal convolutional encoders summarize conditions across multiple time scales, while remote sensing provides daily vegetation context. A hierarchical graph neural network learns dynamic relationships among the ecosystem fluxes across different EC towers and meteorological covariates for each of the towers measured fluxes. During training, observed flux values are selectively hidden, teaching the network to reconstruct missing measurements from environmental conditions and information transferred from neighboring EC towers. Separate daily and half hourly models predict net ecosystem exchange of CO₂ (NEE) and evapotranspiration (ET). Architecture selection and validation used three development towers, excluding one tower at a time. Five seeded models were trained on all three towers and combined as a median ensemble. A fourth tower was excluded from training, architecture selection, and validation for evaluation under novel field conditions. On the excluded field, daily R² values were 0.846 for NEE and 0.889 for ET, with RMSE values of 1.37 g C m⁻² d⁻¹ and 0.67 mm d⁻¹. Half hourly R² values were 0.866 for NEE and 0.856 for ET, with RMSE values of 2.85 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ and 0.030 mm per half hour. Qin et al. (2025) reported daily NEE R² of 0.63 and RMSE of 2.32 g C m⁻² d⁻¹ for a site calibrated ecosys model at a cotton EC site. Bu et al. (2024) reported ET R² values of 0.74 and 0.87 and RMSE values of 0.030 mm per half hour and 0.35 mm d⁻¹ for a physically based two source energy balance model across six dryland EC sites. This framework exceeded these reported process based daily NEE and ET R² benchmarks while matching the reported half hourly ET RMSE. The utility of this framework is then demonstrated by virtually replicating EC measurements across paired semiarid cotton fields to compare microalgae biofertilizer effects on crop water relations and gross primary production.

title: Development of a Multi-Year, High-Resolution Snow Cover Time Series from Trail Camera Imagery Using Machine Learning
authors: Ting Zheng, James-Robert Caulkins, Jennifer Stenglein, Phillip Goodling, Jennifer Fair, Kyra Shaw, Wyatt Joseph Cummings, Benjamin Zuckerberg and Philip A Townsend
main_session: Machine Learning for Snow: Model Development, Applications, and Lessons Learned II Poster
abstract: Seasonal snow cover plays a critical role in regional hydrology, wildlife habitat, and land-atmosphere energy exchange. However, ground-based snow observations remain sparse relative to the spatial and temporal resolution needed to capture local variability, while satellite-derived snow cover products can be unreliable in areas with high vegetation heterogeneity. Camera trap networks deployed for wildlife monitoring, such as Snapshot Wisconsin, offer an underused source of daily, site-level imagery that can be repurposed for environmental monitoring. Specifically, we use trail camera images to quantify surface snow cover, with the ultimate objective being to either validate or improve existing snow cover data. We adapted the USGS Streamflow Rank Estimation model, originally developed for streamflow classification from time-lapse imagery via the Flow Photo Explorer platform, to estimate percent snow cover from daily time-lapse photographs in the Snapshot Wisconsin camera network. The model was validated against a human-labeled dataset spanning a range of snow conditions, lighting, and vegetation contexts. Model performance showed strong agreement with human-labeled snow cover percent estimates with a mean absolute error of 4.8%, and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.969, demonstrating that an existing image-classification framework developed for a different environmental variable can be effectively transferred to snow cover estimation. We applied the trained model to the full archive of daily time-lapse photographs (approximately 4 million images) from the Snapshot Wisconsin project, generating a continuous daily snow cover percentage time series from 2017 to 2026 for 6,533 camera sites distributed across Wisconsin. Continuing work includes evaluating this dataset against local weather station snow depth records and remote sensing snow indices derived from harmonized Landsat/Sentinel-2 imagery. From this, we plan to use the generated data to tune the snow indices to generate accurate maps of snow cover. This dataset offers new opportunities to examine snow phenology, interannual variability, and local-scale heterogeneity in snow cover across the state, with applications for hydrology, wildlife ecology, and citizen-science-driven environmental monitoring

title: Benchmarking Geospatial Foundation Models for High-Resolution Snow Water Equivalent Estimation in the Western US
authors: Mahya Hashemi, Catherine M Breen, Carrie Vuyovich, Jeffrey S Deems, Kat J Bormann, Brennan Bean, Abbie Liel, Jeannette M Torrents and John D Bolten
main_session: Machine Learning for Snow: Model Development, Applications, and Lessons Learned I Oral
abstract: Accurate, spatially distributed snow water equivalent (SWE) estimates are critical for water resource management and infrastructure design, yet current operational products are too coarse to resolve snow variability in mountainous terrain, where the optimal scale is 100-300 m. In the U.S., the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) develops the ASCE 7 standard design ground snow loads from approximately 8,000 sparse ground stations interpolated to 800-m maps, which can over-smooth estimates in topographically complex regions. As a result, design loads in these regions may not reflect local terrain conditions, and higher-resolution estimates would enable more efficient designs where appropriate while maintaining structural safety targets. Geospatial foundation models pretrained on massive Earth observation archives offer a data-efficient path to high-resolution SWE retrieval. We fine-tune Earth observation foundation models, including Prithvi-EO-2.0, TerraMind, Clay, and AlphaEarth, to generate 30-m SWE estimates across Colorado, fusing Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 optical imagery with downscaled climate forcing, terrain features, and passive microwave brightness temperatures. The models are trained on airborne lidar-derived SWE from the Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) over Colorado and California watersheds and tested on unseen sites within Colorado, while watersheds in Wyoming, Washington, and Utah, spanning maritime, intermountain, and continental snow climates, are held out as completely unseen regions to assess spatial generalization. We benchmark these vision-transformer-based foundation models against a 3D-CNN, ConvLSTM and LSTM model trained from scratch to quantify the accuracy and data-efficiency gains of pretrained representations. We will present model performance evaluated against held-out ASO acquisitions and independent point observations from approximately 900 SNOTEL stations, along with temporal generalization to water years excluded from training. These results will support improved snow load estimates in ASCE 7 structural design standards, delivered through the publicly available ASCE Hazard Tool. This work demonstrates a scalable pathway for producing spatially continuous, high-resolution SWE in complex terrain with limited labeled data.

title: Toward near real-time estimates of land surface carbon and water fluxes at management-relevant scales
authors: Paul C Stoy, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, Biological Systems Engineering, Madison, United States, Sadegh Ranjbar, PhD Candidate, Yale University, Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, New Haven, CT, United States, Ankur R Desai, University of Wisconsin Madison, Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences, Madison, WI, United States and Qunying Huang, University of Wisconsin Madison, Department of Geography, Madison, WI, United States
main_session: Next-Generation Spatiotemporal Decision Science: AI/ML, Quantum Mathematics, and Earth System Analytics I Oral
abstract: The advent of machine learning, foundation models, multi-platform remote sensing, and measurement networks creates a path forward for estimating land surface carbon dioxide and water fluxes at spatial scales that align with ecosystem management, and at low latencies for decision-making. We describe efforts to provide hourly, 30 m estimates of land surface carbon dioxide and water fluxes with a latency of less than one day. We first summarize our open-access ALIVE (Advanced Baseline Imager Live Imaging of Vegetated Ecosystems) data product that provides hourly estimates of surface fluxes by combining geostationary satellite (GOES-R) data with High Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) meteorological data and a lightweight histogram-based boosting regressor model trained on eddy covariance observations (‘ALIVE_Hourly’) across the CONUS. ALIVE_Hourly provides epistemic (model), aleatoric (data) and total uncertainties to benchmark model improvements. The 2 km (at nadir) native resolution of ALIVE_Hourly is insufficient for most land management applications, so it must be ‘downscaled’ to finer spatial resolutions. Polar-orbiting satellites and data products like VIIRS and Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 provide a means to do so, but their observations come less frequently. Foundation models built from HLS provide rich layers upon which to infer land surface function, but are updated less frequently still. We downscale ALIVE using a knowledge-guided diffusion super-resolution (KGDiffSR) model with a frozen Diffusion Prior for SR (StableSR) backbone in a two-step process that accounts for its ~4 to 8 × downscaling factor. First, we enhance 2 km GOES-R ABI bands to VIIRS-like resolution (375 m) with a KGDiffSR model trained on large-scale GOES-R and VIIRS imagery pairs. We then explore the ability of KGDiffSR to downscale super-resolved GOES-R ABI bands (375 m) to 30 m spatial resolution with HLS augmented with Google AlphaEarth embeddings. The resultant imagery has similar spectral resolution to apply existing ALIVE algorithms for flux estimation, and we do so to demonstrate a proof-of-concept. The order-of-magnitude scale mismatch introduces uncertainties that must be overcome to generate defensible estimates of surface fluxes in space and time, which points to a clear path forward for doing so.

title: In-season Crop N Status Diagnosis Using Cross-scale Sensing to Support Adaptive N Management
authors: Zhao Jiang, Kaiyu Guan, Ignacio Ciampitti, Sheng Wang, Alyssa K Whitcraft and Leonardo Bosche
main_session: Satellite Solutions for Agricultural Monitoring, Drought, and Water Management I Oral
abstract: Adaptive nitrogen (N) management requires near-real-time diagnosis of crop N status. For many field crops, the optimum N rate varies widely among fields and years, driven by soil properties and weather during the growing season. Existing recommendation tools are hard to scale up and to apply universally across many fields. The Nitrogen Nutrition Index (NNI, the ratio of actual to critical N concentration at comparable plant biomass) provides a physiological benchmark for plant N nutritional status. Ground-based NNI measurements are labor-intensive and destructive, and therefore sparse, whereas remote sensing data provide upscaling capabilities across time and space, enabling field-level in-season N management and retrospective historical analysis. We derived regional NNI maps for the US Midwest from 2011 to 2020 using a cross-scale sensing approach, in which airborne hyperspectral observation provides accurate crop N trait retrievals and abundant quasi-labels for scaling up to satellite data. We analyzed the spatiotemporal patterns of the regional crop N status and the yield responses to NNI using yield maps from an independent model. The 10-yr crop N status results show clear spatial patterns driven by N fertilizer rate and soil properties. Temporal variability of crop N status shows significant impacts of in-season rainfall via N leaching and runoff. The yield-NNI relationship and its environmental drivers provide a baseline for region-specific N management strategies to match crop N demand and reduce N losses. For the 2026 growing season, we expanded this framework to include 15 additional on-farm N-rate trials across Illinois, Iowa, and Indiana. We collected airborne hyperspectral data synchronized with the ground measurements from mid-vegetative to early reproductive stages. These data will strengthen validation of in-season crop N status diagnosis via remote sensing and help identify the earliest growth stage at which satellite-based diagnosis becomes reliable. Frequent revisit of operational multispectral satellites, such as NASA’s HLS, enables timely in-season N monitoring. Combined with the historical baseline, this cross-scale sensing approach advances corn N monitoring from in-season diagnosis toward adaptive N management.

title: Mapping and Characterizing Four Decades of Global, Glacier Darkening (1984–Present) Using Cloud-Computing and AI-Assisted Code Development
authors: Anne Walden Nolin, University of Nevada, Reno, Geography, Reno, United States
main_session: Snow Albedo Dynamics: Drivers, Observations, and Modeling Across Diverse Snow Environments II Poster
abstract: Surface albedo is a first-order control on glacier melt, yet global-scale, high-resolution monitoring of glacier reflectance trends has been limited by the trade-off between spatial resolution and temporal coverage in satellite records. While previous work used MODIS 500-m spatial resolution satellite observations of glacier albedo trends, that coarse resolution omits most alpine glaciers in the RGI. This study presents a framework for computing surface reflectance trends across all glaciers in the Randolph Glacier Inventory (RGI) using the 30-m Landsat surface reflectance archive from 1984 to present, harmonized with Sentinel-2 via the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) product from 2015 onward to increase observation density in the recent record. The annual minimum cloud-free reflectance is computed to isolate end-of-melt-season surface conditions, accounting for cloud and shadow contamination, viewing geometry effects, and terrain illumination corrections, with long-term trends estimated using the Theil-Sen slope estimator with Mann-Kendall significance testing. This global-scale, multi-decadal analysis is implemented in Google Earth Engine, with code development assisted by the AI model Claude (Anthropic). Derived reflectance trends are validated against the MODIS MCD43A3 broadband albedo product over their period of overlap (2000-present). Reflectance trends are aggregated to the 19 RGI first-order regions, and for each region, changes in surface reflectance are assessed in the context of concurrent regional temperature and precipitation trends from the ERA5/ERA5-Land reanalysis. The hypothesis is that regional decreases in glacier reflectance are primarily driven by increasing summer temperatures, via retreat-driven bare-ice exposure at lower elevations, rather than by trends in precipitation, and that regions with the strongest summer warming will show the most pronounced darkening regardless of precipitation trend. This four-decade, glacier-resolved reflectance record, aggregated regionally and linked to a global climate baseline, will provide a basis for attributing surface darkening to specific forcing mechanisms and for constraining albedo parameterizations in glacier mass balance models.

title: Validating spaceborne lidar-optical fusion for wildfire-driven canopy height and biomass change mapping in Alaska
authors: Ali Zarringhalam, University of Maryland College Park, College Park, United States, Laura Duncanson, University of Maryland, Department of Geographical Sciences, College Park, United States and Paul M Montesano, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center | SSAI, Greenbelt, MD, United States
main_session: The Resilience and Vulnerability of Arctic and Boreal Ecosystems to Change VI Poster
abstract: Wildfires are a major source of forest carbon loss and greenhouse gas emissions. Recent studies indicate that wildfires are increasing in frequency and severity across boreal forests. While wildfire-driven aboveground biomass (AGB) change in boreal forests have been studied for decades, the accuracy of these change estimates remains largely unvalidated. Moreover, spaceborne lidar timeseries remain under-utilized for large-scale mapping of forest structural change, and the potential of deep learning models that encode spatial forest structure for change estimation remains relatively unexplored. We investigate how effectively deep Convolutional Neural Networks can measure wildfire-induced canopy height change in boreal forests by integrating Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) and topographic data supervised by ICESat-2 (ATL08) canopy height measurements. We train a UNet model, compare its performance against a baseline Random Forest model from a prior study, and validate the results against pre- and post-fire airborne lidar data in Alaska. UNet improves post-fire Pearson correlation and canopy height change estimates relative to the baseline, particularly for large canopy losses (>2.5 m). Augmenting the training data with fire-coincident ATL08 samples improves large loss detection but introduces an artifact in fire-adjacent pixels, highlighting a challenge in applying patch-based deep learning methods in heterogeneous disturbed landscapes. Using the enhanced UNet model, we mapped AGB change from 2019 to 2024 across Alaska and characterize patterns of AGB change and wildfire-induced AGB losses across Alaska’s ecoregions and land cover classes. We further evaluate the implications for the state’s AGB balance over the study period.

title: SMAFuse: SMA-guided Physics-informed Learning for Field-level Tillage Practice Mapping from Multi-modal Satellite Time Series
authors: Zhixian Lin, Kaiyu Guan, Sheng Wang, Mr. Haozheng Ma and Qu Zhou
main_session: Satellite Solutions for Agricultural Monitoring, Drought, and Water Management II Poster
abstract: Tillage practices strongly influence soil conservation and carbon cycling, yet field-level tillage information remains difficult to monitor consistently over large agricultural regions. Satellite remote sensing offers a scalable solution, but tillage-related signals are often indirect, temporally uncertain, and confounded by crop residue type, soil background, and moisture conditions. Here, we propose SMAFuse, a Spectral Mixture Analysis (SMA)-guided physics-informed fusion framework for field-level tillage practice mapping (conventional, reduced, and no-till) from multi-modal satellite time series. The framework integrates optical HLS observations, SAR backscatter, climate variables, and soil ancillary information through temporal deep learning. To incorporate residue-related physical knowledge, SMAFuse uses SMA-derived residue signals as weak physical supervision through an auxiliary residue-prediction task, encouraging the optical latent representation to encode physically meaningful residue information. Evaluated on around 1,000 field-level sites (augmented to 13,571 grid-level samples) in the U.S. Midwest, SMAFuse outperformed TempCNN, XGBoost, and random forest baselines, achieving weighted F1 scores of 0.836 at the grid level and 0.865 at the field level. The improvement was particularly evident for conventional tillage, the most challenging and underrepresented class. Additional comparisons indicate that SMA-guided physical supervision was more effective than simply adding SMA features as model inputs. These results suggest that SMA-derived residue signals can provide useful physical guidance for deep learning models and improve the robustness of satellite-based tillage classification. Overall, SMAFuse offers a promising pathway toward scalable and dynamic field-level monitoring of tillage practices by bridging interpretable residue physics with multi-modal satellite time-series learning.

title: Near-Real-Time Biotic Stress Crop Anomaly Surveillance Using Earth Observation and Crop Modelling
authors: Natacha Kalecinski, iCube, University of Strasbourg, Strasbourg Cedex, France, Yuval Sadeh, Monash University, School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment, Melbourne, VIC, Australia, Gerald Blasch, International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center, CIMMYT Mexico, Texcoco, Mexico and Inbal Becker-Reshef, University of Maryland, Department of Geographical Sciences, College Park, United States
main_session: Satellite Solutions for Agricultural Monitoring, Drought, and Water Management II Poster
abstract: Crop diseases threaten food production, yet field surveillance is costly, spatially incomplete, and often begins only after visible damage is widespread. Earth-observing satellites provide frequent, large-scale monitoring of crop condition, but distinguishing potential biotic stress from drought, heat, nutrient limitations, management practices, and normal crop development on a large scale remains a major challenge. We present a phenology aware prototype framework for near-real-time detection of unexplained crop stress anomalies across the major U.S. wheat and maize growing regions. The framework was developed within the Global Surveillance and Advisory System (GSAS) project. The prototype integrates multi-year Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) optical imagery, Landsat land surface temperature, USDA Crop type maps, Daymet weather data, APSIM crop-growth simulations, and a DEM to estimate expected crop conditions. Historical observations are filtered by crop type, grouped into similar environments, and aligned by developmental stage using APSIM-derived phenology and cumulative growing degree days. Within each crop, environmental, and phenological group, historical optical, thermal, and weather observations define variable-specific reference distributions that characterize expected conditions and natural variability using robust statistics-based models. Current-season observations are compared with expected values to compute standardized vegetation and weather anomalies. Weather information is used to distinguish anomalies associated with abnormal rainfall or temperature from those that remain unexplained. The framework is being evaluated against independent field observations of crop diseases across major U.S. growing regions. Persistent, spatially coherent unexplained anomalies are prioritized through spatial alerts and multi-year time-series diagnostics. The alerts are not disease diagnoses but identify locations where crop responses deviate from expected trajectories and warrant further investigation, supporting targeted surveillance, and disease-risk modelling. Initial results from ongoing U.S. testing will be presented, with discussion of future adaptation to other agricultural systems, including smallholder farming regions in Asia and Africa.

title: Preliminary Evaluation of a Siberia-Trained Boreal Forest Classifier Using Field Reference Plots in Canada and Alaska
authors: Femke van Geffen, Birgit Heim, Stefan Kruse, Bas van Driel and John Bolte
main_session: The Resilience and Vulnerability of Arctic and Boreal Ecosystems to Change VI Poster
abstract: This ongoing study assesses whether a Random Forest classifier trained on eastern Siberian boreal forest data can be applied to independent boreal regions without local retraining. The SiDroForest framework is implemented with Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel observations to classify summergreen and evergreen forest pixels from seasonal spectral information, with mixed forest represented by their relative occurrence at plot level. Preliminary validation in Canada includes 29 field-classified evergreen plots with usable HLS overlap, containing 6,063 HLS pixels. Predictions with confidence below 0.70 are treated as uncertain. Model predictions are summarized within each plot and compared with its field-assigned forest type. Pixel-weighted agreement with the evergreen plot labels is 88.4%, while agreement exceeds 95% at 13 plots and is at least 75% at 25 of 29 plots. Lower agreement occurs at plots with greater predicted summergreen representation or heterogeneous canopy structure, although these relationships have not yet been tested statistically. Results are preliminary and should be interpreted cautiously because the current reference dataset is dominated by evergreen plots and pixels within plots are not independent observations. Ongoing work will add field-classified plots and extend the assessment to summergreen, evergreen, and mixed forest in additional regions of Alaska and Siberia. Further statistical analysis is needed to quantify plot-level uncertainty, test site- and class-specific effects, and determine whether observed differences reflect systematic limits to geographic transferability

title: Mapping Maple Distribution across the Conterminous United States (CONUS) by Exploiting Irregular Landsat and Sentinel-2 Time Series with Deep Learning
authors: Minghao Wang and Hankui Zhang, South Dakota State University, Geospatial Sciences Center of Excellence, Department of Geography and Geospatial Sciences, Brookings, United States
main_session: Science and Applications Enabled by Remote Sensing Data Fusion, Time Series Analysis, and AI II Poster
abstract: Maple (genus Acer ) distribution information is ecologically and economically crucial.
