However, large-area mapping from moderate-resolution satellite time series is constrained not only by classifier design but also by the semantic and spatial compatibility among reference labels, field plots, and the observed canopy signal. We developed a framework to map maple distribution in forest across the conterminous United States (CONUS) at 30 m resolution for 2022. National Park Service (NPS) vegetation inventory polygons classified based on the U.S. National Vegetation Classification were converted into binary maple and non-maple labels. We matched Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) observations to each park’s mapping year, removed edge pixels, and masked evergreen and nonforest pixels. Raw irregular HLS time series were classified directly, without compositing, using a hierarchical Transformer with separate Landsat and Sentinel-2 branches and Shuttle Radar Topography Mission terrain features. Results were generated with a five-model soft-voting ensemble. The ensemble achieved an F1-score of 0.78 on the NPS test set and 0.60 on an independent National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) dataset constructed to approximate the NPS labeling style. TreeMap 2016, a national 30 m forest type map derived from Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) plot data, was evaluated on the NEON dataset constructed to approximate the FIA labeling style using 2016 observations and achieved an F1 of 0.45. These results demonstrate that the proposed maple distribution map from raw irregular satellite time series is feasible, and we will make the CONUS product publicly available.

title: Assessment of the Circumarctic Landcover Units (CALU) at the Northern Forest Edge in Alaska and North West Canada
authors: Birgit Heim, Annett Bartsch, Mareike Wieczorek, Lea Enguehard, Jacob Schladebach, Femke van Geffen, Rustam Khairullin, Helena Bergstedt, Santosh K Panda, Glenn Patrick Juday, Dr. Go Iwahana, PhD, Katey M Walter Anthony, Kunyan Hao, Laura Schild, Simeon Lisovski and Stefan Kruse
main_session: The Resilience and Vulnerability of Arctic and Boreal Ecosystems to Change V Poster
abstract: The Circumarctic Landcover Units (CALU) land cover product was developed to improve upon existing land cover for the tundra. CALU has been extended both geographically and thematically to include the northern forest edge at 10 m spatial resolution.CALU was created by fusing Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral satellite data. Across the northern treeline and forest transition zone, the combined effects of disturbances—including wildfire, windthrow, and snow damage—and different stages of forest succession create a fine-scale mosaic of land surface types, ranging from tundra and open woodland to dense-canopy forest regeneration. Regional in situ land cover data is limited. We aggregated vegetation plot observations, UAV LiDAR and multispectral imagery from our field work in 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 and higher level containing 3-D forest structure and tree classification. In addition to quantitative accuracy metrics, visual assessment of spatial patterns provides an important complementary perspective. Accordingly, we evaluate the CALU classification by combining multiple lines of evidence, including quantitative agreement statistics, expert regional knowledge, and field observations in Alaska and North West Canada. title: An Open-Science Framework Leveraging Commercial Earth Observation Data for Analysis-Ready Surface Water Products
authors: Hannah G Pankratz, Eric Ross Anderson, Amanda Markert, Franz Josef Meyer, Joseph H Kennedy, Timothy Mayer, Alexander Melancon and Micky Maganini
main_session: Leveraging Commercial Earth Observation Data for Rapid Disaster Response Poster
abstract: Accurate, fine-scale surface water extent mapping requires aligning commercial Earth Observation data with established science baselines. While NASA’s Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) program provides access to commercial high-resolution optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) constellations, a critical gap remains in generating replicable analysis-ready data (ARD) to meet growing commercial and operational demand for reliable and consistent surface water extent maps. This study presents an open-science framework that ingests commercial optical (PlanetScope, 3 m and Vantor, sub-meter) and X-band SAR (ICEYE and Umbra) imagery to produce standardized surface water extent products modeled after NASA’s OPERA Dynamic Surface Water Extent (DSWx-HLS and DSWx-S1) product specifications. The workflow standardizes CSDA imagery by ingesting or generating Level 2 optical surface reflectance and SAR radiometrically terrain corrected products. To match the fine spatial resolution of commercial imagery, high-resolution LiDAR DEMs are incorporated throughout Level 2 processing and surface water derivation. Resulting optical and SAR pipelines yield classified outputs, including open water, cloud/shadow masks, height above nearest drainage masks, and layover/shadow masks. Initial case studies throughout the United States demonstrate performance across different ecoregions, urban and rural settings, and complex terrain, laying the groundwork for global expansion. By producing open-source code, training datasets, and uncertainty metrics, this effort bridges private-sector commercial capabilities with NASA open-science standards to produce ARD products. The resulting framework enables rapid derivation of water extent maps, significantly advancing disaster response and surface water monitoring across public and private sectors.

title: Predicting Hazard Impacts on Crop Yield in Coastal-Inland Agricultural Systems
authors: Remon Ahmed Mishu and Zijun Yang, University of North Carolina at Wilmington, Department of Earth and Ocean Sciences, Wilmington, NC, United States
main_session: Satellite Solutions for Agricultural Monitoring, Drought, and Water Management II Poster
abstract: Agricultural productivity across the North American coastal plain is affected by hydroclimatic extremes and growing soil salinization. Short-term flooding and gradual saltwater intrusion (SWI) affect soil moisture, salinity, and crop health in ways that are difficult to observe. For instance, canopy greenness may remain relatively normal while grain yield is negatively affected. Thus, conventional vegetation-index monitoring may not adequately quantify these losses. Predicting crop responses is further complicated by the need to represent multiple interacting hazards and link their combined effects to yield outcomes. In this study, we develop a deep learning framework for predicting compound hazard impacts on corn and soybean, the two major crops of the North Carolina Coastal Plain, by integrating multi-source satellite imagery, including Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) and Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), and environmental datasets. Annual crop masks are derived from the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Cropland Data Layer (CDL) to extract the spatial distribution of corn and soybean. Optical vegetation and moisture indices (e.g., NDVI, EVI2, NDMI) are complemented by SAR backscatter (e.g., VV, VH, RVI), which senses soil moisture and vegetation water content. An integrated deep learning framework is trained on these time series, into which flood exposure, soil salinity, and meteorological observations are jointly considered. The framework is validated against county-level USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) yields from 2018 to 2024, using leave-one-year-out and leave-one-county-out cross-validation to assess model’s robustness against spatial and temporal variability, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to interpret yield impacts to environmental drivers. Results show that satellite time series alone overestimate yield in drought and flood years, while multisource data improves model performance. By quantifying impacts of interacting environmental stressors on crop yield, the proposed framework holds strong potential for anticipating compound hazard impacts and supporting adaptive management in vulnerable coastal agricultural systems.

title: Improving in-season crop phosphorus and potassium status monitoring via cross-scale sensing and self-supervised learning
authors: Mr. Haozheng Ma, Kaiyu Guan, Zhao Jiang, Sheng Wang, Andrew J Margenot, Ezra Moses and Michael Douglass, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, United States
main_session: Satellite Solutions for Agricultural Monitoring, Drought, and Water Management II Poster
abstract: Monitoring crop nutrient status is essential for improving fertilizer management, increasing nutrient-use efficiency, and reducing the environmental impacts of agricultural production. However, remote sensing studies of crop nutrients have predominantly focused on nitrogen, while phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) have received substantially less attention. Though critical for crop energy transfer, root development, and reproductive growth, the relatively low tissue concentration, subtle spectral response, and limited availability of field observations of P and K challenge remote sensing retrieval. This study applies a cross-scale framework for monitoring P and K in corn and soybean. Replicated P and K fertilization rate field experiments in central Illinois with (bi)weekly leaf nutrient concentrations were measured throughout the growing season. Airborne hyperspectral imagery was acquired concurrently with field sampling for ground measurements to train partial least squares regression models for estimating crop P and K concentrations (%) and uptake (kg ha -1 ) at 0.5-m resolution. To extend nutrient monitoring from experimental fields to larger areas, we further integrate NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) data with self-supervised learning. A representation model is pretrained on multitemporal HLS imagery and subsequently fine-tuned using spatially aggregated nutrient estimates derived from the airborne hyperspectral models. This strategy leverages fine-resolution airborne observations to inform moderate-resolution satellite retrievals while accounting for the spatial scale mismatch and the limited availability of ground-truth data for satellite-based nutrient monitoring. The developed framework helps alleviate the limited availability of crop P and K observations, and identifies a pathway for scalable, multitemporal monitoring of crop nutrient status. By linking field measurements, airborne hyperspectral imagery, and HLS time series, this study aims to advance comprehensive P and K assessment for precision nutrient management in corn and soybean systems, facilitate its transfer to other cropping systems, and support management practices such as removal-based variable-rate fertilizer application.

title: Field-Level Detection of Cover Crop Adoption and Growth Across the U.S. Cotton Belt Using a Phenology and Environment Guided Framework
authors: Saibo Li, Kaiyu Guan, Sheng Wang, Qu Zhou, Yide Xu, Xiaocui Wu and Zhangliang Chen
main_session: Satellite Solutions for Agricultural Monitoring, Drought, and Water Management II Poster
abstract: Cover crops provide important agroecological benefits, particularly in cotton agroecosystems that are vulnerable to soil erosion and water limitation. Satellite remote sensing enables large-scale cover crop monitoring, but existing approaches primarily focus on cover crop occurrence, overlooking seasonal growth dynamics that strongly influence their agroecological benefits. Moreover, detecting and characterizing cover crops across the U.S. Cotton Belt remains challenging due to its diverse cropping systems and substantial environmental heterogeneity. Here, we developed a phenology- and environment-guided framework to detect field-level cover crop adoption and characterize seasonal growth dynamics across U.S. cotton agroecosystems from 2016 to 2024. Specifically, Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) time series were used to extract winter vegetation phenological characteristics and distinguish potential cover crops from overwintering main crops. County-level cover crop statistics from the USDA Census of Agriculture were then integrated with climate and soil variables using interpretable machine learning to calibrate and predict spatially and temporally dynamic detection thresholds for cover crop growth intensity, thereby reducing weed interference. The results showed that the framework substantially outperformed conventional fixed-threshold approaches, achieving an R² of 0.85 and an RMSE of 2.84% compared to county-level cover crop adoption statistics. Sand content and mean dew point temperature were the dominant controls on detection thresholds, with their interactions indicating that cover crop detectability is strongly regulated by local soil–climate conditions. Applying the framework across the U.S. Cotton Belt revealed a significant increase in cover crop adoption from 2016 to 2024. Adoption was consistently highest in cotton, followed by soybeans, corn, and peanuts, with increasing trends observed for most major crop types. Cover crop seasonal growth dynamics showed that longer growing periods were generally associated with greater vegetation growth intensity across years and crop types. Longer growing periods were concentrated in western cotton-growing regions, particularly Texas, whereas higher cover crop growth intensity occurred mainly in Alabama and southern Texas. Our work provides a scalable approach for simultaneously mapping cover crop adoption and characterizing seasonal growth dynamics across environmentally heterogeneous agricultural landscapes, supporting field-scale evaluation of cover crop ecosystem services and climate-smart agricultural management.

title: Moderate-resolution Satellite Time Series Reveal Coupled Management–climate Controls on Global Cropland Phenological Shifts
authors: ABSTRACT WITHDRAWN
main_session: Science and Applications Enabled by Remote Sensing Data Fusion, Time Series Analysis, and AI II Poster
abstract: Satellite-observed crop phenology is widely used to assess vegetation responses to environmental change, yet phenological variation in croplands is also strongly shaped by management, complicating its interpretation as a climate signal. We developed a break-aware framework to characterize and attribute annual cropland phenological shifts using dense, moderate-resolution Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) time series. The framework integrates stochastic continuous change detection, temporal-break classification, annual phenology extraction from filtered Enhanced Vegetation Index trajectories, and attribution of year-to-year shifts to cropping-intensity change, crop-type change, agricultural drought, other disturbances, or within-regime gradual shifts. We applied the framework to 50 cropland-dominated HLS tiles spanning seven major agricultural regions and retrieved annual green-up and dormancy dates from 2016 to 2024. The HLS-derived dates showed strong cross-product agreement with MCD12Q2, with correlations of 0.964 for green-up and 0.988 for dormancy. Area-adjusted assessment of break detection and classification yielded an overall accuracy of 97.96%. Within-regime gradual shifts, mostly driven by climate change, accounted for 53.1% of the absolute annual green-up shift and 48.7% of the dormancy shifts, whereas cropping-system changes contributed 38.4% and 46.7%, respectively. Crop-type change contributed slightly more than intensity change to green-up shifts, whereas intensity change was the dominant management contribution to dormancy shifts. These results demonstrate that satellite-observed cropland phenology represents a coupled environmental–management signal. Explicitly accounting for cropping-system changes is therefore critical for accurately interpreting large-scale cropland phenological shifts and disentangling management effects from climate forcing.

title: Multi-satellite data fusion for improved field-scale evapotranspiration mapping on Google Earth Engine
authors: Hui LIU, Cornell University, School of Integrative Plant Science, Ithaca, NY, United States, Yun Yang, Cornell University, School of Intergrative Plant Science, Ithaca, NY, United States, Martha Anderson, USDA Agricultural Research Service, Hydrology and Remote Sensing Laboratory, Beltsville, United States, Feng Gao, USDA-ARS Hydrology and Remote Sensing Laboratory, Beltsville, United States, Christopher Hain, NASA Marshall Space Flight Cetner, Huntsville, United States, Vikalp Mishra, NASA,Marshall Space Flight Center, Short-term Prediction Research and Transition [SPoRT] Center, Huntsville, United States, John M Volk, Desert Research Institute, Division of Hydrologic Sciences, Reno, United States and Yanghui Kang, Virginia Tech University, Department of Biological Systems Engineering, Blacksburg, United States
main_session: Science and Applications Enabled by Remote Sensing Data Fusion, Time Series Analysis, and AI II Poster
abstract: Accurate field-scale evapotranspiration (ET) data with high spatiotemporal resolution is crucial for characterizing surface energy and water balance dynamics and guiding water resource management. OpenET, implemented on Google Earth Engine (GEE), provides field-scale ET estimates and relies mainly on Landsat data. Although Landsat thermal infrared (TIR) observations are effective for field-scale ET mapping, the ~8-day revisit interval of the combined Landsat 8/9 constellation provides insufficient temporal sampling for short-term ET dynamics. This study presents a framework to improve the spatiotemporal resolution of ET mapping by integrating TIR observations from ECOSTRESS and VIIRS with Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel (HLS) data on GEE. Land surface temperature (LST) data from Landsat, ECOSTRESS and VIIRS were sharpened to 30-m resolution using the Data Mining Sharpener (DMS) algorithm. These sharpened LST data, along with 30-m Leaf Area Index (LAI) and albedo derived from HLS, were used as inputs to the GEE-based Disaggregated Atmosphere-Land Exchange (DisALEXI) model to produce daily 30-m ET estimates. ET estimates were validated against flux tower observations and compared with baseline Landsat-derived ET at six sites with varying land cover and climatic conditions. Results indicated that incorporating ECOSTRESS and VIIRS generally improved ET estimation accuracy, reducing average MAE (mm/day) by 8.64% (1.12 to 1.02, daily), 14.40% (1.00 to 0.85, weekly), 16.37% (0.82 to 0.69, monthly) relative to Landsat-only baselines. This GEE-based framework establishes a prototype workflow for integrating new satellite data sources into the OpenET modeling framework, supporting sustainable agriculture and water resource management.

title: Toward Integrated Earth Observation Applications for Agriculture at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center
authors: Vikalp Mishra, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, AL, United States, Christopher Hain, NASA Marshall Space Flight Cetner, Huntsville, United States, Aparna Phalke, PhD, The University of Alabama in Huntsville, Earth System Science Center, Huntsville, United States, Lee Ellenburg, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Huntsville, United States, Siddharth Chaudhary, University of Alabama in Huntsville, NASA ODSI, Huntsville, AL, United States, Ashutosh S Limaye, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, United States and Alex Goberna, Universities Space Research Association Huntsville, Huntsville, United States
main_session: Satellite Solutions for Agricultural Monitoring, Drought, and Water Management II Poster
abstract: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) has developed a wide range of Earth observation (EO) capabilities for agriculture, spanning satellite- based monitoring, AI/ML + process-based modeling and data assimilation, and operational decision support. This presentation showcases several ongoing agriculture-focused activities across different research groups and projects at MSFC, and highlights how, together, they represent an emerging integrated capability rather than a set of isolated efforts. Together, these efforts align into four themes: (a) Direct satellite applications use EO products to characterize agricultural land use, crop development, and surface conditions, for example, HLS data for planting date estimation and crop type mapping; (b) Integrated satellite and modeling efforts combine observations with land surface, hydrologic, and crop models to extend beyond what either provides alone, for example, assimilating satellite soil moisture into crop models to better estimate irrigation effects, or ingesting satellite-driven planting dates into models; (c) Integrated frameworks link crop information with water availability and climate resilience to address agricultural questions that cross traditional domains, for example, a coupled framework for robust assessment of water availability and irrigation demand, or a coupled crop, land, and weather model to assess the environmental impact of resilience efforts like irrigation; (d) Decision support translates these capabilities into user-friendly tools and information that inform operational agricultural and water management decisions.The Alabama Irrigation Initiative is a prime example of multiple science activities coming together to inform irrigation adoption and its long-term economic benefits. Presented together, these themes demonstrate the breadth of EO-driven agricultural work underway at MSFC and its progression from foundational satellite applications toward integrated decision support. We discuss opportunities to strengthen connections across these efforts and to present a coherent, integrated solution to relevant stakeholders.

title: Mapping Ponding Severity Gradients and Crop Phenological Response to a Rapid Inundation Event Using Daily 3 m Satellite Imagery
authors: Christy Gibson, Trent Ford, Talon Becker, Connor Sible, Boris Camiletti, Esther Ngumbi and Sunoj Shajahan
main_session: Sustainable Global Agrifood Systems: Reducing Carbon, Water, and Biodiversity Footprints of Agricultural Production with Improved Land Management II Poster
abstract: Excess moisture rivals drought as a driver of yield loss across the US Midwest, yet the spatial structure of inundation damage remains poorly resolved. Within a single field, prolonged ponding, partial saturation, and unaffected upland occur across micro-topographic gradients of a few centimeters, producing divergent crop outcomes that field-average monitoring cannot capture. Quantifying that structure is a prerequisite for evaluating whether management practices buffer inundation stress and for estimating regional losses with useful precision. We characterized a multi-day inundation event that affected Champaign County, Illinois, in June 2026, during which cumulative rainfall exceeded 300 percent of normal on soils already at field capacity, producing surface ponding that persisted for days at early vegetative crop stages. Using near-daily 3 m PlanetScope imagery integrated with 30 m Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel time series, we delineate ponded areas within individual fields and derive severity gradients from ponding persistence and dry-down trajectory, quantify affected area at field, farm, and county scales, and assess crop phenological response across those gradients, including emergence timing, greenup, and growth rate through the season. This work would evaluate severity metrics derived at 3 m and reproduced at 30 m, which determines whether the approach extends regionally using freely available imagery. Ground-truth validation against field-measured soil moisture, soil biogeochemistry, and end-of-season yield is planned as the next phase of this work.

title: Compressing a Geospatial Foundation Model for Onboard Land-Degradation Forecasting: When Knowledge Distillation Helps, and When It Does Not.
authors: Gabriel Diaz Ireland, Darwin Geospatial, AI Engineering Department, St Petersburg, United States, Victor Manuel Tenorio, Rey Juan Carlos University, Signal Theory and Communications and Telematics Systems and Computing, Madrid, Spain, Sandupal Dutta, Johns Hopkins University, Department of Earth & Planetary Sciences, Baltimore, MD, United States, Irene Molero Cuenca, Rey Juan Carlos University, Darwin Geospatial, Madrid, Spain and Benjamin F Zaitchik, Johns Hopkins University, Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Baltimore, United States
main_session: Satellite Solutions for Agricultural Monitoring, Drought, and Water Management II Poster
abstract: Satellite monitoring of land degradation is largely reactive: full scenes are downlinked and processed on the ground regardless of relevance, which limits how quickly a small satellite could flag emerging soil loss on its own. We test whether a geospatial foundation model can be compressed enough for onboard inference without losing the skill that makes it useful. We distill the 364.5-million-parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M teacher into a 1.19-million-parameter MobileNetV3 student — a 307-fold reduction — training both on multi-temporal NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 tiles to predict pixel-wise Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Bare Soil Index (BSI) sixty days ahead, and we vary the training-set size from 500 to 44,000 chips. On held-out agricultural data the student reaches a coefficient of determination R2 = 0.794 against the teacher's 0.828, retaining about 96% of its predictive skill in a model 307 times smaller. Output-level distillation further improves accuracy over an identically sized student trained on ground truth alone, with the gain concentrated at full data scale, while more elaborate transfer schemes add nothing. Compression of this foundation model is therefore nearly lossless for the forecasting target, and distillation delivers a real but data-scale-dependent gain — a concrete guide to when a tiny onboard model should inherit a large one.

title: Advancing GeoAI for operational services in the Hindu Kush Himalaya: Opportunities and Challenges
authors: Sudip Pradhan, International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), Kathmandu, Nepal and Birendra Bajracharya, ICIMOD, Kathmandu, Nepal
main_session: Frontiers of Geospatial Artificial Intelligence and Capacity Building: Translating Research to Action III Oral
abstract: The Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) is a globally significant mountain system spanning eight countries, harbouring exceptional biodiversity, and sustaining water, food, energy, and livelihoods for nearly two billion people. It faces escalating threats from climate change, environmental degradation, rapid socioeconomic transformation, and rising disaster risk. As a SERVIR hub for HKH, we developed information services combining Earth observation and geospatial science to address these challenges, including high-impact weather assessment, flood early warning, land cover monitoring, forest fire and drought monitoring. Recent advances in Geo-AI provide unprecedented opportunities to enhance these services through automated mapping, faster analysis, and generating deeper insights. Our Geo-AI strategy focused on two complementary directions. First, we used foundation models to generate high-quality geospatial information layers. For example, we applied the Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M-TL foundation model with TerraTorch to produce land cover maps from seasonal Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel composites over Nepal's Koshi Province. The model was trained using Collect Earth Online reference data used for National Land Cover Monitoring System of Nepal developed earlier by SERVIR. We evaluated using two variants, frozen linear probe and LoRA-adapted UPerNet decoder. Second, we developed prototype of an agentic natural language geospatial analysis pipeline based on a LangGraph multi-agent framework with pgvector retrieval. The Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model enabled users to query structured, spatial, and raster datasets using plain language while automatically generating analytical summaries and visualizations. Despite promising results, operationalizing these tools remains constrained by fragmented geospatial data ecosystems, limited high-performance computing infrastructure, shortage of interdisciplinary expertise, weak institutional readiness, and insufficient collaboration among institutions in the region. Addressing these requires a comprehensive capacity development framework encompassing human skills, institutional governance, digital infrastructure, interoperable data ecosystems, and strengthened regional partnerships to accelerate Geo-AI adoption across the HKH.

title: Multi-Sensor Satellite Flood Detection in Bihar, India
authors: Andrew Gillreath-Brown, Austin Madson and Jennifer R Marlon
main_session: Advancing Flood Science and Applications Using Earth Observations and Data-Driven Approaches II Oral
abstract: Bihar is India’s most flood-prone state, where roughly 76% of the population in north Bihar lives under constant threat of flooding. During the June-October monsoon, rainfall and snowmelt from Nepal flow through five major Himalayan rivers into the Bihar lowlands, adding to local precipitation and raising flood risk as water moves toward the Ganges. Timely information on the extent, severity, and timing of flooding is critical for flood preparedness, adaptation planning, and early warning systems. However, village-level flood records spanning multiple years remain scarce for the region. We combined two independent satellite products, Sentinel-1 (S1) synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS), to generate village-level flood estimates for 556 villages in Bihar for 2016–2025. S1 backscatter data were pre-processed and compared against per-orbit, dry-season backscatter baselines using a z-score anomaly detection technique. Water extent was classified through a valley-emphasis Otsu thresholding method with an adaptive seeding technique using dual-pol data. We then derived a custom Random Forest (RF) model trained on an exhaustive set of manually labeled samples, stratified by land-cover subcategory (e.g., flooding, ponds, rivers, rice fields, built-up areas, roads), sensor (Sentinel-2, Landsat, mixed), and season (monsoon vs. dry), comprising 5,665 labeled pixels (49% wet, 51% dry) distributed across Bihar’s full spatial extent and the 2016–2025 study period to minimize spatial autocorrelation. HLS data were pre-processed in Google Earth Engine and used to compute the appropriate spectral indices (i.e., NDWI and MNDVI) and to acquire multiple spectral bands (i.e., Green, Red, NIR, and SWIR1) that were then passed into the RF model for classification. Together, these two products track surface water change across seasons with an increased temporal coverage than any single sensor, particularly during the cloud-heavy monsoon when the majority of flooding occurs. This multi-sensor, village-level flood record provides an objective foundation for evaluating flood exposure and supporting early warning and adaptation planning in one of South Asia’s most flood-vulnerable regions.

title: Agribound: An open-source framework unifying geospatial foundation models and agentic AI for global agricultural field boundary mapping
authors: Sayantan Majumdar, Jeremy Rapp, Jayden Atkin, Matt Bromley, Justin L Huntington, Peter ReVelle, Soheil Nozari, Ryan Smith, Md Fahim Hasan, Eric Jensen, David Ketchum and Samapriya Roy
main_session: Frontiers of Geospatial Artificial Intelligence and Capacity Building: Translating Research to Action III Oral
abstract: Accurate agricultural field boundaries are critical for crop monitoring, irrigation water accounting, and land-change science, yet the growing ecosystem of deep-learning and geospatial foundation models (GFMs) for boundary delineation remains fragmented across incompatible codebases, input conventions, and output schemas. Comparing models on the same area, imagery, and metrics can take weeks of engineering, and two problems persist: boundary models segment every visually distinct region rather than fields, and supervised models require regionally representative labels that do not exist for much of the Global South. We present agribound, an open-source, cloud-native Python framework unifying seven delineation engines behind a single function call: YOLO-based instance segmentation (Delineate-Anything), multi-country semantic segmentation (Fields of The World), Mask R-CNN (GeoAI), a satellite-pretrained DINOv3 vision transformer, the Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model, unsupervised embedding clustering (AlphaEarth, TESSERA), and multi-engine ensembling. It spans ten satellite/aerial sources from 1984 to present, building cloud-masked composites in Google Earth Engine. Automatic land-use/land-cover filtering removes non-agricultural polygons; a zero-training pipeline combining embedding clustering, crop-probability filtering, and SAM2 refinement maps fields anywhere without labels; and a unified fine-tuning and evaluation harness enables controlled comparison across sensors, resolutions (1-30 m), and landscapes. We benchmark all engines across six continents and demonstrate multi-decadal irrigation water accounting in New Mexico, USA. An LLM-orchestrator interface decomposes natural-language requests (e.g., map irrigated fields in this area for 2024) into agribound tool calls, autonomously selecting sensor, engine, and filtering strategy. By reducing the barrier from weeks of engineering to a single call and enabling practitioners without machine-learning expertise or labeled data to map fields, agribound offers the geospatial community an open capacity-building resource and a reproducible testbed for evaluating present and future foundation models on equal footing, accelerating the translation of Earth Observation data into actionable insights.

title: Benchmarking Earth Observation Foundational Models: Lessons learned comparing their Downstream Land Cover Outputs
authors: Emil A Cherrington, University of Alabama in Huntsville, Earth System Science Center, Huntsville, AL, United States
main_session: Frontiers of Geospatial Artificial Intelligence and Capacity Building: Translating Research to Action III Oral
abstract: Even in the current era of big Earth observation (EO) data, the ability to accurately and rapidly classify land cover remains a key scientific challenge. To that end, multiple recent efforts have focused on developing Foundation Models (FMs) trained on large datasets that can facilitate the rapid generation of products which can transform EO imagery into informational products on which decisions can be based. For instance, in 2023, NASA partnered with IBM to develop the Prithvi geospatial FM, whose downstream applications include the classification of land cover, and the identification of flooded areas and burn scars. In parallel, in 2025, Google released its AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) dataset to serve as an input to land cover classification efforts. Using the ~23,000 km 2 sized Central American country of Belize as a case study, our team embarked on a series of land cover classification experiments to test the accuracy of different models. To date, over two hundred experiments were run, using models ranging from the Prithvi-100M model to bespoke deep learning models of varying architectures, and leveraging datasets such as the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 effort. Classification accuracies were evaluated quantitatively using in-situ data provided by local partners, in addition to qualitative assessment of outputs. This presentation will focus on the lessons learned in comparing outputs generated using the Prithvi geospatial FM with outputs generated using different models and approaches, including data derived from the AEF dataset. The implications for the broader EO user community will also be discussed.

title: ASTRA: An Apollo-Style Lunar Mission Architecture for the Mapping and Sampling of Permanently Shadowed Regions
authors: Brayden Sanderson, Shashwath Dinesh, Avania Bhattacharya, Beau Elder, Madelyn Nedimyer, Anuraag Pillai, Galileo Solis and Hunter Zamora, NASA SEES STEM Enhancement in Earth Science program, Austin, United States
main_session: BRIGHT STaRS: Bright Students Training as Research Scientists Poster Session Poster
abstract: The lunar south pole has become the primary target of current lunar exploration efforts due to its Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs), which act as cosmic freezers preserving unanalyzed volatiles, pristine regolith, and primordial water ice. Current human landing architectures, including Starship HLS and Blue Moon Mk2, are complex systems that require orbital refueling, a technique not proven to close. Additionally, comprehensive mapping and subsurface characterization of PSRs remain areas of active development. Drawing from the proven Apollo mission architecture, the team proposes ASTRA: the Apollo-style Sampling and Topographical Reconnaissance Architecture. Rather than relying on massive, integrated landing systems, ASTRA employs a smaller-scale and more efficient lunar lander for a two-person crew, removing the requirement of unproven orbital refueling. Furthermore, the lander launch utilizes a ballistic lunar transfer (BLT) into Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit (NRHO), minimizing propellant requirements and increasing payload capacity. The lander is complemented by a novel autonomous robotics stack to enable holistic mapping and sampling of Shackleton Crater, an ideal region to study PSRs.

title: In-Domain Gains, Out-of-Domain Costs: Quantifying Cross-Site Transfer in Fine-Tuned Foundation Models for Urban Land Cover
authors: Jack Garner, NASA SEES STEM Enhancement in Earth Science program, Austin, TX, UNITED STATES, Grant Nowotny, NASA SEES STEM Enhancement in Earth Science program, Fulshear, United States, Aditya Kaul, NASA SEES STEM Enhancement in Earth Science program, Fremont, United States, Ishaan Soni, NASA SEES STEM Enhancement in Earth Science program, Bengaluru, India and Leema Malhis, NASA SEES STEM Enhancement in Earth Science program, Woodbridge, United States
main_session: BRIGHT STaRS: Bright Students Training as Research Scientists Poster Session Poster
abstract: Geospatial satellite transformer models are crucial for interpreting Earth observations that inform climate forecasting, zoning policy, and disaster response. However, satellite data can be noisy in rapidly changing or urban areas. Key issues such as spectrally mixed pixels and building occlusion can affect visible foliage levels, degrading model classification ability. Using the GLOBE Observer program, we collected 3,600 ground samples (5-meter footprints) at 36 Manhattan locations and paired them with Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel imagery. Utilizing this data, we fine-tuned the Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model to improve urban land cover mapping. We compared model performance across two labeling strategies: hard labels, which force each mixed pixel into one class, and soft (fractional) labels, which train the model toward the true built-up fraction. To combat severe class imbalance towards built-up labels, we evaluated class-weighted and focal-loss training and report precision-recall performance for the minority class. Our fine-tuning method improved separability over the pretrained representation. Building upon these results, we will conduct a controlled test of cross-site generalization across four additional locations: Fulshear, Texas; Fremont, California; Bengaluru, India; and Woodbridge, Virginia. Each site will be used to fine-tune the same Prithvi model with an identical 3,600-sample pipeline, isolating the location of ground sample data. Each model will then be evaluated across all five sites, producing a transfer matrix that separates in-domain accuracy from cross-site transfer. Based on analysis to date, we believe that fine-tuning will improve in-domain classification accuracy but decrease cross-site performance due to differences in urban morphology, vegetation composition, and local spectral characteristics. However, we expect geographically or environmentally similar locations to exhibit better transferability than dissimilar locations.

title: Development of a UAV Imagery-Based Visibility Classification Algorithm and an Operational Decision-Support System for UAM Corridors
authors: Minseok Kim, Siwon Kim, Kiramat Hussain, Gwanjae Lee, Kyung-Hwan Kwak and Jonggun Kim
main_session: Fog: Connecting Atmosphere, Ocean, Land, Ecosystems, and Society I Poster
abstract: Safe Urban Air Mobility (UAM) requires visibility along flight corridors to be secured in advance, but conventional ground-based sensors measure visibility only in one direction at a fixed point and cannot track it as an aircraft moves along the 300-600 m corridor altitude band. This study develops an algorithm that classifies UAM corridor visibility from RGB imagery on an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), and a system that secures this information in advance to support operational decisions. Rather than being mounted on the UAM aircraft, the technique uses prior remote UAV flights to secure corridor visibility proactively. Across 35 flight sessions from June 2024 to April 2026 at Chuncheon and the Ulsan K-UAM testbed, 13,590 images were collected and labeled as Good, Normal, or Bad. To avoid subjective labeling, a Dark Channel Prior classifier combining a Koschmieder-based fog density metric and an image clarity metric assigned physically consistent labels. Four models were compared: EfficientNet-B0, XGBoost, DINOv2, and ConvNeXtV2-Tiny, reaching 99.45%, 99.06%, 99.01%, and 98.44% accuracy on the validation set, a spread of only 1.01 points. A near real-time pipeline streams UAV imagery via RTMP, converts it to HLS with ffmpeg, runs inference, and delivers results over WebSocket to a React and Cesium.js 3D dashboard on Google Cloud Platform, color-coding each corridor section by visibility class so operators can judge feasibility immediately. This work shows that UAM corridor visibility can be classified and visualized in near real time using only a UAV RGB camera and deep learning, without dedicated meteorological equipment. Future work includes domain adaptation across regions and seasons and multi-UAV corridor-wide mapping. □ Keywords Urban Air Mobility (UAM), Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Visibility Classification, Deep Learning, Dark Channel Prior (DCP), Operational Decision Support Acknowledgements This work was funded by the Korea Meteorological Administration Research and Development Program under Grant RS-2024-00404042.

title: Fine-resolution Fuel Characterization for Near Real-time Wildfire Susceptibility Assessment: From Ignition Probability to Burn Potential
authors: Tuo Feng, Dar A Roberts, Max Moritz, Stuart Sweeney, Haijun Li and Alan Murray
main_session: Cooperative Strategies for Wildland Fire Science and Management: Integrating Earth Observation Science, Technologies, and Operations to Enhance Community and Ecosystem Resilience IV Poster
abstract: Near Real-time monitoring of wildfire susceptibility is essential for early warning and pre-fire intervention. The expansion of Earth observation archives provides opportunities to capture biophysical properties of vegetative fuels across various scales, thereby supporting inference of spatially-explicit wildfire susceptibility. However, the extent to which scaling impacts the accuracy in fire danger modeling remains largely unknown, constraining understanding of fire - fuel feedbacks and operational implementation of risk assessment. This study leverages full-collections of MODIS and HLS archives spanning the last decade across Southern California to quantify the effectiveness of finer-resolution fuel measurements in improving detection of point-scale ignition probability and patch-level burn potential. The fractional estimates of major fuel types were retrieved via spectral mixture analysis, and subsequently combined with live and dead fuel moisture content and extinction thresholds to generate an ensemble fire potential index (eFPI) at both MODIS and HLS scales. Further, we developed XGBoost models with multi-resolution imagery as inputs and compared their respective accuracy in capturing fuel ignitability and the likelihood that an ignition would successfully initiate a burn. Assessment of the eFPI and XGBoost models across different scales suggests that finer-resolution multispectral imagery provides substantial improvements in characterizing both ignition probability ( AUC eFPI&MODIS = 0.70; AUC eFPI&HLS = 0.76; AUC XGBoost&MODIS = 0.79; AUC eFPI&HLS = 0.83), and subsequent burn potential ( AUC eFPI&MODIS = 0.73; AUC eFPI&HLS = 0.79; AUC XGBoost&MODIS = 0.85; AUC eFPI&HLS = 0.93). Despite the higher accuracy, XGBoost models exhibited limited transferability across time, with models trained on samples from fire / no-fire season showing substantial declines in predictive performance when applied to opposite seasons, whereas the predictions from the eFPI framework demonstrated stronger temporal stability. This study informs the strategic selection of multi-spectral imagery for wildfire susceptibility modeling, and offers guidelines on developing near real-time products to support operational risk monitoring.

title: Evaluating 30-m and 500-m Satellite-Derived Crop Phenology Using UAV and Field Observations
authors: Ms. Peiyu Du, Xiaoyang Zhang, Yongchang Ye, Maitiniyazi Maimaitijiang and Yu Shen
main_session: Understanding Phenological Responses, Changes, and Feedback: Patterns, Mechanisms, and Consequences I Poster
abstract: Crop phenology is important for agricultural management and yield forecasting. Satellite vegetation indices are used for phenology monitoring, but index sensitivity and spatial resolution may produce inconsistent estimates. This study aims to (1) compare vegetation indices for crop phenology detection and (2) evaluate phenology derived from 30-m and 500-m satellite observations through comparisons with UAV and visual field observations. Data were collected in 2024 over four corn and soybean fields near Brookings, South Dakota. The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Two-band Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI2), and Kernel Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (KNDVI) were calculated from 30-m Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 (HLS), native 500-m Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) Nadir BRDF-Adjusted Reflectance, a 30-m HLS–VIIRS fusion time series, and UAV observations. The Spatiotemporal Shape-Matching Model generated the fusion time series, and the Hybrid Piecewise Logistic Model detected six phenological transition dates from greenup onset to dormancy onset. Dates derived from the four remote-sensing datasets were intercompared and compared with visual field observations. Preliminary results indicate that vegetation-index performance depended on the datasets compared. When each satellite product was compared with UAV observations, KNDVI produced the smallest average phenological differences for native VIIRS and the HLS–VIIRS fusion product, whereas NDVI produced the smallest differences for HLS. NDVI agreed most closely with visual field observations. Across indices and stages with available field observations, UAV-derived dates had the smallest average absolute differences from visual observations, followed by HLS, the HLS–VIIRS fusion product, and native VIIRS. Across data sources, maturity onset was relatively consistent with visual observations, whereas senescence onset was detected 23–44 days earlier and dormancy onset was generally detected later. These results demonstrate that crop phenology differences depend jointly on vegetation index, observation scale, data source, and phenological stage, providing guidance for interpreting 30-m and 500-m satellite-derived crop phenology.

title: Evolutionary Optimisation Algorithms for PROSAIL Inversion Using Harmonised Landsat Sentinel Data: A Decadal Case Study on Rainfed Corn
authors: Nitish Singh and Soumyashree Kar, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Centre of Studies in Resources Engineering, Mumbai, India
main_session: Remote Sensing of Terrestrial Ecosystems: Monitoring, Understanding, and Management Across Scales I Poster
abstract: Inversion of the PROSAIL radiative transfer model remains constrained by an inherently ill-posed, multimodal cost surface, particularly when applied to Harmonised Landsat Sentinel (HLS) time series spanning multiple sensors. Conventional look-up-table (LUT) inversion samples the parameter space coarsely and can miss narrow global minima, motivating derivative-free, population-based optimisation as an alternative. This study benchmarks four evolutionary optimisation algorithms - Genetic Algorithm (GA), Differential Evolution (DE), Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO), and Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) - against LUT-based inversion of PROSPECT-D coupled with 4SAIL, applied to HLS L30 (Landsat 8/9) and S30 (Sentinel-2) reflectance time series over rainfed corn fields in Story County, Iowa, USA, spanning 2016 to 2025. Corn pixels are identified year-by-year from the USDA Cropland Data Layer. All algorithms are evaluated for retrieval of leaf area index (LAI), leaf chlorophyll content (Cab), and equivalent water thickness (Cw), addressing the correlated, multi-parameter retrieval problem characteristic of PROSAIL's ill-posedness. Retrievals are validated against MODIS MCD15A3H LAI and, where available, in-situ AmeriFlux measurements. Performance is compared in terms of retrieval accuracy (RMSE, bias, R-squared), computational efficiency (convergence iterations, cost-function evaluations), and stability across the ten-year HLS harmonised record. The comparison quantifies the accuracy-efficiency trade-off relevant to operational, large-area biophysical retrieval, and clarifies whether population-based, derivative-free evolutionary algorithms outperform LUT inversion in navigating the multimodal cost surface introduced by cross-sensor variability within the harmonised time series. Findings inform algorithm selection for PROSAIL-based crop biophysical monitoring at continental scale.

title: Developing a National-Scale Fuel Type Mapping Framework for the New Zealand Wildfire Prediction System
authors: Paul Seibert, Taejin Park and Jessica McCarty
main_session: NISAR Applications: Soil Moisture, Hydrology, and Societal Impacts II Poster
abstract: As wildfire activity in New Zealand is expected to increase with climate change, accurately characterizing wildfire fuels is essential for improving fire danger prediction and forecasting. Existing fire danger prediction systems rely primarily on meteorological observations and weather models but often lack detailed spatial information on fuel type and condition. Satellite remote sensing offers continuous observations of vegetation that can improve fire danger assessments by capturing spatiotemporal variability in fuel characteristics. Recent improvements in satellite remote sensing have substantially increased the spatial and temporal resolution of Earth observation datasets, enabling more detailed characterization of vegetation structure, composition, and condition across landscapes. We are developing a national-scale fuel type mapping framework to support a satellite imagery-informed wildfire prediction system for New Zealand. This framework combines optical observations from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) with radar observations from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) Geocoded Covariance (GCOV) product to generate quarterly fuel type maps across New Zealand. Optical and synthetic aperture radar observation provide complementary spectral and structural characteristics, improving discrimination among wildfire fuel classes across diverse ecosystems. Model development is informed by in situ fuels data and evaluated using a crowd sourced national fuel type dataset. This presentation describes the framework architecture, multisensor data integration workflow, and preliminary classification performance. This work provides a framework for incorporating satellite-derived fuel type information into operational wildfire forecasting systems and demonstrates the value of multisensor Earth observations for wildfire risk assessment.

title: AfricaIR10: A 10 m AI‑Enabled Irrigated–Rainfed Cropland Map of Africa Using Google DeepMind’s AlphaEarth Foundation Data and Self‑Supervised Machine Learning
authors: Dr. Pardhasaradhi Teluguntla, Prasad Thenkabail, Adam Oliphant, Itiya Aneece, Daniel Foley and Jake Lawton
main_session: From Pixels to Practice: Remote Sensing and Machine Learning Driving Agricultural Innovation I Oral
abstract: High-resolution and continental-scale characterization of irrigated and rainfed croplands is fundamental for agricultural water accounting, food security monitoring, climate adaptation, and sustainable land and water resource management. This is true across the continent of Africa, where existing 30-m land cover products are limited in their ability to resolve the continent's highly fragmented smallholder production systems, dispersed irrigation schemes, and heterogeneous rainfed agricultural landscapes. Here, we present AfricaIR10 , the first continental 10-m irrigated–rainfed cropland map for Africa (2025), derived from Google DeepMind's AlphaEarth 64-band multimodal geospatial embeddings using a self-supervised, agroecological zone (AEZ)-stratified machine learning framework implemented on Google Earth Engine. AfricaIR10 achieves robust generalization across Africa's diverse agroecological and climatic conditions. AfricaIR10 achieves an overall accuracy of 95.5%, while the irrigated croplands obtained producer’s and user’s accuracy of 90.6% and 88.1% and the rainfed croplands obtained producer’s and user’s accuracy of 96.4% and 97.5% respectively. The product identifies 63.5 million hectares (Mha) of irrigated cropland, 236.7 Mha of rainfed cropland, and 300.3 Mha of total cropland across all 54 African countries. In addition, comparisons with three existing global cropland products and recent Africa‑focused datasets show strong agreement in major irrigation regions while revealing substantial underestimation of smallholder irrigation and fragmented rainfed cropland in coarser products. AfricaIR10 delivers unprecedented 10-m spatial resolution and thematic fidelity for quantifying agricultural water use, irrigation extent, crop production potential, climate vulnerability, and basin-scale water stress across Africa. AfricaIR10 provides a scalable baseline for consistent, high-resolution monitoring by integrating next-generation Earth observation datasets, including AlphaEarth Foundation, Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) and NISAR. It supports hydrological modeling, agricultural water accounting, climate adaptation, and evidence-based decision-making to improve Africa's food and water security.

title: From sink to source: 30 m mapping of cropland net ecosystem carbon balance across the U.S. Corn Belt
authors: Xian Wang, Kimberly A Novick, Mallory Barnes, Chao Wang and Kesondra Key
main_session: From Pixels to Practice: Remote Sensing and Machine Learning Driving Agricultural Innovation I Oral
abstract: In croplands, soil organic carbon (SOC) is the primary long-term carbon storage pool. But SOC changes so slowly against a large background stock that detecting annual change requires repeated, high-precision sampling, which is impractical at regional scale. Net ecosystem carbon balance (NECB), defined as what a field takes up minus what leaves (including harvest), offers an annual flux-based alternative that captures the full ecosystem carbon balance, rather than inferring it from a slowly changing stock. However, NECB has neither been mapped at high resolution nor used to evaluate cropland carbon dynamics across large regions. In this study, we produced an observation-constrained, 30 m NECB product for corn and soybean fields across the Corn Belt states from 2017 to 2022. We first produced gap-free 30 m monthly reflectance by fusing HLS and MODIS reflectance, then derived vegetation, moisture, and respiration proxies. These, with Daymet meteorological variables, were used to upscale eddy covariance net ecosystem productivity (NEP) in a random forest model. The model predicts daily NEP (R² = 0.73) and year-to-year anomalies reasonably well (R² = 0.64). We then computed NECB as 30 m predicted NEP minus 30 m grain carbon export (QDANN yield × carbon fraction) and leaching losses (IPCC Tier 1). Our results show that, although cropland is a strong carbon sink through NEP (approximately 222±131 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹), accounting for harvest export and leaching losses turns cropland into a net carbon source of about 94±79 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹ across the Corn Belt. Climate extremes further amplified the net carbon source in both event years: in 2019, flooding delayed planting, lowering annual NEP and reducing planted areas; in 2020, summer drought and the August derecho suppressed corn NEP during the peak growing season. Meanwhile, the carbon source shrank under cover cropping relative to conventional practices, with corn reduced by about 30 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹ (p < 0.001) and soybean shifting from a source to near neutral (+2 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹, p < 0.001). Thus, NECB offers a scalable, observation-based approach for tracking cropland carbon source-sink status and its sensitivity to climate extremes and management practices, supporting field-to-regional carbon monitoring and carbon-market applications.

title: Leveraging AI for watershed-scale transport to subgrid-scale wetland processes in LSMs
authors: Gil Bohrer, Katherine Bossert, Parisa Pourabedini, Ayushi Pandey, Asmita Murumkar, Yufan Wu, Rongjun Qin and Ting Zhu
main_session: Frontiers in Biogeochemical, Ecosystem, and Earth System Modeling: Integrating AI, Data-Driven, and Process-Based Approaches III GeoBurst Poster
abstract: Wetlands are the largest terrestrial source of methane and are responsible for the largest uncertainty in global methane syntheses. Land surface models (LSMs) are challenged by the large flux variability of wetlands. Since they do not resolve watershed-scale lateral exchange, LSMs poorly predict hydrological dynamics of throughflow rates and water surface elevations, which greatly affect CO2 and methane fluxes. Detailed decade-long observations at OWC wetlsand suggest that hydraulic dynamics play a strong role in modulating fluxes. Furthermore, the vertical uptake of carbon by local photosynthesis only accounts for 1/3 of the available carbon for methane generation. The major carbon source for methane generation in our site seems to be dissolved organic matter (DOM) loading from the river supplying the wetland. We developed PG-Net, a physics-guided machine-learning framework for wetland hydrology and biogeochemistry. PG-Net uses a hierarchical transformer architecture: a Water Balance Transformer enforces mass balance, and a Nutrient & DOC Transformer models biochemical processes. PG-Net ingest feature layers related to the watershed structure and weather and using observations from USGS river gauges and water quality sites to train the model to predicts inflow rate, water elevation, and DOM loading into each wetland within a large watershed. Further improvement is achieved with a Hydrology-Aware Graph Network that models wetland connectivity through river networks and incorporates memory for watershed-scale temporal dependencies. To improve the input for these models we developed a machine learning approach to reduce inconsistencies in scaled precipitation products by combining watershed information, observations from NOAA weather stations, and spatially scaled satellite and reanalysis products of precipitation. We also developed an improved approach for EC data gapfilling, utilizing NASA HLS vegetation and water indices as feature vectors in addition to the classically utilized meteorological observation at the EC tower, with Conditional Score-based Diffusion models for Imputation (CSDI). The result is more realistic in terms of both the dynamics and the variation of the gap-filled fluxes, even over longer gaps, and can supplement missing observations for the training of the network.

title: Increasing the usability and actionability of Earth observation data through the Satellite Needs Working Group process
authors: Pontus Olofsson, PhD, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, AL, United States, Natasha Sadoff, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, SSAI, Ocean Ecology Laboratory, Greenbelt, United States and Emily Caitlin Adams, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, United States
main_session: Advancing and Scaling Impact with NASA Earth Observations and Modeling I Poster
abstract: The Satellite Needs Working Group (SNWG) is a US Government effort to identify and address Earth observation needs of civilian federal agencies. NASA, as one of the main satellite Earth data providers, plays an important role in the operation of SNWG: with funding from the Earth Action Program, NASA leads the assessment of agencies’ needs, stakeholder engagement, and the management and implementation of the various solutions designed to address needs. The portfolio of solutions has grown to 25. This presentation will focus on the impact of these solutions across federal agencies and how this impact is contributing to the NASA Earth Science to Action strategy. Examples will include how the Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 dataset is supporting cattle ranching and crop farming; how the muti-sensor OPERA project is helping to support the Clean Water Act; and how near real-time products from the TEMPO satellite mission are ensuring rapid detection of harmful pollutants.

title: Integrating TEMPO, Atmospheric Composition, and Weather Data for Continuous 24-Hour NO₂ Exposure Estimates in Health Applications
authors: Yun Hang, Aodong Mei, Zhengyi Cui, Kari North, Yang Liu, Xiong Liu, Qian Xiao and Hao Feng
main_session: Effectively Using Climate and Weather Data for Health Applications II Poster
abstract: High-resolution hourly nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) exposure estimates are important for environmental health studies but remain difficult to generate because satellite observations are affected by cloud cover, retrieval quality, and the lack of nighttime measurements. NASA TEMPO satellite mission provides hourly daytime observations of tropospheric NO₂ over North America, offering new opportunities for exposure assessment if the observations can be extended to continuous 24-hour fields. We developed the Foundation Model-Oriented Reconstruction Modeling Architecture for TEMPO (FORMAT) to reconstruct continuous tropospheric NO₂ by integrating TEMPO observations with GEOS-CF fields, static spatial predictors, and meteorological embeddings derived from the Prithvi WxC foundation model. The reconstructed tropospheric NO₂ fields were then used to estimate hourly 1-km surface NO₂ concentrations across the United States. Compared with conventional interpolation methods and GEOS-CF alone, FORMAT more accurately reconstructed missing tropospheric NO₂ observations. The resulting surface NO₂ model achieved an R² of 0.864 in 10-fold cross-validation. The reconstructed hourly NO₂ fields captured expected spatial and temporal patterns, with higher concentrations across major metropolitan areas, including the Northeast Corridor, Southern California, Houston, Dallas–Fort Worth, and Chicago, and lower concentrations in rural regions. To evaluate their utility for health applications, we linked the exposure estimates with hourly cardiac emergency dispatch records in New York City. A 10 ppb increase in hourly NO₂ was associated with higher odds of cardiac emergency dispatch (OR = 1.045, 95% CI: 1.005–1.086, p = 0.028; n = 13,352). This work demonstrates a practical approach for combining satellite observations, atmospheric composition forecasts, and meteorological information to generate continuous hourly NO₂ exposure estimates. The resulting dataset provides a health-ready exposure product that supports studies requiring fine spatial and temporal resolution and illustrates how TEMPO observations can be more effectively used in environmental health applications.

title: Satellite and UAS Remote Sensing Synergy for Large-Scale Crop Disease Mapping Using Deep Learning
authors: Maitiniyazi Maimaitijiang, Santosh Subedi, Mr. Ubaid Janjua and Shyam Solanki
main_session: From Pixels to Practice: Remote Sensing and Machine Learning Driving Agricultural Innovation II Poster
abstract: Timely, accurate, and fine-scale mapping of crop disease extent within farmers’ fields is essential for quantifying crop losses, supporting crop insurance claims, identifying disease hotspots, and characterizing field- and landscape-scale disease risk for long-term management planning. Satellite imagery provides the spatial coverage and repeated observations needed for large-scale disease monitoring but is often limited by the availability of reliable, spatially explicit reference data. This study presents a hierarchical UAS–satellite remote sensing synergy framework for large-scale crop disease mapping, using soybean white mold as a case study. High-resolution UAS multispectral imagery and field observations were collected from multiple soybean fields in South Dakota, USA, from 2023 to 2025. UAS-based deep learning models were developed to identify white mold symptoms and generate spatially continuous, field-scale disease extent maps. These maps were subsequently aggregated to corresponding satellite pixel footprints to produce pixel-level reference labels for training and validating separate deep learning models using Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 (HLS) and PlanetScope multispectral imagery. The two satellite data sources were evaluated independently to characterize the trade-off between the finer spatial detail and more frequent observations provided by PlanetScope and the radiometric consistency and open availability of HLS. The satellite-based models reproduced the major spatial patterns of disease occurrence observed in the UAS-derived reference maps, although their ability to represent small and spatially fragmented disease patches varied with spatial resolution. The results demonstrate the potential of a hierarchical field-to-UAS-to-satellite framework for extending detailed field-scale disease observations across larger agricultural areas. Although demonstrated using soybean white mold, the proposed framework could potentially be adapted to other crop diseases and support large-scale disease surveillance, targeted field scouting, crop-loss assessment, site-specific management, and long-term disease-risk mapping.

title: Resolving seasonal – and unseasonal – forage greening along a desert-alpine gradient using a spatially distributed time-lapse camera network
authors: Christian John, Michigan Technological University, College of Forest Resources and Environmental Science, Houghton, MI, United States, Bradyn O'Connor, University of California Davis, Wildlife Fish and Conservation Biology, Davis, CA, United States, Tom Stephenson, California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Sierra Nevada Bighorn Sheep Recovery Program, Bishop, CA, United States and Eric Post, University of California Davis, Wildlife, Fish, and Conservation Biology, Davis, CA, United States
main_session: Understanding Phenological Responses, Changes, and Feedback: Patterns, Mechanisms, and Consequences II Oral
abstract: Plant growth in seasonally arid environments is limited by moisture availability, and in alpine regions can be additionally restricted by persistent snow cover. For altitudinal migrants, these limiting factors shape the annual forage landscape by driving spatial heterogeneity in the phenology of palatable plant species. One such migrant is the Sierra Nevada Bighorn Sheep (“Sierra bighorn”), an endangered alpine specialist endemic to the Sierra Nevada Mountains (California, USA). Sierra bighorn move seasonally between the low-elevation Owens Valley, a transition zone between the Great Basin and Mojave Deserts, and the High Sierra, a rugged stretch of peaks towering >2000m in elevation over the mountain range’s eastern escarpment. We deployed a network of 135 time-lapse cameras across the eastern Sierra in an effort to track patterns of snow cover and plant growth to inform conservation and management of Sierra bighorn (starting 2018, and ongoing). Seasonal variation in plant greenness was tracked using the Green Chromatic Coordinate, and was compared with seasonal patterns of variation in NDVI from the Harmonized Landsat/Sentinel product (HLS). Plant green-up timing occurred predictably later in the year with increasing elevation and in association with snow cover dynamics. We identify a fine-scale, species-specific greening signal associated with rainfall, even during autumn when plants would normally be senescent, indicating that some plants readily take in available moisture even outside the typical growing season. Notably, plant species that exhibited unseasonal greening are among the preferred forage species of Sierra bighorn. Sierra bighorn migrated earlier following late-summer precipitation that led to autumn green-up of some low-elevation plant species, suggesting that unseasonal rains may provide foraging benefits during times of resource scarcity. We furthermore find that relatively fine-scale data streams such as HLS may be limited in their capacity to discern certain greening events, revealing the value of targeted, in-situ remote sensing applications for tracking patterns of landscape phenology.

title: Forecasting the Risk and Impacts of Spongy Moth Defoliation across the United States
authors: Xiangtao Xu, Cameron Scholl, Eva-Marie Metz, Christian Frankenberg and Christine L Goodale
main_session: Remote Sensing of Terrestrial Ecosystems: Monitoring, Understanding, and Management Across Scales III Oral
abstract: Forest pest outbreaks can alter forest carbon sinks and ecosystem services and have broad reaching impacts on the forest structure and composition. Effective management of outbreaks requires knowledge of when and where outbreaks may occur in advance. However, outbreak dynamics often depend on a complex suite of biogeographical, meteorological, and ecophysiological factors, which challenges the forecasting of outbreaks. In this study, we explore the spatial patterns and environmental drivers and impacts of defoliation from a major forest pest in northeastern temperate forests ( Lymantria dispar dispar , LDD) to better understand its near-term and long-term risks and impacts. We generate maps of growing-season defoliation based on satellite imagery across the North American range of LDD at a 30m resolution using the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel data fusion product. We then integrate these maps with TROPOMI SIF to quantify productivity declines due to defoliation. Using machine learning, we separate the effects of climatic anomalies, landcover conditions, forest and insect phenology, and spatial and temporal autocorrelation in LDD populations on the probability and severity of defoliation. Preliminary analyses in New York state estimated that 5,500 km 2 of forest area was defoliated from 2020 to 2023, with the maximum decline in daily gross primary productivity ranging from 15-40% compared to years without defoliation. Outbreak risk was best predicted by a warm and dry growing season the year prior, consistent with drivers of infection by host-specific pathogens. Ongoing analyses aim to further address 1) how accurately can near-term LDD defoliation risk be predicted from preceding conditions, 2) what long-term changes to defoliation risk look like based on recent patterns, 3) under what conditions are the impacts of LDD defoliation on temperate forest productivity most severe? Improved understanding of LDD dynamics and consequences will provide both valuable guidance for the immediate management of LDD and better insight into modeling the impacts of defoliator outbreaks om future carbon dynamics in temperature forests.

title: Ventenata dubia in Montana: Statewide Inventory, Remote Sensing-Based Prediction, and Invasion Risk Assessment
authors: Ming Shen, Rustin Bielski-pimlott, Jessica J Mitchell, Di Yang, Rebekah Fields and Neva Tall Bear
main_session: Remote Sensing of Terrestrial Ecosystems: Monitoring, Understanding, and Management Across Scales III Oral
abstract: Ventenata dubia (VEDU) is a relatively new and rapidly spreading invasive annual grass in the western United States. Its broad habitat tolerance degrades native habitats, reduces forage yield, and increases wildfire risk. Ventenata has proved difficult for producers to identify and has been known to facilitate plant viruses. This research aims to inventory the distributions of VEDU and surrounding grass species in Montana, integrate field observations with multisource remote sensing imagery to develop identification models, and evaluate invasion risk to support future management and control efforts. A multiyear inventory strategy was implemented to survey suitable VEDU habitats across Montana. More than 3,000 field samples were collected between 2018 and 2024, covering landscapes ranging from large meadows in western Montana to eastern counties near the borders of North and South Dakota. These field observations were integrated with Landsat 8, Sentinel-2, Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS), and PlanetScope imagery to develop VEDU identification models and compare model performance among sensors. Our results indicate that VEDU identification accuracy varies across elevation zones. Sentinel-2 imagery substantially reduced data costs and processing time; however, PlanetScope imagery provided more suitable images for temporal analysis. Phenological observations showed that VEDU tends to senesce earlier than native perennial bunchgrasses but later than associated nonnative annual grasses. By combining remotely sensed probability of ventenata occurrence maps with habitat-suitability maps, we developed a statewide invasion-risk map to inform future monitoring, management, and control. This work establishes a continuous, multiyear field survey dataset of VEDU distribution across Montana and provides an integrated framework for remote sensing-based identification and invasion risk assessment. The resulting datasets and maps can support targeted monitoring and management of VEDU in Montana and the workflow can be extended to other regions in the western United States.

title: NASA Earth Action: Delivering Societal Returns on America’s Investment in Satellite Remote Sensing and Earth Science
authors: Thomas Paul Wagner, NASA Headquarters, Washington, DC, United States
main_session: Advancing and Scaling Impact with NASA Earth Observations and Modeling II Oral
abstract: NASA’s Earth Action program (EA) accelerates the use of Earth observations for decision-making; helping build a safer, stronger, and more prosperous nation. This presentation describes EA's approach, priorities, and opportunities for the AGU Earth science community. It is intended for current PIs, potential proposers, students and any other interested parties. EA aims to empower all levels of government and the public and private sectors with actionable Earth information. The portfolio spans agriculture, disasters, energy, health, air quality, water, wildland fires, energy, resource conservation, and other areas. Projects are supported across NASA centers, academia, and the private sector with awards that range from single-investigator projects to multi-institution consortia supporting broad objectives. Program outcomes range from regional to national scales set on land, sea and air. There is strong emphasis on technology transfer with growing support for private sector engagement. In addition to satellite remote sensing, the program capitalizes on NASA's advanced Earth models and extensive data holdings by developing application-specific tools, interfaces, and datasets. Some of the most widely used remote sensing datasets, such as the Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) product, are produced by EA's SNWG program. AI is a growing focus area, especially to reduce the barrier to entry for new users and reduce the time required to develop applications. Training is supported at all scales with self-paced, on-line approaches (ARSET) through to expert-guided development projects (EarthRISE Developers Academy). Access to commercial data is provided through the CSDA program, which also fosters the broader space economy by developing new use-cases and applications. As NASA evolves its satellite mission teams into DARTs (Data, Applications, Research, Technology), the future promises an expanded portfolio with more opportunities for scientists to get involved in applications. Finally, the program is increasing efficiency for proposers. The new ROSES 2025 solicitation A.13 "Accelerating Earth Solutions" is open to proposals from any relevant sector and covers Needs and Opportunities, Solutions Development, and Scaling Impact for national benefit.

title: A Multimodal Method to Reconstruct High Resolution Surface Temperatures at High Altitudes
authors: Kyung Yoon Kim, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States and Venkataraman Lakshmi, Johns Hopkins University, Environmental Health and Engineering, Baltimore, United States
main_session: Advances in Flood and Landslide Hazard Mapping in Mountainous and Data-Scarce Regions Poster
abstract: Elevation dependent warming has been documented to destabilize the cryosphere at high altitudes, endangering mountain communities and infrastructure. However, both the paucity of in situ observations and the challenges of disaggregating surface signals in complex topography have been persistent constraints in the implementation of satellite-based temperature retrievals for early warning systems (e.g., landslide induced GLOFs). The volume of both deep learning algorithms and publicly available gridded datasets (e.g., Landsat, ECOSTRESS, VIIRS, Sentinel-2, ERA5-Land) may offer a potential solution. Until a more definitive source of high-resolution surface temperature estimates is released (e.g., Harmonized Landsat Sentinel LST), a trustworthy method for downscaling temperature estimates where surface observations are limited (e.g., cloudiness) is needed. This work leverages a combination of remotely sensed, modeled reanalysis, and in situ datasets at multiple spatiotemporal scales to attempt at reconstructing surface temperatures at selected sites with a sufficient period of record. Deep learning models are benchmarked at the point and/or pixel scale for further consideration. The applicability of a robust all-weather, high spatiotemporal resolution temperature product will be far-reaching if/when the day comes, given the rapid rate at which both temperature is rising and technology is advancing.

title: ECO 2 Bench: A Benchmark for Machine-Learning Upscaling of Ecosystem Carbon Fluxes
authors: Yilun Zhao, Virginia Tech, Department of Biological Systems Engineering, Blacksburg, United States, Trevor Keenan, University of California, Berkeley, Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management, Berkeley, United States, Maoya Bassiouni, USGS Pacific Islands Water Science, Honolulu, United States and Yanghui Kang, Virginia Tech, Department of Biological Systems Engineering, Blacksburg, Virginia, United States
main_session: Advances in Measurements, Synthesis, and Modeling of Greenhouse Gas Fluxes from Natural Ecosystems II Poster
