abstract: Accurate estimates of ecosystem carbon fluxes are essential for carbon accounting and understanding ecosystem responses to environmental change. Eddy-covariance towers directly measure carbon exchange, but their spatial coverage remains limited. Machine learning has become essential to upscale tower observations to regional and global scales with remote-sensing and environmental data. However, the lack of standardized benchmarks constrains rigorous model evaluation, methodological innovation, and the development of reproducible workflows. Here, we present ECO2Bench , a benchmark for machine-learning upscaling of daily gross primary productivity (GPP) and net ecosystem exchange (NEE). ECO 2 Bench comprises a curated dataset, baseline models, and consistent evaluation protocols. The dataset contains 36,273 daily samples from global eddy-covariance towers spanning 2016–2024, pairing flux measurements with satellite, meteorological, soil, and land-cover information. A key innovation is the inclusion of tower-centered Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 images covering 1.5 × 1.5 km at 30 m resolution, enabling image-based modeling of fine-scale spatial heterogeneity. The baselines include tabular models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and MLP) and convolutional neural networks (SimpleCNN and ResNet18). In 10-fold cross-validation, tabular models achieved R² values of 0.64-0.67 for GPP and 0.36-0.41 for NEE, while SimpleCNN and ResNet18, which use fine-scale spatial information, achieved higher R² values of 0.69 and 0.72, respectively, for GPP and 0.42 and 0.44, respectively, for NEE. Additionally, we used ECO 2 Bench to evaluate advanced frameworks based on the Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation models, which achieved the best performance with R² values reaching 0.73 for GPP and 0.45 for NEE, highlighting the value of generalizable representations learned from large-scale satellite data. By providing standardized multimodal data, high-resolution imagery, baseline models, and evaluation metrics, ECO 2 Bench provides a reproducible testbed for comparing models, measuring progress, and advancing image-based deep learning model approaches for ecosystem carbon-flux upscaling.

title: Evaluating Geospatial Foundation Model for Transferable Subfield-Scale Crop Yield Prediction
authors: Samar Ranjit, Dr. Eunsang Cho, Ph.D., Simon Kraatz, Martha Anderson, Dr. Jisung Chang, Feng Gao and Michael H Cosh
main_session: Multimodal AI and Remote Sensing for a Profitable Climate-Smart and Resilient Agriculture I Poster
abstract: Geospatial foundation models are emerging as powerful tools in Earth observation, where large-scale pretraining yields transferable spatial, spectral, and temporal representations that hold strong potential for applications such as large-scale crop yield prediction. However, their ability to generalize to observed subfield-scale crop-yield variability remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the transferability of a dense regression framework built around a pretrained Prithvi-EO-2.0 encoder for fine-scale soybean, corn, and wheat yield prediction using large-scale U.S. agricultural datasets. Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 observations from 2020–2024 are composited monthly over crop-specific growing seasons and organized into standardized image chips at 30 m resolution. The modeling framework combines the Prithvi-EO-2.0 encoder with a UPerNet decoder and convolutional regression head to generate spatially continuous yield estimates. USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service county-level yield data for soybeans, corn, and wheat are used during the initial training stage, while Cropland Data Layer crop masks identify relevant pixels for each crop. Independent fine-scale yield-monitor observations for all three crops from the USDA Beltsville Agricultural Research Center provide external ground truth for fine-tuning and evaluating model performance on observed within-field yield variability. Strict temporal holdout experiments assess generalization to previously unseen growing seasons. This study aims to determine whether a model initialized with globally pretrained Earth-observation representations and adapted using large-scale county-level yield supervision can transfer to finer-scale agricultural conditions. By advancing the emerging integration of large geospatial foundation models into agriculture, this study provides a step toward a scalable pathway from county-level supervision to subfield-scale yield assessment, supporting targeted management and sustainable agricultural decision-making.

title: Crop Damage and Loss from Disasters: A Geospatial Foundation Model Framework and Benchmark
authors: Esmaeel Adrah, Jamon Van Den Hoek, Scott C Sheridan and He Yin
main_session: From Detection to Decision: Environmental and Societal Impacts of Disaster and Conflict in the Era of AI and New Earth Observation II GeoBurst Poster
abstract: Remote sensing assessments of agricultural disasters often conflate physical hazard footprint (extent), biophysical crop disruption (damage), and yield/economic shortfall (loss). Because simple change detection is confused by crop phenology or cloud artifacts, robust mapping requires modeling the crop's "expected-normal" state as a comparison baseline. We present a framework and benchmark operationalizing the extent–damage–loss distinction on cropland. That includes: (1) constructing the first benchmark linking U.S. county-level insurance records into typed, timed, and spatially explicit damage maps, and (2) developing a GeoFM-based framework mapping damage and loss via the deviation between an expected-normal baseline and the observed state in embedding space. Analyzing ~2,000 CONUS county-disaster pairs (flood, hail, tornado, drought) with USDA Risk Management Agency (RMA) records across 2024–2025, we propose to build a benchmark data via a cause-routed pipeline. We deploy an "inverted design", leveraging the in-distribution generalization of GeoFMs to model the baseline rather than damage itself. We utilize frozen encoders (NASA-IBM Prithvi-EO-2.0, TerraMind) model for the per-pixel expected-normal state from historical baselines and compute the damage as the distance (cosine, Mahalanobis dM ) between this baseline and post-disaster observations, which a downstream model bridges to county-level loss. Our preliminary results evaluating thresholds (P90, P95, P98) yields peak performance at P95: Prithvi dM for hail (IoU 0.691, F1 0.817) and Prithvi cosine for flood (IoU 0.746, F1 0.855). Our GeoFM framework and benchmark spanning discrete floods to continuous drought define the limits of observation-based loss assessment and motivate future, temporally predictive GeoFM architectures.

title: GeoAI and Remote Sensing for Conflict, Displacement, and Environmental Change
authors: Kexin Song, Yale University, School of the Environment, New Haven, CT, United States and Luke Sanford, Yale University, School of Environment, New Haven, United States
main_session: From Detection to Decision: Environmental and Societal Impacts of Disaster and Conflict in the Era of AI and New Earth Observation III Oral
abstract: Documenting violent conflicts is fundamentally constrained by restricted ground access, yet the demand for reliable, scalable, and timely evidence is essential for humanitarian response and post-conflict recovery. To address this challenge, we present a GeoAI-enabled framework that combines satellite time series, foundation models, and causal inference. Using the 2017 Rohingya genocide as a case study, we demonstrate how Earth observations and GeoAI can support social science research where traditional fieldwork is difficult. Our framework consists of four components. First, we detect conflict-related damage using Google AlphaEarth foundation model embeddings and machine learning classifiers. Second, we reconstruct the spatiotemporal trajectories of conflict and forced displacement using the NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) data and the COntinuous monitoring of Land Disturbance (COLD) algorithm. Third, we characterize local economic disruption using Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) nighttime lights as proxy. Finally, we apply causal inference to evaluate the impacts of conflict and refugee camp exposure on natural and built environments. This integrated approach yields previously inaccessible evidence, including anticipatory signals of population displacement that precede peak violence, quantified cascading environmental and socioeconomic impacts, and distinct post-conflict recovery trajectories. Together, these findings hold important implications for guiding rapid humanitarian response, informing recovery planning, and strengthening long-term resilience.

title: Advancing Evapotranspiration Estimation through Multi-Satellite Data Fusion
authors: Yun Yang, Martha Anderson, Hui LIU, Weina Duan, Jiaxin Wang and Christopher Hain
main_session: Advancing Measurements and Modeling of Invisible Components of Water Budget: Challenges, Opportunities, and Applications II Oral
abstract: Evapotranspiration (ET) is a fundamental component of the terrestrial water budget, linking the water, energy, and carbon cycles and providing an essential constraint for understanding ecosystem processes and land–atmosphere interactions. However, accurately estimating ET across spatial and temporal scales remains challenging because no single satellite system provides the spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and thermal observations needed for operational monitoring. Multi-satellite data fusion has therefore become a critical strategy for advancing satellite-based ET estimation. This presentation introduces recent advances in GEE-DisALEXI, a cloud-based modeling framework that integrates the physically based DisALEXI energy balance model with Google Earth Engine to enable scalable, multi-sensor ET estimation. The framework fuses complementary observations from Landsat, Sentinel-2, Harmonized Landsat Sentinel (HLS), ECOSTRESS, MODIS, VIIRS, and geostationary satellites, leveraging their respective spatial, temporal, and spectral strengths to overcome cloud contamination, revisit limitations, and different spatial resolutions. Recent developments in very high resolution ET mapping using commercial satellite will also be presented, highlighting the framework ranging from regional to field and sub-field scales. The presentation will also discuss emerging opportunities to integrate new Earth observation systems to further improve ET estimation and monitoring. Combining physically based modeling, multi-sensor data fusion, and cloud computing provides a scalable foundation for advancing satellite-based ET estimation and improving our understanding of water use at different scales.

title: Multimodal Remote Sensing Foundation Models for Scalable, Cloud-Robust Crop Mapping in Climate-Smart Agriculture
authors: Han Ma, Shunlin Liang, Wenyuan Li and Husheng Fang
main_session: Multimodal AI and Remote Sensing for a Profitable Climate-Smart and Resilient Agriculture II Oral
abstract: Accurate, timely, and scalable crop mapping is essential for climate-smart agricultural management, food-security assessment, and economically viable decision-making under increasing climate stress. Although satellite-based crop classification has advanced rapidly, persistent challenges—including smallholder field fragmentation, frequent cloud contamination, heterogeneous crop calendars, limited reference data, and poor model transferability across regions—continue to constrain operational applications. This presentation summarizes recent progress in multimodal remote sensing foundation models for agricultural mapping, with emphasis on scalable crop-type mapping across Asia. First, we introduce AgriFM , a remote sensing foundation model trained on more than 25 million images from MODIS, Landsat, and Sentinel-2. AgriFM was evaluated on five agricultural downstream tasks and consistently outperformed conventional deep learning methods and state-of-the-art general-purpose remote sensing foundation models, demonstrating the value of agriculture-specific pretraining and multi-sensor representation learning. Second, we discuss paddy rice mapping across Asia from 2018 to 2023 using Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 data and the NASA–IBM geospatial foundation model, highlighting the potential of foundation models for multi-year, continental-scale crop monitoring. The main focus will be our latest work on joint multi-crop mapping of corn, soybean, winter wheat, and rice across Asia in 2021 using a multimodal foundation-model framework that integrates Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 optical time series. By combining cloud-penetrating radar observations with optical spectral and phenological information, the approach improves robustness to missing data and cloud cover while enhancing generalization across diverse agroecological zones. The resulting crop maps provide high-resolution information relevant to yield forecasting, resource allocation, risk assessment, and climate-resilient agricultural planning. This work illustrates how multimodal AI and standardized remote sensing data fusion can help bridge the gap between foundation-model development and actionable, field-relevant agricultural monitoring.
